shelves.title: Levothyroxine in pregnancy: subclinical hypothyroidism and TPO-positive euthyroid women — two large RCTs, both null
shelves.question: Does levothyroxine treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism, hypothyroxinemia, or thyroid-peroxidase-antibody-positive euthyroid status in pregnancy improve offspring cognition, live birth, or pregnancy outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Hypothyroidism/drug therapy · Pregnancy Complications/drug therapy · Thyroxine/therapeutic use · Iodide Peroxidase/immunology · Live Birth · Preconception Care
shelves.balance: Two large randomized trials point the same way: levothyroxine started in pregnancy for subclinical hypothyroidism or hypothyroxinemia did not improve children's IQ at 5 years (Casey 2017), and levothyroxine given before conception to euthyroid TPO-antibody-positive women did not raise live-birth rates (TABLET 2019). A 2024 meta-analysis of the RCTs agrees. This does not touch overt hypothyroidism in pregnancy, which is treated on other grounds and has never been placebo-tested. Proposed stamp: LIKELY — the null is strong and concordant across two large trials, but the label scale reserves higher certainty for Level A benefit claims and these are null results in defined sub-populations.

cards.headline: Casey 2017: treating subclinical hypothyroidism or hypothyroxinemia in pregnancy did not improve child IQ
cards.summary: Casey: treating subclinical hypothyroidism or hypothyroxinemia in pregnancy did not improve child IQ at 5 years (median 97 vs 94 , P=0.71; hypothyroxinemia 94 vs 91, P=0.30), nor any other neurocognitive or pregnancy outcome.
cards.people: 677 women with subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH >=4.00 mU/L, normal free T4) randomized at mean 16.7 weeks of gestation, and 526 with hypothyroxinemia (normal TSH, low free T4) at mean 17.8 weeks; singleton pregnancies screened before 20 weeks. Mean maternal age is not stated in the record's abstract.
cards.result: Median child IQ at 5 years was 97 (95% CI 94 to 99) on levothyroxine vs 94 (92 to 96) on placebo in the subclinical-hypothyroidism trial (P=0.71), and 94 (91 to 95) vs 91 (89 to 93) in the hypothyroxinemia trial (P=0.30). No significant differences in any other neurocognitive or pregnancy outcomes; adverse events low in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Treatment began at a mean of ~17 weeks — after much of early fetal brain development — so the trial does not test preconception or first-trimester initiation. IQ scores were missing for 4% of children.
cards.source: Casey BM, Thom EA, Peaceman AM, et al. Treatment of Subclinical Hypothyroidism or Hypothyroxinemia in Pregnancy. N Engl J Med. 2017;376(9):815-825. PMID 28249134 · NCT00388297.

cards.headline: TABLET 2019: levothyroxine before conception did not raise live-birth rates in TPO-positive euthyroid women
cards.summary: TABLET: levothyroxine before conception did not raise live-birth rates in TPO-positive euthyroid women ( 37.4% vs 37.9% ; relative risk 0.97 [0.83 to 1.14]).
cards.people: 952 euthyroid women with thyroid peroxidase antibodies and a history of miscarriage or infertility, from 49 UK hospitals (19,585 women screened); 476 assigned levothyroxine 50 mcg daily, 476 placebo, started before conception and continued through pregnancy. Mean age is not stated in the record's abstract.
cards.result: Live birth after at least 34 weeks: 37.4% (176/470) on levothyroxine vs 37.9% (178/470) on placebo — relative risk 0.97 (95% CI 0.83 to 1.14), absolute difference -0.4 percentage points (95% CI -6.6 to 5.8). No significant differences in pregnancy loss, preterm birth, or neonatal outcomes. Serious adverse events 5.9% vs 3.8% (P=0.14).
cards.watchOut: A single fixed 50 mcg dose was used without titration to TSH targets; the result applies to euthyroid TPO-positive women, not to women with abnormal TSH.
cards.source: Dhillon-Smith RK, Middleton LJ, Sunner KK, et al. Levothyroxine in Women with Thyroid Peroxidase Antibodies before Conception. N Engl J Med. 2019;380(14):1316-1325. PMID 30907987 · ISRCTN15948785.

cards.headline: 2024 meta-analysis of the pregnancy RCTs: no live-birth or miscarriage benefit from levothyroxine
cards.summary: The 2024 pooled analysis of the pregnancy RCTs agrees: no live-birth or miscarriage benefit — the preconception intervals are wide, from small studies.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
cards.people: 5 preconception-treatment studies (768 participants) and 8 treatment-during-pregnancy studies (2,622 participants) in subclinical hypothyroidism, pooled by Sankoda et al. 2024.
cards.result: Preconception levothyroxine: no significant effect on live birth (relative risk 1.41, 95% CI 0.84 to 2.36), pregnancy (relative risk 1.73, 0.88 to 3.39), or miscarriage (relative risk 0.46, 0.11 to 2.00) — wide intervals from small studies. Treatment during pregnancy: no higher live-birth rate (relative risk 1.03, 0.98 to 1.09) and no lower miscarriage rate (relative risk 1.01, 0.66 to 1.53).
cards.watchOut: The one positive signal — less preterm birth in the subgroup with TSH >4.0 mU/L (relative risk 0.47, 0.20 to 1.10) — is a subgroup finding whose interval crosses 1.0; it is hypothesis-generating only and is fenced here, not carded as a benefit.
cards.source: Sankoda A, Suzuki H, Imaizumi M, et al. Effects of Levothyroxine Treatment on Fertility and Pregnancy Outcomes in Subclinical Hypothyroidism: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Thyroid. 2024;34(4):519-530. PMID 38368537. No registry ID on the record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the fence for this shelf
cards.summary: Two large concordant null trials plus a concordant meta-analysis: routine levothyroxine for these subclinical states in pregnancy has no demonstrated benefit — LIKELY, for the null.
cards.people: Pregnant or preconception women with subclinical hypothyroidism, hypothyroxinemia, or TPO antibodies with normal thyroid function — the populations actually randomized.
cards.result: Two large concordant null RCTs plus a concordant 2024 pooled analysis: routine levothyroxine for these subclinical states in pregnancy has no demonstrated benefit on child IQ, live birth, miscarriage, or preterm birth. Proposed stamp: LIKELY.
cards.watchOut: Fence: this shelf does NOT cover overt hypothyroidism in pregnancy (never placebo-tested; treatment remains standard), women with TSH above 10 mU/L, or treatment begun before conception for subclinical hypothyroidism with TSH >4.0 — the 2024 subgroup signal there is unverified and fenced. Shelf #354 owns subclinical hypothyroidism treatment in non-pregnant adults (TRUST) and is not re-carded here.

shelves.title: Levothyroxine + liothyronine combination vs levothyroxine alone: no consistent benefit in the trials
shelves.question: In adults with hypothyroidism who remain symptomatic on levothyroxine, does adding liothyronine (T3) improve symptoms, mood, quality of life, weight, or lipids compared with levothyroxine alone?
shelves.mesh: Hypothyroidism/drug therapy · Thyroxine/administration & dosage · Triiodothyronine/administration & dosage · Drug Therapy, Combination · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: Across 11 randomized trials and 1,216 patients, pooled symptom, mood, quality-of-life, weight, and lipid outcomes show no difference between combination T4+T3 and T4 alone (Grozinsky-Glasberg 2006). The honest complication is preference: about half of blinded trial participants say they prefer the combination, a signal one meta-analysis found indistinguishable from chance (2019) and a later one found positive but highly heterogeneous (2025). Preference is not measured symptom benefit. Proposed stamp: LIKELY — no consistent objective benefit across many trials; the preference-subgroup question remains open and is fenced as such.

cards.headline: Pooled RCTs (2006): combination T4+T3 matched T4 alone on every symptom and metabolic outcome
cards.summary: The 2006 pooled RCTs: T4+T3 matched T4 alone on every measured outcome — pain, depression, anxiety, fatigue, quality of life, weight and lipids, with standardised differences of ~0.00.
cards.people: 11 randomized trials, 1,216 adults with clinical hypothyroidism, pooled by Grozinsky-Glasberg et al. 2006. Age and sex mix are not stated in the record's abstract.
cards.result: No difference between combination and monotherapy for bodily pain (standardized mean difference 0.00, 95% CI -0.34 to 0.35), depression (0.07, -0.20 to 0.34), anxiety (0.00, -0.12 to 0.11), fatigue (-0.12, -0.33 to 0.09), quality of life (0.03, -0.09 to 0.15), body weight, total cholesterol, triglycerides, LDL, or HDL. Adverse events did not differ.
cards.watchOut: Trials were short and used varying T3 doses and ratios; the pooled null is about average effects in unselected hypothyroid patients, not about a genetically or symptomatically defined subgroup, which no included trial isolated.
cards.source: Grozinsky-Glasberg S, Fraser A, Nahshoni E, et al. Thyroxine-triiodothyronine combination therapy versus thyroxine monotherapy for clinical hypothyroidism: meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2006;91(7):2592-2599. PMID 16670166. No registry ID on the record.

cards.headline: Preference meta-analysis (2019): about half preferred the combination — not distinguishable from chance
cards.summary: The 2019 preference meta-analysis: 46.2% preferred the combination — not distinguishable from chance (P=0.231).
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of blinded RCTs
cards.people: 7 blinded randomized trials, 348 hypothyroid individuals, pooled by Akirov et al. 2019.
cards.result: Pooled proportion preferring combination T3/T4 over T4 alone was 46.2% (95% CI 40.2% to 52.4%), with P=0.231 for the difference from chance and low heterogeneity (I2=18%). Preference tracked TSH, mood, and symptom measures in sensitivity analyses, but not quality of life or body weight.
cards.watchOut: Preference in a crossover trial can be driven by feeling any change at all, including T3 side effects that partly unblind treatment; a preference count is not an efficacy outcome.
cards.source: Akirov A, Fazelzad R, Ezzat S. A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Patient Preferences for Combination Thyroid Hormone Treatment for Hypothyroidism. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne). 2019;10:477. PMID 31396154. No registry ID on the record.

cards.headline: Preference network meta-analysis (2025): preference for combination confirmed, but with high heterogeneity
cards.summary: The 2025 preference network meta-analysis: 52% preferred combination or desiccated thyroid vs 24% T4 alone (relative risk 2.20, a relative measure of stated preference) — with high heterogeneity (I²=81%) .
cards.type: Systematic review, meta-analysis and network meta-analysis of RCTs
cards.people: 11 RCTs (8 crossover), 1,135 patients with hypothyroidism, pooled through April 2024. Age and sex mix are not stated in the record's abstract.
cards.result: 24% of patients preferred levothyroxine alone, 52% preferred levothyroxine+liothyronine or desiccated thyroid extract, and 24% had no preference; meta-analytic relative risk of preferring combination was 2.20 (95% CI 1.38 to 3.52) — a relative measure of stated preference, not of symptom scores. Heterogeneity was high (I2=81%); excluding 4 studies reduced it (I2=24%) without changing the result (relative risk 1.97, 1.52 to 2.54).
cards.watchOut: This 2025 preference result and the 2019 null preference result cannot both be read at face value; the pooled trials overlap and the endpoint is subjective. It does not overturn card 1's null on measured symptoms, mood, and quality of life.
cards.source: Treatment Preferences in Patients With Hypothyroidism. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2025;110(3):887-900. PMID 39290156. No registry ID on the record. (First author not listed in the extracted record fields used for this pack — see summary.md.)

cards.headline: Synthesis: the fence for this shelf
cards.summary: Objective outcomes show no consistent benefit across the trials; the preference signal is real but unstable — LIKELY, for no consistent objective benefit.
cards.people: Adults with hypothyroidism, including those with persistent symptoms on levothyroxine alone.
cards.result: Measured outcomes — symptoms, mood, cognition, quality of life, weight, lipids — show no consistent advantage for adding T3 across more than a thousand randomized patients. A genuine but unstable preference signal exists in crossover trials. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (for no consistent objective benefit).
cards.watchOut: Fence: no verified trial isolates a responder subgroup (e.g., by deiodinase genotype), so no subgroup claim is carded. Preference data are fenced off from efficacy: they justify a shared-decision conversation, not a claim that combination therapy works better.

shelves.title: Graves' orbitopathy: teprotumumab reverses proptosis; glucocorticoids mainly calm inflammation
shelves.question: In active, moderate-to-severe Graves' orbitopathy (thyroid eye disease), what do teprotumumab and intravenous glucocorticoids each achieve — proptosis reversal, activity-score improvement, diplopia, quality of life?
shelves.mesh: Graves Ophthalmopathy/drug therapy · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use · Receptor, IGF Type 1/antagonists & inhibitors · Methylprednisolone/therapeutic use · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Exophthalmos/drug therapy
shelves.balance: Teprotumumab is the treatment that moves proptosis: in the phase 3 OPTIC trial 83% had a >=2 mm proptosis response vs 10% on placebo, with concordant phase 2 results. Intravenous glucocorticoids, in the EUGOGO-era randomized comparison, beat oral glucocorticoids on overall response (87.8% vs 63.4%) but reduced proptosis by only ~1.6 mm — they mainly suppress inflammation and activity scores. No head-to-head trial of teprotumumab vs IV glucocorticoids was verified. Proposed stamp: LIKELY.

cards.headline: OPTIC (2020): teprotumumab produced a proptosis response in 83% vs 10% on placebo
cards.summary: OPTIC: teprotumumab produced a proptosis response in 83% vs 10% on placebo (number needed to treat 1.36), with mean proptosis change −2.82 vs −0.54 mm .
cards.people: 83 patients with active thyroid eye disease (41 teprotumumab, 42 placebo), intravenous infusions every 3 weeks for 21 weeks, outcomes at week 24. Age and sex mix are not stated in the record's abstract.
cards.result: Proptosis response (>=2 mm reduction): 83% (34/41) vs 10% (4/42), P<0.001 (number needed to treat 1.36). Overall response 78% vs 7%; Clinical Activity Score 0 or 1 in 59% vs 21%; mean proptosis change -2.82 mm vs -0.54 mm; diplopia response 68% (19/28) vs 29% (8/28); GO-QOL overall score change 13.79 vs 4.43 points (P<=0.001 for all). Most adverse events were mild or moderate; two serious events on teprotumumab, one an infusion reaction leading to discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: A 24-week trial in active disease: durability after stopping, and effect in chronic/inactive fibrotic disease, are not answered here. Orbital imaging substudy included only 6 patients.
cards.source: Douglas RS, Kahaly GJ, Patel A, et al. Teprotumumab for the Treatment of Active Thyroid Eye Disease. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(4):341-352. PMID 31971679 · NCT03298867.

cards.headline: Phase 2 trial (2017): the same proptosis and activity benefit, seen earlier and smaller
cards.summary: The 2017 phase 2 trial saw the same benefit, earlier and smaller: response 69% vs 20% , already separated by week 6 (43% vs 4%).
cards.people: 88 patients with active, moderate-to-severe thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy, randomized to teprotumumab or placebo, 8 infusions over 24 weeks. Age and sex mix are not stated in the record's abstract.
cards.result: Primary response (>=2-point Clinical Activity Score reduction plus >=2 mm proptosis reduction at week 24): 69% (29/42) on teprotumumab vs 20% (9/45) on placebo, P<0.001. Effect was rapid: at week 6, 43% vs 4% had responded. The only drug-related adverse event was hyperglycemia in patients with diabetes, controlled by adjusting diabetes medication.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2, single primary endpoint at 24 weeks; hyperglycemia is a real monitoring point in patients with diabetes — the population SourceMed readers treat most.

cards.headline: IV vs oral glucocorticoids (2001): IV won on response and tolerability, but proptosis fell only ~1.6 mm
cards.summary: Marcocci 2001: IV glucocorticoids beat oral on overall response ( 87.8% vs 63.4% ) but reduced proptosis by only ~1.6 mm — they mainly suppress inflammation and activity.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (single-blind, EUGOGO-era, with orbital radiotherapy in both arms)
cards.people: 82 consecutive patients with moderate-to-severe active Graves' ophthalmopathy; both groups also received orbital radiotherapy and radioiodine for hyperthyroidism; 12-month follow-up. Groups did not differ in age or gender mix per the record's abstract, which gives no pooled mean age.
cards.result: Responders: 87.8% (36/41) with IV methylprednisolone vs 63.4% (26/41) with oral prednisone (P<0.02). Proptosis fell from 23.2 to 21.6 mm (IV) and 23.0 to 21.7 mm (oral) — a ~1.5 mm change, far smaller than teprotumumab's. Clinical Activity Score fell to 1.7 (IV) vs 2.2 (oral), P<0.01 for the final-score difference. Diplopia disappeared in 48.1% (IV) vs 36.4% (oral), not significantly different. IV treatment was better tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Both arms also received orbital radiotherapy, so the glucocorticoid-only effect cannot be isolated; this is a 2001 trial with an older regimen, and there is no placebo arm — the comparison is IV vs oral, not steroid vs none.
cards.source: Marcocci C, Bartalena L, Tanda ML, et al. Comparison of the effectiveness and tolerability of intravenous or oral glucocorticoids associated with orbital radiotherapy in the management of severe Graves' ophthalmopathy: results of a prospective, single-blind, randomized study. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2001;86(8):3562-3567. PMID 11502779. No registry ID on the record (pre-registration era).

cards.headline: Synthesis: the fence for this shelf
cards.summary: A division of labour the trials support: teprotumumab reverses proptosis (two concordant RCTs); glucocorticoids calm activity; no head-to-head trial exists — LIKELY.
cards.people: Patients with active, moderate-to-severe Graves' orbitopathy.
cards.result: Division of labor supported by the trials: teprotumumab reverses proptosis (two concordant RCTs, large absolute effects); glucocorticoids — IV better than oral — mainly reduce inflammatory activity, with only ~1.5 mm proptosis change in the randomized comparison. Proposed stamp: LIKELY.
cards.watchOut: Fence: no verified head-to-head RCT compares teprotumumab with IV glucocorticoids, so no card claims superiority of one over the other; teprotumumab trials cover active disease over 24 weeks, not chronic inactive disease or long-term durability.

shelves.title: Low-risk papillary thyroid cancer after surgery: radioactive iodine or not — two noninferiority trials say it can be omitted
shelves.question: After total thyroidectomy for low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer, does omitting postoperative radioactive iodine (ablation) worsen recurrence or event rates compared with routine ablation? What does active-surveillance cohort evidence add for microcarcinoma?
shelves.mesh: Thyroid Neoplasms/radiotherapy · Thyroid Neoplasms/surgery · Iodine Radioisotopes/therapeutic use · Thyroidectomy · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Disease-Free Survival
shelves.balance: Two phase 3 noninferiority trials now agree: in low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer after total thyroidectomy, a no-ablation follow-up strategy was noninferior to routine radioiodine — ESTIMABL2 at 3 and 5 years (event-free 95.6% vs 95.9% at 3 years; 93.2% vs 94.8% at 5 years) and the UK IoN trial at 5 years (recurrence-free 97.9% vs 96.3%). Active-surveillance cohorts for papillary microcarcinoma are supportive context only and are labeled observational. Proposed stamp: LIKELY.

cards.headline: ESTIMABL2: no radioiodine was noninferior to ablation at 3 years — and the result held at 5 years
cards.summary: ESTIMABL2: omitting radioiodine was noninferior at 3 years (event-free 95.6% vs 95.9% ) — and the result held at 5 years (93.2% vs 94.8% ; difference −1.6% [−4.5 to 1.4]).
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial, phase 3 (noninferiority), with pre-specified 5-year follow-up report
cards.people: 776 patients enrolled with low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer after total thyroidectomy (82.7% female, median age 52.9 years); 730 evaluable at 3 years and 698 at 5 years. Radioiodine arm received 1.1 GBq after recombinant human TSH.
cards.result: At 3 years, patients without a functional, structural, or biologic event: 95.6% (95% CI 93.0 to 97.5) without radioiodine vs 95.9% (93.3 to 97.7) with it — difference -0.3 percentage points (two-sided 90% CI -2.7 to 2.2), meeting the 5-point noninferiority criterion. At 5 years: 93.2% vs 94.8% event-free, difference -1.6% (90% CI -4.5 to 1.4), noninferiority confirmed; 5-year events were structural/functional in 11 patients and biologic in 31. No treatment-related adverse events were reported in the 3-year report.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is a composite dominated by biologic abnormalities (thyroglobulin/antibody changes), not recurrence or death; events were more frequent when postoperative thyroglobulin on hormone therapy exceeded 1 ng/mL. Applies to the trial's low-risk definition only.
cards.source: Leboulleux S, Bournaud C, Chougnet CN, et al. Thyroidectomy without Radioiodine in Patients with Low-Risk Thyroid Cancer. N Engl J Med. 2022;386(10):923-932. cards.headline: IoN (UK, 2025): no ablation was noninferior for 5-year recurrence-free survival
cards.summary: IoN (UK, 2025): no ablation was noninferior for 5-year recurrence-free survival ( 97.9% vs 96.3% ) — only 17 recurrences in the whole trial.
cards.people: 504 patients (77% female) with completely resected low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer at 33 UK centres, randomized to 1.1 GBq ablation or no ablation; median follow-up ~6.8 years (no ablation) and 6.6 years (ablation). Mean age is not stated in the record's abstract.
cards.result: Only 17 recurrences occurred in total (8 without ablation, 9 with). Five-year recurrence-free rates: 97.9% (95% CI 96.1 to 99.7) without ablation vs 96.3% (93.9 to 98.7) with ablation in the intention-to-treat analysis (97.9% vs 96.9% per-protocol) — noninferior within the pre-set 5-percentage-point margin.
cards.watchOut: Recurrence was rare in both arms, so the trial excludes large harm from omission but cannot exclude small absolute differences; the trial remains in active follow-up, and eligibility included some pT3/N1a patients — broader than ESTIMABL2's low-risk definition, so the two trials' populations are not identical.

cards.headline: Active surveillance of papillary microcarcinoma (Kuma Hospital cohort): only 7.1% came to conversion surgery — observational context
cards.summary: Active surveillance of papillary microcarcinoma (Kuma cohort — observational context ): only 7.1% came to conversion surgery, and rates fell as experience accumulated.
cards.type: Retrospective cohort (labeled observational — context only, not randomized evidence)
cards.people: 2,288 patients with low-risk papillary microcarcinoma managed by active surveillance at a single Japanese centre. Age and sex mix for the whole cohort are not stated in the record's abstract.
cards.result: 162 patients (7.1%) underwent conversion surgery more than 12 months after starting surveillance: 57 for disease progression, 43 by patient preference, 31 by physician preference, 24 for associated thyroid/parathyroid disease, 7 for other reasons. Conversion rates fell over calendar time as experience accumulated.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the fence for this shelf
cards.summary: Two independent phase 3 noninferiority trials agree: routine postoperative radioiodine can be omitted in low-risk disease — LIKELY.
cards.people: Patients after total thyroidectomy for low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer, as defined by the two trials; microcarcinoma surveillance patients are a separate, pre-surgical population.
cards.result: Omitting routine postoperative radioiodine in low-risk disease is supported by two independent phase 3 noninferiority trials with concordant results at 3-5 years. Proposed stamp: LIKELY.
cards.watchOut: Fence: nothing here applies to intermediate- or high-risk cancer, gross extrathyroidal extension, or distant metastases. The randomized endpoint is events/recurrence, not mortality — no mortality claim is made or implied. The surveillance cohort is observational context and carries no stamp of its own.

shelves.title: Primary hyperparathyroidism: parathyroidectomy vs surveillance — one 10-year RCT (SIPH)
shelves.question: In mild primary hyperparathyroidism, does parathyroidectomy improve quality of life, bone density, or fracture outcomes compared with observation without treatment over 10 years?
shelves.mesh: Hyperparathyroidism, Primary/surgery · Parathyroidectomy · Quality of Life · Bone Density · Absorptiometry, Photon
shelves.balance: The entire randomized evidence base is one Scandinavian trial (SIPH, 191 patients, 10 years). Surgery improved bone density at every measured site versus observation (a surrogate) and produced one better SF-36 domain (vitality) of uncertain clinical significance; it did not reduce fractures, and psychiatric symptom scores improved equally in both groups. Observation was stable and safe over a decade in this mild-disease population. Single-trial shelf: stamp capped at POSSIBLE, and the topic file flags this shelf for the developer's personal verdict (slow lane). Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: SIPH quality of life (10 years): surgery better on one SF-36 domain only — vitality
cards.summary: SIPH at 10 years: parathyroidectomy beat observation on one SF-36 domain only — vitality (65.1 vs 57.4, P=0.017); psychopathology scores improved equally in both groups, and observation was stable across the decade.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (the SIPH trial, quality-of-life report)
cards.people: 191 patients with mild primary hyperparathyroidism from Sweden, Norway, and Denmark (95 parathyroidectomy, 96 observation), enrolled 1998-2005, followed 10 years. Age and sex mix are not stated in the record's abstract.
cards.result: After 10 years the surgery group scored better on SF-36 vitality (65.1 +/- 20.2 vs 57.4 +/- 22.7; P=0.017); no differences in any physical subscale. Comprehensive Psychopathological Rating Scale symptom scores improved in both groups with no between-group difference. The observation group's SF-36 scores were stable across the decade.
cards.watchOut: One significant domain out of many, with an effect the authors themselves call subtle and of uncertain clinical significance; a single trial with no replication. The abstract reports no registry ID for SIPH — this pack states that plainly rather than supplying one.
cards.source: Pretorius M, Lundstam K, Hellstrom M, et al. Effects of Parathyroidectomy on Quality of Life: 10 Years of Data From a Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial on Primary Hyperparathyroidism (the SIPH-Study). J Bone Miner Res. 2021;36(1):3-11. PMID 33125769. No registry ID on the record.

cards.headline: SIPH bone density (10 years): surgery gained BMD at all sites vs observation — but fractures did not differ
cards.summary: SIPH bone density: surgery gained bone density at all sites while observation lost it — but fractures did not differ ; bone density is a surrogate and is fenced as such.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (the SIPH trial, bone-health report)
cards.people: The same SIPH cohort: 191 randomized (96 observation, 95 surgery); 129 (64 observation, 65 surgery) followed the full 10 years. Age and sex mix are not stated in the record's abstract.
cards.result: Significant treatment effect of surgery on BMD at all analyzed compartments (P<0.001), largest at lumbar spine and femoral neck; mean T-score change differences ranged from 0.41 (33% radius) to 0.58 (lumbar spine) in favor of surgery. BMD fell significantly at all sites under observation. Fracture frequency did not differ between groups in either modified intention-to-treat or per-protocol analysis.
cards.watchOut: BMD is a surrogate: the trial showed denser bones without fewer fractures, and the authors conclude observation could be considered safe for many patients with mild disease over 10 years regarding bone health. One-home note: cards 1 and 2 are two outcome reports of the SAME single trial — SIPH counts once toward the evidence base.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the fence for this shelf
cards.summary: One 10-year trial (its two reports count once): bone density and possibly vitality improve; fractures and broad quality of life do not — capped at POSSIBLE by the single-trial rule.
cards.people: Patients with mild (asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic) primary hyperparathyroidism — the SIPH population.
cards.result: One 10-year RCT: surgery improves bone density (surrogate) and possibly vitality; it has not been shown to reduce fractures or broadly improve quality of life or psychiatric symptoms, and observation was stable over a decade. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE — capped there because the shelf rests on a single trial, per the single-trial rule.
cards.watchOut: Fence: no mortality, kidney-stone, or cardiovascular outcome claim is carded — SIPH's reports verified here do not establish them. No in-flight parathyroidectomy-vs-observation RCT was found in the 2026-11-08 sweep. Flagged slowLane for the developer's personal verdict as a single-flagship-RCT shelf.

shelves.title: Subclinical hyperthyroidism: treat or watch — associations are real but modest, and no trial shows treatment prevents events
shelves.question: In endogenous subclinical hyperthyroidism (low TSH, normal free T4, no symptoms), do the observed risks of atrial fibrillation, coronary events, mortality, and fracture justify treatment, and has any randomized trial shown treatment prevents those outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Hyperthyroidism/diagnosis · Hyperthyroidism/mortality · Atrial Fibrillation/mortality · Coronary Disease/mortality · Fractures, Bone/etiology · Hip Fractures/etiology
shelves.balance: Pooled prospective cohorts associate subclinical hyperthyroidism with more atrial fibrillation, coronary mortality, and hip fracture — but the hazard ratios (1.24-1.68 in the individual-participant analyses) sit inside the 0.5-2.0 band that this library does not count as solid evidence, rising above it only in the smallest TSH<0.10 subgroups with few events. The one randomized treatment trial (elderly, TSH<0.1) compared radioiodine with methimazole — both worked biochemically — but had no observation arm, so whether treating changes any clinical outcome is untested. Observational-dependent shelf, flagged for the developer's personal verdict. Proposed stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Pooled cohorts (Collet 2012): subclinical hyperthyroidism tracks with AFib and coronary death — hazard ratios 1.24 to 1.68
cards.summary: Collet 2012 (10 pooled cohorts): hazard ratios 1.24 for total mortality, 1.29 coronary death, 1.21 coronary events and 1.68 atrial fibrillation — every headline ratio inside this library’s 0.5–2.0 not-solid band , printed on the card.
cards.type: Individual-participant pooled analysis of prospective cohorts (observational)
cards.people: 52,674 participants from 10 cohorts; 2,188 (4.2%) had endogenous subclinical hyperthyroidism (TSH <0.45 mIU/L, normal free T4, no thyroid medication). Coronary events analyzed in 22,437; incident atrial fibrillation in 8,711.
cards.result: Age- and sex-adjusted hazard ratios for subclinical hyperthyroidism vs euthyroidism: total mortality 1.24 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.46), coronary heart disease mortality 1.29 (1.02 to 1.62), coronary events 1.21 (0.99 to 1.46), incident atrial fibrillation 1.68 (1.16 to 2.43). Risks of coronary mortality and atrial fibrillation were higher at TSH <0.10 mIU/L than at 0.10-0.44 (P for trend 0.03).
cards.watchOut: FENCE: every one of these ratios lies between 0.5 and 2.0 — by this library's standing rule for observational evidence, ratios in that band are NOT solid evidence, however precise. These are associations in people who developed subclinical hyperthyroidism, not effects of any treatment, and residual confounding (illness lowering TSH) cannot be excluded.
cards.source: Collet TH, Gussekloo J, Bauer DC, et al. Subclinical hyperthyroidism and the risk of coronary heart disease and mortality. Arch Intern Med. 2012;172(10):799-809. PMID 22529182. No registry ID on the record (observational pooling).

cards.headline: Pooled cohorts (Blum 2015, JAMA): hip-fracture hazard ratio 1.36; higher only in the TSH<0.10 stratum
cards.summary: Blum 2015: hip-fracture hazard ratio 1.36 [1.13 to 1.64]; the one estimate beyond the fence — spine fracture 3.57 at TSH <0.10 — rests on 8 events .
cards.people: 70,298 participants from 13 prospective cohorts (US, Europe, Australia, Japan); 2,219 (3.2%) had subclinical hyperthyroidism; 762,401 person-years of follow-up, 2,975 hip fractures.
cards.result: Hip fracture hazard ratio for subclinical hyperthyroidism vs euthyroidism 1.36 (95% CI 1.13 to 1.64); any fracture 1.28 (1.06 to 1.53); nonspine fracture 1.16 (0.95 to 1.41); spine fracture 1.51 (0.93 to 2.45). At TSH <0.10 mIU/L: hip fracture 1.61 (1.21 to 2.15), any fracture 1.98 (1.41 to 2.78), spine fracture 3.57 (1.88 to 6.78) — the spine estimate rests on 8 events. Endogenous-only analyses were similar (hip 1.52, 1.19 to 1.93). No association for subclinical hypothyroidism.
cards.watchOut: FENCE: the headline ratios again sit inside the 0.5-2.0 not-solid band; only the small TSH<0.10 spine subgroup crosses 2.0, on 8 events with a wide interval. The authors' own conclusion: further study is needed to determine whether treating prevents fractures — that study still does not exist (see card 3).

cards.headline: The only randomized treatment trial (Azizi 2021): radioiodine vs long-term methimazole in the elderly — both controlled TSH; no watch arm
cards.summary: Azizi 2021, the only treatment trial: radioiodine vs long-term methimazole — both controlled TSH and there was no observation arm , so treat-vs-watch cannot be answered by it.
cards.people: 83 patients aged >=65 years with subclinical hyperthyroidism and TSH <0.1 mU/L (from 306 screened), randomized to radioiodine (n=41) or long-term methimazole (n=42); 71 completed 60 months of follow-up.
cards.result: After a fixed 15 mCi radioiodine dose, 66% became hypothyroid and 34% euthyroid at 60 months. On methimazole (tapered to ~3.7 mg/day by year 5), 94% were euthyroid and 2 developed spontaneous hypothyroidism. Minor adverse events occurred in both groups in the first 4 months; no deaths or serious side effects over 60 months.
cards.watchOut: There is no untreated/observation group, so this trial cannot say whether treating subclinical hyperthyroidism prevents atrial fibrillation, fracture, or death — it shows two ways to normalize TSH in the elderly with TSH<0.1. Small (83 randomized) and single-centre-programme evidence.

shelves.title: Levothyroxine over-replacement: a suppressed TSH tracks with atrial fibrillation and fracture — observational harm evidence
shelves.question: In patients taking levothyroxine, is a suppressed (or low) TSH associated with atrial fibrillation, cardiovascular events, and fractures, and where does the risk begin — suppressed TSH only, or any low TSH?
shelves.mesh: Thyrotropin/blood · Atrial Fibrillation/etiology · Thyroxine/blood · Fractures, Bone/epidemiology · Hormone Replacement Therapy/adverse effects · Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology
shelves.balance: The classic signal is Sawin 1994 (Framingham): a TSH <=0.1 mU/L carried a relative risk of atrial fibrillation of 3.1 — the one estimate here that clearly crosses the library's 2.0 observational fence. In people actually taking thyroxine (Tayside cohort), a fully suppressed TSH (<=0.03) tracked with more cardiovascular disease (HR 1.37), dysrhythmia (HR 1.6), and fractures (HR 2.02), while a low-but-not-suppressed TSH showed no increased risk; a large case-control study adds a levothyroxine dose-response for fracture. All of it is observational — no trial has randomized patients to TSH targets and counted events. Harm/observational shelf, flagged for the developer's personal verdict. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Sawin 1994 (Framingham): TSH <=0.1 tripled the relative risk of atrial fibrillation over 10 years
cards.summary: Sawin 1994 (Framingham): TSH ≤0.1 carried a threefold 10-year atrial fibrillation risk (28% vs 11%; adjusted relative risk 3.1 [1.7 to 5.5]) — fenced on the card as a low-TSH-from-any-cause cohort, not a levothyroxine population.
cards.people: 2,007 Framingham participants aged >=60 without atrial fibrillation at baseline (814 men, 1,193 women); only 61 had a low TSH (<=0.1 mU/L) and 187 a slightly low TSH (0.1-0.4). Ten-year follow-up.
cards.result: Cumulative 10-year atrial fibrillation incidence was 28% with low TSH vs 11% with normal TSH (absolute difference 17 percentage points); age-adjusted incidence 28 vs 10 per 1,000 person-years (P=0.005). Adjusted relative risk 3.1 (95% CI 1.7 to 5.5) — a relative measure that crosses this library's 2.0 fence for observational harm signals. Slightly low TSH (0.1-0.4) was NOT significantly different from normal.
cards.watchOut: These were clinically euthyroid older persons with low TSH from any cause — not a levothyroxine-treated population — so Sawin anchors the TSH level, not the drug. The low-TSH group was small (61 people, 13 events).
cards.source: Sawin CT, Geller A, Wolf PA, et al. Low serum thyrotropin concentrations as a risk factor for atrial fibrillation in older persons. N Engl J Med. 1994;331(19):1249-1252. PMID 7935681. No registry ID on the record (pre-registration era cohort).

cards.summary: Flynn 2010 (Tayside): on long-term thyroxine, a suppressed TSH — not merely a low one — tracked with events: hazard ratios 1.37 (cardiovascular) and 1.6 (dysrhythmia), both labeled inside the 0.5–2.0 not-solid band ; only fracture ( 2.02 ) touches the fence.
cards.people: 17,684 patients on thyroxine replacement in Tayside, Scotland (1993-2001 data), categorized by TSH: suppressed (<=0.03 mU/L), low (0.04-0.4), normal (0.4-4.0), or raised (>4.0). Age and sex mix are not stated in the record's abstract.
cards.result: Versus normal TSH, suppressed TSH carried adjusted hazard ratios of 1.37 (95% CI 1.17 to 1.60) for cardiovascular disease, 1.6 (1.10 to 2.33) for dysrhythmias, and 2.02 (1.55 to 2.62) for fractures. A low but not suppressed TSH showed no increased risk (hazard ratios 1.1, 1.13, and 1.13). Raised TSH was also harmful (1.95, 1.80, 1.83) — the risk curve is U-shaped.
cards.watchOut: FENCE: the cardiovascular (1.37) and dysrhythmia (1.6) ratios sit inside the 0.5-2.0 not-solid band; only the fracture ratio (2.02) touches the fence line. Observational: patients whose TSH is suppressed may differ from others (dose requests, illness, adherence) in ways adjustment cannot fully remove.

shelves.title: Graves' disease: long-term low-dose methimazole vs radioiodine vs surgery — remission, relapse, and the hypothyroidism trade
shelves.question: For Graves' hyperthyroidism, how does long-term low-dose methimazole compare with conventional-duration antithyroid treatment, radioiodine, and surgery on remission/relapse, hypothyroidism, and safety?
shelves.mesh: Graves Disease/drug therapy · Methimazole/therapeutic use · Antithyroid Agents/therapeutic use · Iodine Radioisotopes/therapeutic use · Recurrence · Graves Ophthalmopathy/etiology
shelves.balance: The strongest randomized finding is about duration: continuing low-dose methimazole for a total of 60-120 months instead of stopping at 18-24 months cut post-withdrawal relapse from 53% to 15% in adults (Azizi 2019), a result that held at 84 months of extended follow-up (56% vs 17% recurrence) and was echoed in a juvenile trial. Safety over up to a decade of low-dose therapy was reassuring in these trials (skin reactions and two liver-enzyme elevations, all early). Direct randomized comparisons against radioiodine are thin — the Cochrane review found only two small RCTs — and surgery has no randomized comparison here. The trade is stated plainly: radioiodine and surgery end hyperthyroidism definitively at the price of near-certain hypothyroidism; long-term methimazole preserves the gland but requires years of therapy. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (for the long-term methimazole remission benefit).

cards.headline: Azizi 2019 (adults): methimazole for 60-120 months cut relapse after withdrawal to 15%, vs 53% with conventional duration
cards.summary: Azizi 2019 (adults): methimazole for 60–120 months cut relapse after withdrawal to 15% vs 53% ; in the same cohort’s extended follow-up, recurrence by 84 months was 17% vs 56% (P<0.001).
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial, with extended 84-month follow-up report (2024)
cards.people: 302 consecutive adults with a first episode of Graves' hyperthyroidism; after 18-24 months of methimazole, 258 were randomized to continue low-dose methimazole (total 60-120 months, n=130) or stop (n=128), then followed 48 months after withdrawal. Sex mix is not stated in the record's abstract.
cards.result: Hyperthyroidism recurred within 48 months of withdrawal in 15% (18/119) of the long-term group vs 53% (65/123) of the conventional group — an absolute reduction of about 38 percentage points. In the extended follow-up of the same cohort (PMID 38165576), recurrence by 84 months post-withdrawal was 17% (20/118) vs 56% (67/120), P<0.001. Safety: 14 cutaneous reactions and 2 liver-enzyme elevations, all in the first 18 months; no further methimazole reactions over up to 118 additional months.
cards.watchOut: One research group's programme (Iran) provides most of the long-term evidence; relapse predictors (TRAb, T3, age) matter — the benefit is an average. Registry ID as printed on the record is IRCT/5143 (an Iranian registry entry in abbreviated form); no NCT number exists on the record.
cards.source: Azizi F, Amouzegar A, Tohidi M, et al. Increased Remission Rates After Long-Term Methimazole Therapy in Patients with Graves' Disease: Results of a Randomized Clinical Trial. Thyroid. 2019;29(9):1192-1200. PMID 31310160 · IRCT5143 (as listed on the record). Extended follow-up: Azizi F, et al. Endocrine. 2024;84(2):577-588. PMID 38165576.

cards.headline: Azizi 2019 (juvenile Graves'): long-term methimazole nearly tripled the 4-year cure rate
cards.summary: Azizi 2019 (juvenile Graves’): long-term methimazole nearly tripled the 4-year cure rate ( 88% vs 33% ), with only 3 cutaneous reactions and no other adverse events.
cards.people: 66 consecutive patients with untreated juvenile Graves' hyperthyroidism; after a median 22 months of methimazole, 56 were randomized to continue low-dose methimazole or stop; 24 per group completed the protocol, with 48 months of post-withdrawal follow-up.
cards.result: Hyperthyroidism was cured in 92% (1 year) and 88% (4 years) after withdrawal in the long-term group vs 46% and 33% in the short-term group — roughly a threefold higher 4-year cure rate with long-term therapy. Only 3 cutaneous reactions and no other adverse events over up to 120 months of methimazole; required dose fell from 5.17 mg/day at 22 months to 3.5 mg/day by 96-120 months.
cards.watchOut: Small, single-programme, juvenile-only trial (24 completers per arm) — supportive of the adult finding, not independent proof for adults; percentages rest on small denominators.
cards.source: Azizi F, Takyar M, Madreseh E, et al. Long-term Methimazole Therapy in Juvenile Graves' Disease: A Randomized Trial. Pediatrics. 2019;143(5):e20185534 (pages not listed on the record). PMID 31040197. No registry ID on the record.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2016: radioiodine vs antithyroid drugs — only two RCTs met the bar, and long-term outcome differences were unknown
cards.summary: Cochrane 2016: only two RCTs met the bar for radioiodine vs antithyroid drugs, and long-term outcome differences were unknown from randomised evidence.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomized trials
cards.people: 2 RCTs, 425 adults with Graves' disease (204 radioiodine, 221 methimazole for 18 months), each with at least 2 years of follow-up.
cards.result: Health-related quality of life appeared similar between radioiodine and methimazole, but no quantitative data were reported and evidence quality was low. The review's framing conclusion: despite how common Graves' disease is, whether radioiodine and antithyroid medication differ on long-term outcomes was unknown from randomized evidence as of the 2015 search.
cards.watchOut: A 2016 review with a September 2015 search — it predates the long-term methimazole trials on this shelf, so its 'unknown' applies to radioiodine-vs-drug comparisons, not to the duration question answered by cards 1-2. Ophthalmopathy outcomes carried high risk of performance/detection bias in at least one included trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the fence for this shelf
cards.summary: One strong randomised claim: long-term low-dose methimazole produces far higher durable remission than conventional courses, with no late toxicity signal — LIKELY, for that duration claim.
cards.people: Patients with Graves' hyperthyroidism choosing among continued antithyroid drug therapy, radioiodine, and surgery.
cards.result: Randomized evidence supports one strong claim: long-term low-dose methimazole (60-120 months) produces far higher durable remission after withdrawal than conventional 18-24-month courses, with no late-emerging toxicity signal in these trials. Proposed stamp: LIKELY, applying to that duration claim.
cards.watchOut: Fence: there is no adequately powered randomized comparison of long-term methimazole against radioiodine or surgery on relapse, hypothyroidism, ophthalmopathy, or quality of life — head-to-head claims among the three definitive strategies are NOT carded. Surgery appears in this shelf only as the non-randomized third option in the trade-off framing. The Korean population cohort sometimes cited for atrial-fibrillation differences by treatment method (PMID 36387909) is observational and was not carded.

shelves.title: After total thyroidectomy: routine calcium + calcitriol vs symptom-guided replacement for transient hypocalcemia
shelves.question: After total thyroidectomy, does routinely giving oral calcium plus calcitriol to everyone prevent symptomatic transient hypocalcemia better than PTH- or symptom-guided selective supplementation?
shelves.mesh: Thyroidectomy/adverse effects · Hypocalcemia/prevention & control · Calcitriol/administration & dosage · Calcium, Dietary/administration & dosage · Vitamin D/administration & dosage · Postoperative Care
shelves.balance: Routine prophylaxis works for symptoms: in the largest RCT, adding calcitriol 1 mcg twice daily to routine calcium cut tetany from 7.4% to 0% and severe day-3 hypocalcemia from 27.2% to 9.9%, and a meta-analysis of the RCTs found symptomatic hypocalcemia in 4% with calcitriol+calcium vs 19% with calcium alone and 31% with nothing (odds ratio ~0.31-0.32, a relative measure). A randomized PTH-guided strategy shows the selective alternative is also safe: patients with a day-1 PTH >=10 pg/mL were discharged without supplements and only 10% had transient symptoms. The question is symptoms and length of management, not permanent hypoparathyroidism — no card here touches that. Proposed stamp: LIKELY.

cards.headline: Tartaglia 2005: routine calcitriol 1 mcg twice daily + calcium abolished tetany (0% vs 7.4%)
cards.summary: Tartaglia 2005: routine calcitriol 1 mcg twice daily + calcium abolished tetany (0% vs 7.4% with no calcitriol); severe day-3 hypocalcemia 9.9% vs 27.2%.
cards.people: 417 consecutive total-thyroidectomy patients in Italy, all given calcium salts 500 mg three times daily, randomized to calcitriol 0.5 mcg twice daily (n=104), calcitriol 1 mcg twice daily (n=111), or no calcitriol (n=202). Age and sex mix are not stated in the record's abstract.
cards.result: Postoperative tetany: 2.9% (0.5 mcg group), 0% (1 mcg group), 7.4% (no calcitriol), P=0.03. Paresthesias: 28.8%, 17.1%, 22.3% (P=0.19, not significant). Severe hypocalcemia on day 3: 23.1%, 9.9%, and 27.2% (P=0.001) — an absolute reduction of about 17 percentage points for the 1 mcg dose vs none. Intact PTH at treatment discontinuation did not differ from preoperative levels.
cards.watchOut: Everyone received calcium, so this tests adding calcitriol, not calcium vs nothing; the unequal group sizes (202 controls vs ~105 per dose arm) and single-centre design temper precision. Outcome is transient biochemical/symptomatic hypocalcemia, not permanent hypoparathyroidism.
cards.source: Tartaglia F, Giuliani A, Sgueglia M, et al. Randomized study on oral administration of calcitriol to prevent symptomatic hypocalcemia after total thyroidectomy. Am J Surg. 2005;190(3):424-429. PMID 16105530. No registry ID on the record (pre-registration era).

cards.headline: Cayo 2012: a single day-1 PTH identifies who can safely skip routine supplementation
cards.summary: Cayo 2012: a day-1 PTH ≥10 identifies who can safely skip routine supplements (10% transient symptoms, all managed as outpatients); below 10, 48% developed symptoms.
cards.type: Prospective randomized study of a PTH-guided selective strategy
cards.people: 143 total-thyroidectomy patients; management randomized/stratified by morning-after-surgery (POD1) PTH: >=10 pg/mL (n=112, 78%) received no supplementation unless symptomatic; <10 pg/mL (n=31) were randomized to calcium, calcium+calcitriol, or none.
cards.result: Of patients with POD1 PTH >=10, 11 (10%) reported transient hypocalcemic symptoms, all managed with outpatient calcium — supporting discharge without routine supplements in that group. Of those with PTH <10, 15 (48%) developed symptoms and 5 required intravenous calcium. Predictors of symptoms: younger age (odds ratio 1.59) and PTH <10 (odds ratio 1.08 per the record's abstract).
cards.watchOut: The PTH<10 subgroup was too small (n=31) for the authors to determine whether calcium alone or calcium+calcitriol is needed there — so this card supports selective supplementation by PTH, not a verdict on which supplement the high-risk group needs.
cards.source: Cayo AK, Yen TWF, Misustin SM, et al. Predicting the need for calcium and calcitriol supplementation after total thyroidectomy: results of a prospective, randomized study. Surgery. 2012;152(6):1059-1067. PMID 23068088. No registry ID on the record.

shelves.title: Benign thyroid nodules: radiofrequency ablation vs surgery — a young field with no adequate head-to-head trial
shelves.question: For symptomatic benign thyroid nodules, how does radiofrequency ablation compare with surgery on volume reduction, symptom relief, complications, and the loss of definitive histology?
shelves.mesh: Thyroid Nodule/surgery · Radiofrequency Ablation · Laser Therapy · Thyroidectomy · Catheter Ablation/adverse effects · Organ Size
shelves.balance: The topic file's flag is borne out: there is no adequately powered randomized trial of RFA against surgery. What exists: Italian RCTs of RFA against laser ablation (12-month volume reduction 70.9% vs 60.0% for laser), a Brazilian RFA-vs-thyroidectomy randomized comparison with only 5 patients per arm, and large observational series pooling to a 1.35% major-complication rate for RFA. RFA shrinks nodules by roughly two-thirds over a year and relieves pressure/cosmetic scores, but leaves tissue in place and yields no histology; surgery removes the nodule definitively. Certainty is capped accordingly. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE at best, per the topic file's flag.

cards.headline: LARA II (2021): RFA shrank nodules 70.9% at 12 months — but the randomized comparator was laser ablation, not surgery
cards.summary: LARA II: RFA shrank nodules 70.9% at 12 months vs laser’s 60.0% (P=0.024) — but the randomised comparator was laser, not surgery ; the 6-month LARA report showed the same pattern (64.3% vs 53.2%).
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (RFA vs laser ablation)
cards.people: 60 patients with a solitary solid/predominantly solid benign nonfunctioning nodule with pressure symptoms or cosmetic problems (single Italian centre), randomized 1:1 to a single RFA or laser session; 29 per group completed 12 months.
cards.result: Volume reduction rate at 12 months: 70.9% +/- 16.9% (RFA) vs 60.0% +/- 19.0% (laser), P=0.024. Technical success (>50% reduction) did not differ significantly. Compression scores improved from 4.6 to 1.3 (RFA) and 4.6 to 1.6 (laser); cosmetic scores from 3.4 to 1.3 and 3.4 to 1.4 — within-group gains with no significant between-group difference. The 6-month LARA report (PMID 32056501) showed the same pattern (64.3% vs 53.2%).

cards.headline: The only randomized RFA-vs-thyroidectomy comparison found: 5 patients per arm

cards.headline: Synthesis: the fence for this shelf
cards.summary: RFA reproducibly shrinks benign nodules by roughly two-thirds and relieves pressure and cosmetic scores; surgery alone removes the nodule and yields histology — POSSIBLE at best.
cards.people: Patients with symptomatic, biopsy-benign thyroid nodules choosing between ablation and surgery.
cards.result: RFA reproducibly shrinks benign nodules by ~60-71% over 6-12 months in randomized ablation-vs-ablation trials, improves symptom and cosmetic scores, and carries a ~1.35% pooled major-complication rate in experienced hands. Surgery remains the only option that removes the nodule and provides histology. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE — the topic file's ceiling for this young field.
cards.watchOut: Fence: no claim of equivalence or superiority to surgery is carded — that trial has not been done at adequate size. Volume reduction is not nodule elimination: regrowth, repeat sessions, and missed-occult-malignancy risk over long horizons are unquantified in the carded evidence. In-flight note: the 2024 randomized activity in this field compares ablation technologies with each other (microwave vs RFA, PMID 39436295), not ablation with surgery.
cards.source: Synthesis of cards 1-3 on this shelf.

shelves.title: Hormone replacement for chronic hypoparathyroidism: rhPTH(1-84) and palopegteriparatide
shelves.question: Can parathyroid-hormone replacement free patients with chronic hypoparathyroidism from high-dose calcium and active vitamin D — REPLACE (rhPTH 1-84) and the PaTHway programme (palopegteriparatide)?
shelves.mesh: Calcium Citrate/administration & dosage · Drug Therapy, Combination · Headache/chemically induced,diagnosis · Hypoparathyroidism/diagnosis,drug therapy,epidemiology · Injections, Subcutaneous · Parathyroid Hormone/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Recombinant Proteins/administration & dosage,adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two separate phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled programmes reached the same endpoint family. REPLACE (134 patients) found 53% on rhPTH(1-84) versus 2% on placebo achieving at least a 50% reduction in oral calcium and active vitamin D while maintaining serum calcium. PaTHway (84 participants) found 79% on palopegteriparatide versus 5% on placebo meeting its composite of normal serum calcium, independence from conventional therapy and stable dose at week 26, with 93% of treated participants independent of conventional therapy. The PaTHway 52-week report is a post hoc renal-function analysis of the same trial, carded as such and counted once as evidence. Primary hyperparathyroidism surgery is a different question and stays home on Shelf #516.

cards.headline: REPLACE 2013: rhPTH(1-84) let 53% of patients halve their calcium and active vitamin D while keeping serum calcium — versus 2% on placebo
cards.summary: REPLACE 2013: rhPTH(1-84) let 53% of patients halve their calcium and active vitamin D while keeping serum calcium — vs 2% on placebo.
cards.people: 134 adults with hypoparathyroidism of at least 18 months' duration, aged 18–85 years, from 33 sites in eight countries, randomised 2:1 after an optimisation period to rhPTH(1-84) starting at 50 μg daily (90) or placebo (44) for 24 weeks, with titration to 75 or 100 μg permitted and calcium / active vitamin D progressively reduced. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — at least a 50% reduction from baseline in daily oral calcium and active vitamin D dose while maintaining albumin-corrected serum calcium — was achieved by 48 (53%) patients on rhPTH(1-84) versus one (2%) on placebo (percentage difference 51.1%, 95% confidence interval 39.9 to 62.3; p<0.0001). At least one adverse event occurred in 84 (93%) patients on rhPTH(1-84) and 44 (100%) on placebo, with hypocalcaemia, muscle spasm, paraesthesias, headache and nausea most common; serious adverse events occurred in ten (11%) versus four (9%) patients. Six rhPTH(1-84) patients and seven placebo patients discontinued before study end.
cards.watchOut: A 24-week, dose-reduction endpoint trial: it shows PTH replacement can substitute for much of conventional therapy over six months, not that it prevents the long-term renal and other complications of conventional therapy.
cards.source: Mannstadt M et al. Efficacy and safety of recombinant human parathyroid hormone (1-84) in hypoparathyroidism (REPLACE): a double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised, phase 3 study. cards.headline: PaTHway 2023: palopegteriparatide met the normocalcaemia-plus-independence composite in 79% versus 5% on placebo at week 26
cards.summary: PaTHway 2023: palopegteriparatide met the normocalcaemia-plus-independence composite in 79% vs 5% on placebo at week 26.
cards.people: 84 adults with hypoparathyroidism randomised 3:1 to once-daily TransCon PTH (palopegteriparatide, initially 18 μg/d; 61 treated in the efficacy report) or placebo (21), both co-administered with conventional therapy and titrated by a serum-calcium-guided algorithm. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At week 26, 79% (48/61) of participants on palopegteriparatide versus 5% (1/21) on placebo met the composite primary endpoint — normal albumin-adjusted serum calcium (8.3–10.6 mg/dL), independence from conventional therapy (no active vitamin D and at most 600 mg/d of calcium), and no increase in study drug over the prior 4 weeks (p<0.0001). Overall, 93% (57/61) of treated participants achieved independence from conventional therapy, mean 24-hour urine calcium normalised, and Hypoparathyroidism Patient Experience Scale domain scores and the SF-36 Physical Functioning subscale improved significantly versus placebo. Adverse events occurred in 82% (50/61) on palopegteriparatide and 100% (21/21) on placebo, mostly mild (46%) or moderate (46%); there were no study-drug-related withdrawals.
cards.watchOut: Small (84 randomised) and 26 weeks: the composite is dominated by the independence-from-supplements component, and the placebo arm is only 21 participants, so the 5% placebo figure rests on a single responder.

cards.headline: PaTHway 52-week renal analysis 2024: eGFR rose by a mean 9.3 mL/min/1.73 m2 over 52 weeks — a post hoc analysis of the same trial
cards.summary: PaTHway 52-week renal analysis 2024: eGFR rose by a mean 9.3 mL/min/1.73 m² over 52 weeks — a post hoc analysis of the same trial, labelled as such.
cards.type: Post hoc analysis of a phase 3 trial (26-week double-blind placebo-controlled period followed by an open-label extension)
cards.people: Adults with chronic hypoparathyroidism in the PaTHway trial: at week 52, over 95% (78/82) of participants remained enrolled in the open-label extension. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At week 52, 86% of extension participants maintained normocalcaemia and 95% had achieved independence from conventional therapy, with none requiring active vitamin D. Mean (SD) eGFR increased by 9.3 (11.7) mL/min/1.73 m2 from baseline over 52 weeks (P<0.0001), and 43% of participants had an increase of at least 10 mL/min/1.73 m2; in the subgroup with baseline eGFR below 60, the mean increase was 11.5 (11.3) (P<0.001). One case of nephrolithiasis was reported, in a placebo-group participant during blinded treatment; none were reported through week 52 on palopegteriparatide.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc and, after week 26, uncontrolled: without a parallel placebo arm in the extension, the eGFR rise cannot be separated from regression to the mean, supplement withdrawal effects, or natural history. It is a hypothesis about renal preservation, printed as such — the authors themselves call for further investigation.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two PTH-replacement programmes, one result — most patients can come off high-dose supplements; the renal claim is post hoc only
cards.summary: Two PTH-replacement programmes, one result — LIKELY; the renal claim is post hoc only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: REPLACE (134 patients, rhPTH[1-84]) and PaTHway (84 participants, palopegteriparatide; 26-week primary report and 52-week renal analysis are two reports of ONE trial).
cards.result: The randomised evidence is concordant across two different PTH preparations: a 51.1-percentage-point advantage on REPLACE's dose-reduction endpoint (53% vs 2%) and a 79% vs 5% composite success in PaTHway, with 93% of palopegteriparatide participants independent of conventional therapy. That supports LIKELY for the shelf's question — PTH replacement can free patients from high-dose calcium and active vitamin D while maintaining calcium. The renal-function improvement comes from a post hoc, partly uncontrolled analysis and is not part of the stamp. A further 52-week efficacy report of PaTHway found in the currency sweep is the same trial again and is fenced here, not carded a third time.
cards.watchOut: Neither programme was powered for fractures, kidney failure or other long-term complications of hypoparathyroidism; 'freedom from supplements at 6–12 months' is the proven claim.

shelves.title: Differentiated thyroid cancer: lenvatinib and sorafenib
shelves.question: In radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer, do lenvatinib (SELECT) and sorafenib (DECISION) prolong progression-free survival versus placebo — at what toxicity cost?
shelves.mesh: Disease-Free Survival · Iodine Radioisotopes/therapeutic use · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Phenylurea Compounds/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Quinolines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Thyroid Neoplasms/drug therapy,radiotherapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (for progression-free survival; no overall-survival claim is made): Two double-blind phase 3 trials against placebo both prolonged progression-free survival — SELECT: median 18.3 vs 3.6 months on lenvatinib (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.21, 99% CI 0.14 to 0.31 — a relative measure well outside the 0.5–2.0 caution band) with a 64.8% response rate; DECISION: median 10.8 vs 5.8 months on sorafenib (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.76 — a relative measure inside the caution band's lower half, printed with its absolute medians). Toxicity is heavy on both drugs and is printed on both cards. Overall survival was not reached in SELECT and is not claimed for either drug on this shelf; low-risk RAI-omission questions stay home on Shelves #514–#515.

cards.headline: SELECT 2015: lenvatinib stretched median progression-free survival to 18.3 vs 3.6 months — relative hazard 0.21 — with treatment-related effects in most patients
cards.summary: SELECT 2015: lenvatinib stretched median progression-free survival to 18.3 vs 3.6 months — relative hazard 0.21 — with treatment-related effects in most patients.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (placebo patients could cross to open-label lenvatinib at progression)
cards.people: 392 patients with progressive, iodine-131-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer randomised to lenvatinib 24 mg daily (261) or placebo (131). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 18.3 months on lenvatinib and 3.6 months on placebo (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.21, 99% confidence interval 0.14 to 0.31; P<0.001 — a relative measure, printed with its absolute medians), with benefit in all prespecified subgroups. The response rate was 64.8% on lenvatinib (4 complete and 165 partial responses) versus 1.5% on placebo (P<0.001). Median overall survival was not reached in either group. Treatment-related adverse effects occurring in over 40% of the lenvatinib group included hypertension (67.8%), diarrhea (59.4%), fatigue or asthenia (59.0%), decreased appetite (50.2%), decreased weight (46.4%) and nausea (41.0%); 14.2% discontinued lenvatinib for adverse effects versus 2.3% on placebo, and 6 of 20 deaths during the treatment period in the lenvatinib group were considered drug-related.
cards.watchOut: The toxicity ledger is part of the result: two-thirds hypertensive, one in seven stopping for adverse effects, and some treatment-period deaths judged drug-related. Crossover at progression also means the trial cannot cleanly answer overall survival.

cards.summary: Both kinase inhibitors delay progression in radioiodine-refractory disease — LIKELY for progression-free survival only; no survival claim (NETTER-style interim-only survival reporting is not carded as a claim).

shelves.title: Selenium in mild Graves' orbitopathy (EUGOGO)
shelves.question: In patients with mild Graves' orbitopathy, does selenium supplementation improve eye outcomes and quality of life versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antioxidants/therapeutic use · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Graves Ophthalmopathy/drug therapy · Humans · Male · Pentoxifylline/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Quality of Life · Selenium/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one well-conducted trial, reported in P values without absolute rates. In EUGOGO (n=159, mild Graves' orbitopathy), 6 months of selenium improved Graves'-orbitopathy-specific quality of life (P<0.001), reduced eye involvement (P=0.01) and slowed progression (P=0.01) versus placebo, with exploratory 12-month results in the same direction and no adverse events evident; the pentoxifylline arm showed none of these benefits and frequent gastrointestinal problems. The record prints no absolute progression rates or QoL scores, so none are carded and the size of the benefit cannot be stated from the verified record. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single trial, still unreplicated. Scope boundary: moderate-to-severe active Graves' orbitopathy (the teprotumumab question) is a different shelf; this shelf is mild disease only.

cards.headline: EUGOGO: selenium improved quality of life and slowed progression in mild Graves' orbitopathy at 6 months
cards.summary: EUGOGO: selenium improved quality of life and slowed progression in mild Graves' orbitopathy at 6 months
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial (6 months treatment, 6 months follow-up)
cards.people: 159 patients with mild Graves' orbitopathy received selenium 100 µg twice daily, pentoxifylline 600 mg twice daily, or placebo for 6 months. The abstract does not print the arm sizes, mean age, or the sex split.
cards.result: At 6 months, selenium — but not pentoxifylline — was associated with improved quality of life (P<0.001), less eye involvement (P=0.01), and slowed progression of orbitopathy (P=0.01) versus placebo, on a blinded overall ophthalmic assessment and a disease-specific QoL questionnaire (the co-primary outcomes). The Clinical Activity Score fell in all groups, significantly more with selenium. Exploratory 12-month evaluations confirmed the 6-month results. Two placebo patients and one pentoxifylline patient required immunosuppressive therapy for deterioration. No adverse events were evident with selenium; pentoxifylline caused frequent gastrointestinal problems. The abstract prints P values without absolute rates for progression or QoL scores, so no absolute figures are carded.
cards.watchOut: A single European trial in mild disease; the absence of printed absolute rates means the clinical size of the benefit cannot be judged from the record, only its direction and statistical strength. The registry number (NTR524, Netherlands Trial Register) appears in the abstract text; there is no databank entry in this record.
cards.source: Marcocci C et al. Selenium and the course of mild Graves' orbitopathy. N Engl J Med. 2011. PMID: 21591944. Registry ID: NTR524 appears in the abstract text; no databank entry in this record. shelves.title: Cinacalcet in primary hyperparathyroidism
shelves.question: In patients with primary hyperparathyroidism, does cinacalcet normalise serum calcium and lower parathyroid hormone versus placebo?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — direction consistent, magnitude unverifiable from the verified record. The pinned record is a pooled analysis of three multicentre randomised trials (81 patients across the severity spectrum, treatment up to 4.5 years): it reports that cinacalcet reduced serum calcium and increased the proportion achieving normal calcium (≤10.3 mg/dl) similarly in all three severity categories, with a modest PTH reduction — but its abstract prints NO percentages or effect sizes for any of these outcomes. Scope boundary: cinacalcet in dialysis secondary hyperparathyroidism (EVOLVE) is Shelf #296, a different question, and its null result is not imported here.

cards.type: Pooled analysis of three multicentre randomised clinical trials (treatment up to 4.5 years)
cards.people: 81 patients with primary hyperparathyroidism in three categories: failed parathyroidectomy (29), meeting one or more criteria for parathyroidectomy without prior surgery (37), and mild asymptomatic disease (15). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.

The databank lists three registry IDs (NCT00001859, NCT00037518, NCT00936988) without mapping them to the three component trials — noted as such.

shelves.title: Fixed versus dosimetry-calculated radioiodine activity in Graves' disease
shelves.question: In patients with Graves' disease receiving radioiodine, does a fixed activity achieve cure rates comparable to dosimetry-calculated activity?
shelves.mesh: No MeSH terms in the record
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the only randomised comparison is a 40-patient single-centre trial that cannot carry the comparability claim made for it. Success of the first radioiodine dose at 3 months was 60% with a fixed activity versus 65% with dosimetry-calculated activity — 'no statistically significant difference' in a trial with 20 patients per arm is absence of evidence, not evidence of equivalence, and no non-inferiority margin was prespecified in the record. The authors' conclusion that the fixed approach 'may be used' as it is simpler goes beyond what their sample can show, and that overclaim is flagged rather than adopted. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single tiny trial; the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

cards.headline: Jaiswal 2014: first-dose success 60% (fixed) versus 65% (calculated) at 3 months — in 40 patients

cards.people: 40 patients with Graves' disease in an Indian population: 20 received a fixed activity of 185 MBq of iodine-131 and 20 received an activity calculated from gland weight and 24-hour uptake. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Success of the first dose (euthyroid or hypothyroid at 3 months without further therapy) was 60% in the fixed group (8 hyperthyroid, 4 euthyroid, 8 hypothyroid after the first dose) versus 65% in the calculated group (7 hyperthyroid, 8 euthyroid, 5 hypothyroid). The record reports no statistically significant difference between the success rates.
cards.watchOut: With 20 patients per arm, the confidence interval around a 5-point difference spans clinically important inferiority and superiority; the trial's conclusion that the fixed approach may be adopted for convenience overclaims its data and is flagged on this card. The record carries no MeSH terms and no registry ID, and follow-up is only 3 months — late hypothyroidism and retreatment are not captured.

shelves.title: Antithyroid drug dose in Graves' disease (European multicentre trial)
shelves.question: In patients with Graves' disease, does a higher methimazole dose (with levothyroxine add-back) improve remission rates versus a lower titrated dose?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antithyroid Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Drug Administration Schedule · Follow-Up Studies · Graves Disease/drug therapy · Humans · Methimazole/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Recurrence · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a 313-patient multicentre trial with nearly identical long-term relapse rates: after methimazole 10 mg versus 40 mg daily for a year (levothyroxine added as required), relapse at a mean of 4.3 years was 58.3% versus 57.8%, and no baseline variable predicted who would relapse. The stamp stops at POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) because this is a single trial programme and the carded record is its long-term follow-up report. One correction: the topic draft's statement that the higher dose 'caused more adverse events' is not printed in this record's abstract and is not carded; the record's own conclusion is that the dose can safely be kept to the minimum required. Scope boundary: long-term low-dose methimazole versus radioiodine versus surgery as treatment strategies is a different question, homed on its own shelf.

cards.headline: Benker 1998 (European Multicentre Trial): relapse 58.3% on methimazole 10 mg versus 57.8% on 40 mg at ~4.3 years
cards.summary: Benker 1998 (European Multicentre Trial): relapse 58.3% on methimazole 10 mg versus 57.8% on 40 mg at ~4.3 years
cards.type: Prospective, multicentre, randomised trial — long-term follow-up report (mean observation 4.3 ± 1.3 years)
cards.people: 313 patients with Graves' disease randomised to methimazole 10 mg or 40 mg daily for 1 year, with levothyroxine supplementation as required. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The overall relapse rate was 58%, with no difference between doses: 58.3% (10 mg) versus 57.8% (40 mg). The record notes the group's earlier report found 12-month post-treatment relapse rates of 37% and 38% respectively. Age, goitre size, ophthalmopathy, iodine excretion, T4, T3, immunoglobulin levels, therapeutic index and thyroid uptake at entry none predicted relapse (confirmed by Cox regression); five patients became spontaneously hypothyroid without relation to dose.
cards.watchOut: This record is the follow-up report; its abstract does not print the adverse-event comparison the topic draft attributed to the trial, so no harm claim is carded. Pre-registration era: no registry ID in the record. The block-and-replace element (levothyroxine 'as required') also means the comparison is of two dose strategies, not of pure doses.

shelves.title: Benign thyroid nodules: microwave versus radiofrequency ablation — equal shrinkage in one randomised trial
shelves.question: In predominantly solid, nonfunctioning benign thyroid nodules, how do microwave ablation and radiofrequency ablation compare for nodule volume reduction, complications, and durability over two years?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Microwaves/therapeutic use · Radiofrequency Ablation/methods · Thyroid Nodule · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One prospective randomised multicentre trial (152 patients, five Chinese institutions, follow-up at least 2 years) found microwave ablation (MWA) noninferior to radiofrequency ablation (RFA) for shrinking predominantly solid, nonfunctioning benign thyroid nodules: the volume reduction rate differed by −5.6% at 6 months and −2.4% at 2 years (noninferiority met at both), technique efficacy (≥50% volume reduction) was 91% versus 86% (p=.40), and volume change over time did not differ. Safety is the open part: the commonest major complication, voice change, occurred in 6.6% on MWA versus 1.3% on RFA (p=.21) — not statistically different in a trial this size, and the authors state a larger sample is needed to show safety is comparable. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single open-label trial, a volume (not symptom or cancer) endpoint, and an underpowered safety comparison. Cross-point: Shelf #521 covers RFA versus surgery, a different comparison.

cards.headline: Chen 2024: microwave ablation noninferior to radiofrequency ablation for nodule volume reduction at 6 months and 2 years
cards.summary: Chen 2024: microwave ablation noninferior to radiofrequency ablation for nodule volume reduction at 6 months and 2 years
cards.people: 152 participants with nonfunctioning, predominantly solid benign thyroid nodules at five institutions in China, randomised 1:1 to microwave ablation (n=76; mean age 46; 58 women) or radiofrequency ablation (n=76; mean age 50; 56 women), followed for at least 2 years. Primary outcomes: volume reduction rate (VRR) at 6 months and 2 years.
cards.result: MWA was noninferior to RFA for VRR at 6 months (mean difference −5.6%; P=.01 for noninferiority) and at 2 years (mean difference −2.4%; P<.001). VRR change over time did not differ (mixed-effects mean difference 6.9%, 95% CI −0.5 to 13.9; P=.73), and technique efficacy (≥50% volume reduction) was 91% (MWA) versus 86% (RFA) (P=.40). Voice change — the most common major complication — occurred in 6.6% of the MWA group versus 1.3% of the RFA group (P=.21).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-country, and powered for a volume endpoint — not for symptoms, regrowth beyond 2 years, or complications. The 5-point numerical excess of voice change on microwave ablation is exactly the kind of difference a 152-patient trial cannot resolve. Noninferiority on shrinkage does not make the two interchangeable for every nodule location (e.g., near the recurrent laryngeal nerve).
cards.source: Chen S et al. Microwave versus Radiofrequency Ablation in Treating Predominantly Solid Benign Thyroid Nodules: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Radiology. 2024. PMID: 39436295. Registry ID: NCT04046354, from the record.
