shelves.title: Desiccated thyroid extract versus levothyroxine: no symptom or cognition difference; preference split between trials
shelves.question: In primary hypothyroidism stable on levothyroxine, does desiccated thyroid extract differ from levothyroxine in symptoms, neurocognitive function, or patient preference?
shelves.mesh: Cross-Over Studies · Hormone Replacement Therapy · Humans · Hypothyroidism/drug therapy · Quality of Life · Thyroxine/therapeutic use · Tissue Extracts/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Two randomised double-blind crossover trials agree on the main question and disagree on preference. In 70 patients stable on levothyroxine (Hoang 2013, 16 weeks per treatment), desiccated thyroid extract (DTE) produced no differences in symptoms or neurocognitive measures versus levothyroxine, with about 3 lb lower weight on DTE; yet 48.6% preferred DTE, 18.6% preferred levothyroxine, and 32.9% had no preference. In a 75-patient three-arm crossover (Shakir 2021, 22 weeks per arm: levothyroxine, levothyroxine + liothyronine, DTE), there were again no differences in primary or secondary outcomes as a group and preference did not differ — except that the third of patients most symptomatic on levothyroxine preferred and responded to T3-containing treatment. SPLIT: (the treatment made no difference) for symptoms, cognition, and quality of life in the whole groups, in both trials; patient preference favoured DTE in one trial and not the other, with a symptomatic-subgroup signal that is hypothesis-generating, not proven. DTE preparations are animal-derived, fixed-ratio T4/T3 products that are not FDA-approved as safe and effective in the modern sense and vary by maker — a reason the generic claim cannot be stretched product to product.

cards.headline: Hoang 2013: no symptom or neurocognitive difference between DTE and levothyroxine; 48.6% preferred DTE, weight 3 lb lower
cards.summary: Hoang 2013: no symptom or neurocognitive difference between DTE and levothyroxine; 48.6% preferred DTE, weight 3 lb lower
cards.people: 70 patients aged 18–65 with primary hypothyroidism on a stable levothyroxine dose for 6 months, in a randomised double-blind crossover at a tertiary care centre: DTE or levothyroxine for 16 weeks, then crossed over for 16 weeks. Outcomes: biochemical and neurocognitive tests, symptoms, quality of life, weight, and end-of-study preference.
cards.result: There were no differences in symptoms and neurocognitive measurements between the two therapies. Patients weighed less on DTE (172.9 ± 36.4 lb vs 175.7 ± 37.7 lb; P<.001 — about 3 lb). At study end, 34 patients (48.6%) preferred DTE, 13 (18.6%) preferred levothyroxine, and 23 (32.9%) had no preference; in subgroup analysis, those who preferred DTE lost 4 lb on it and reported significantly better subjective symptoms on the general health questionnaire-12 and thyroid symptom questionnaire (P<.001 for both). The authors conclude DTE did not significantly improve quality of life.
cards.watchOut: Preference was measured after patients had experienced both treatments and may track the small weight difference or unblinding cues rather than symptom relief — the formal symptom and cognition measures, taken blinded, showed no difference. Seventy patients, 16 weeks per arm: too small and short for uncommon harms or long-term outcomes.

cards.headline: Shakir 2021: no group differences among levothyroxine, levothyroxine + liothyronine, and DTE; the most symptomatic third preferred T3-containing treatment
cards.summary: Shakir 2021: no group differences among levothyroxine, levothyroxine + liothyronine, and DTE; the most symptomatic third preferred T3-containing treatment
cards.people: 75 hypothyroid patients in a prospective, randomised, double-blind, crossover study, allocated across three treatment arms — levothyroxine (LT4), LT4 + liothyronine (LT3), and DTE — for 22 weeks each. Primary outcomes: thyroid symptom questionnaire (TSQ-36), general health questionnaire (GHQ-12), Wechsler memory scale (VMS-IV), and Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) scores.
cards.result: Serum TSH remained within the reference range on all three arms. There were no differences in primary or secondary outcomes, except a minor increase in heart rate on DTE. Treatment preference did not differ, and neither cause of hypothyroidism nor the Thr92Ala-DIO2 polymorphism modified outcomes. In subgroup analysis, the third of patients most symptomatic on LT4 showed a strong preference for T3-containing treatment, with improved TSQ-36, GHQ-12, BDI, and visual memory scores.
cards.watchOut: The symptomatic-subgroup finding is a subgroup of a 75-patient trial — the right way to read it is as a reason to run a confirmatory trial in symptomatic patients, not as proof they benefit. Preference here did NOT replicate Hoang's DTE preference, which is why this shelf is split rather than positive on preference.

shelves.title: Bedtime versus morning levothyroxine: better blood levels at night, no difference in quality of life
shelves.question: In primary hypothyroidism, does taking levothyroxine at bedtime improve thyroid hormone levels and quality of life compared with the conventional morning fasting dose?
shelves.mesh: Cross-Over Studies · Drug Administration Schedule · Hormone Replacement Therapy/methods · Humans · Hypothyroidism/drug therapy · Quality of Life · Thyroxine/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: One randomised double-blind crossover trial (105 patients with primary hypothyroidism; 90 completed) compared the same levothyroxine dose taken at bedtime versus in the morning, 3 months each. Bedtime intake lowered TSH by 1.25 mIU/L (95% CI 0.60–1.89; P<.001) and raised free T4 by 0.07 ng/dL (P=.01) and total T3 by 6.5 ng/dL (P=.02) relative to morning intake. But quality of life, fatigue, anxiety/depression, symptoms, lipids, BMI, and heart rate did not differ between timings. SPLIT: POSSIBLE for a modest biochemical advantage to bedtime dosing; (the treatment made no difference) for how patients felt or for lipid levels. The practical reading is that bedtime dosing is a legitimate alternative for patients who cannot manage the morning fast — with levels rechecked after any switch — not that everyone should move their dose.

cards.headline: Bolk 2010: bedtime levothyroxine lowered TSH by 1.25 mIU/L and raised free T4 and total T3 versus morning intake; quality of life unchanged
cards.summary: Bolk 2010: bedtime levothyroxine lowered TSH by 1.25 mIU/L and raised free T4 and total T3 versus morning intake; quality of life unchanged
cards.people: 105 consecutive patients with primary hypothyroidism at Maasstad Hospital Rotterdam, in a randomised double-blind crossover: for 6 months each patient took one capsule in the morning and one at bedtime (one containing levothyroxine, the other placebo), switching the active timing after 3 months; 90 completed and were analysed. Primary outcomes: thyroid hormone levels. Secondary: creatinine, lipids, BMI, heart rate, quality of life.
cards.result: Compared with morning intake, bedtime intake decreased thyrotropin by 1.25 mIU/L (95% CI 0.60–1.89; P<.001), increased free thyroxine by 0.07 ng/dL (0.02–0.13; P=.01), and increased total triiodothyronine by 6.5 ng/dL (0.9–12.1; P=.02). Secondary outcomes, including quality-of-life questionnaires (SF-36, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory, and a symptoms questionnaire), showed no significant changes between morning and bedtime intake; plasma lipid levels also did not change significantly.
cards.watchOut: Single crossover trial; the outcomes that moved are blood levels, not symptoms. A TSH fall of 1.25 mIU/L on the same dose means bedtime dosing effectively increases exposure — switching timing without rechecking levels can overshoot in patients already near the bottom of the TSH range. The trial used a double-dummy capsule routine unlike real-world single-tablet use.
cards.source: Bolk N et al. Effects of evening vs morning levothyroxine intake: a randomized double-blind crossover trial. Arch Intern Med. 2010. PMID: 21149757. Registry ID: ISRCTN17436693 (NTR959), from the record. shelves.title: Selenium in Hashimoto thyroiditis: antibodies fell in one small trial; thyroid function did not change
shelves.question: In autoimmune thyroiditis with high thyroid-peroxidase antibody concentrations, does selenium supplementation lower antibody levels or change thyroid function?
shelves.mesh: Antioxidants/therapeutic use · Autoantibodies · Humans · Selenium/therapeutic use · Thyroiditis, Autoimmune/drug therapy · Thyroiditis, Autoimmune/immunology
shelves.balance: The evidence is a single small trial measuring antibodies, not illness. In 70 women with autoimmune thyroiditis and high antibody levels (Gärtner 2002, blinded and placebo-controlled, 3 months), selenium as sodium selenite 200 μg daily (the specific tested preparation — selenium supplements are not well regulated and forms differ by maker) lowered thyroid peroxidase antibody concentrations to 63.6% of baseline versus 88% on placebo, with complete antibody normalisation in 9 of 36 on selenium versus 2 of 34 on placebo (P=0.01). TSH and free thyroid hormone levels did not change in either group, and no clinical outcome — symptoms, progression to hypothyroidism, or levothyroxine need — was shown to improve. The topic draft could not pin a results record for the large CATALYST trial (protocol only at drafting), so this shelf rests on the 2002 trial alone and must be re-checked for CATALYST results at review. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — an antibody surrogate moving in a small, short trial, with thyroid function unchanged.

cards.headline: Gärtner 2002: selenium lowered TPO antibodies to 63.6% of baseline vs 88% on placebo over 3 months; TSH and free hormones unchanged
cards.summary: Gärtner 2002: selenium lowered TPO antibodies to 63.6% of baseline vs 88% on placebo over 3 months; TSH and free hormones unchanged
cards.people: 70 women (mean age 47.5 years) with autoimmune thyroiditis and TPO and/or thyroglobulin antibodies above 350 IU/ml, randomised into age- and antibody-matched groups: 36 received sodium selenite 200 μg orally daily for 3 months and 34 received placebo; all patients took levothyroxine to keep TSH in the normal range. Primary endpoint: change in TPO antibody concentration.
cards.result: Mean TPO antibody concentration fell to 63.6% of baseline in the selenium group (P=0.013) versus 88% in the placebo group (P=0.95). In the subgroup with TPO antibodies above 1200 IU/ml, the mean reduction was 40% on selenium versus a 10% increase on placebo. Nine selenium patients had completely normalised antibody concentrations versus two on placebo (P=0.01), with normalised thyroid echogenicity on ultrasound in those patients. Mean TSH, free T4, and free T3 were unchanged in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Antibodies are a surrogate: the trial does not show that lowering them prevents hypothyroidism, reduces symptoms, or lowers levothyroxine requirements, and thyroid function itself did not move. Three months, 70 women, one German centre, in a population whose baseline selenium status may not match selenium-replete populations. Selenium has a narrow safety margin at supplement doses — this trial is not a dosing recommendation.
cards.source: Gärtner R et al. Selenium supplementation in patients with autoimmune thyroiditis decreases thyroid peroxidase antibodies concentrations. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2002. PMID: 11932302. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). shelves.title: Iodine in pregnancy and child neurodevelopment: no IQ benefit in mild deficiency (a large null trial)
shelves.question: In mildly iodine-deficient pregnant women, does daily iodine supplementation (200 μg) until delivery improve their children's IQ and executive function?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Child · Child, Preschool · Developmental Disabilities · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gestational Age · Humans · Infant · Intelligence · Intelligence Tests · Iodine · Male · Neuropsychological Tests · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications
shelves.balance: Tested properly, in the population where benefit was most plausible, iodine did not help. In a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in Bangalore, India, and Bangkok, Thailand, 832 mildly iodine-deficient pregnant women (median urinary iodine 131 μg/L) took iodine 200 μg daily or placebo until delivery; 313 children were tested at age 5–6 years. Verbal IQ was 89.5 on iodine versus 90.2 on placebo (difference −0.7, 95% CI −2.9 to 1.5; p=0.77), performance IQ 97.5 versus 99.1 (difference −1.6; p=0.44), and the executive-function composite 90.6 versus 91.5 (difference −0.9; p=0.74) — every point estimate slightly favoured placebo, and adverse events in pregnancy did not differ (24 vs 28 women). This answers mild deficiency in areas where schoolchildren were iodine sufficient; it does not address severe deficiency, where iodine's role is established by other evidence. PROPOSED (the treatment made no difference) — one large trial with clinical (neurodevelopmental) endpoints and confidence intervals that exclude a meaningful IQ gain.

cards.headline: Gowachirapant 2017: iodine 200 μg in pregnancy did not improve child IQ or executive function at age 5–6 years
cards.summary: Gowachirapant 2017: iodine 200 μg in pregnancy did not improve child IQ or executive function at age 5–6 years
cards.people: 832 pregnant women in Bangalore, India, and Bangkok, Thailand, entering at mean gestational age 10.7 weeks with mild iodine deficiency (median urinary iodine concentration 131 μg/L, IQR 81–213), randomised 1:1 to iodine 200 μg orally daily or placebo until delivery (mean compliance 87%). Co-primary outcomes in the children at age 5–6 years: WPPSI-III verbal and performance IQ and the BRIEF-P global executive composite; 313 children were analysed for IQ and 315 for executive function.
cards.result: Verbal IQ: 89.5 (SD 9.8) on iodine versus 90.2 (9.8) on placebo (difference −0.7, 95% CI −2.9 to 1.5; p=0.77). Performance IQ: 97.5 (12.5) versus 99.1 (13.4) (difference −1.6, −4.5 to 1.3; p=0.44). BRIEF-P global executive composite: 90.6 (26.2) versus 91.5 (27.0) (difference −0.9, −6.8 to 5.0; p=0.74). Adverse events during gestation or at delivery were reported by 24 women in the iodine group and 28 in the placebo group, with no difference in frequency. The authors conclude daily iodine supplementation in mildly iodine-deficient pregnant women had no effect on child neurodevelopment at age 5–6 years.
cards.watchOut: Only about 38% of randomised women's children contributed outcome data (313 of 832) — a large loss to follow-up over 5–6 years, though analysis was intention-to-treat with mixed-effects models. Some unmasking occurred at an interim analysis at age 2 years. The setting matters: mild maternal deficiency where schoolchildren were already iodine sufficient — the null does not generalise to severe deficiency.
cards.source: Gowachirapant S et al. Effect of iodine supplementation in pregnant women on child neurodevelopment: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2017. PMID: 29030199. Registry ID: NCT00791466, from the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: no neurodevelopment benefit from iodine supplements in mild deficiency — (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: no neurodevelopment benefit from iodine supplements in mild deficiency — (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 832 pregnant women randomised; 313–315 children assessed at age 5–6 years (Gowachirapant 2017).
cards.result: Verbal IQ difference −0.7 points, performance IQ −1.6 points, executive composite −0.9 points — all non-significant and all numerically favouring placebo. PROPOSED (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: A null in mild deficiency is not a licence to ignore iodine nutrition in pregnancy: severe deficiency causes preventable brain damage, and this trial's mothers were only mildly deficient at entry. The claim carded is narrow — supplements did not raise measured IQ in this population.

shelves.title: Advanced medullary thyroid cancer: vandetanib and cabozantinib each roughly halve-to-quarter the progression hazard vs placebo — progression-free survival, not overall survival
shelves.question: In locally advanced or metastatic medullary thyroid cancer, do the multikinase inhibitors vandetanib or cabozantinib improve outcomes compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Carcinoma, Neuroendocrine · Thyroid Neoplasms · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Protein Kinase Inhibitors · Disease Progression · Disease-Free Survival
shelves.balance: LIKELY: two independent double-blind phase 3 trials, each against placebo, show large progression-free survival gains. In ZETA (331 patients), vandetanib 300 mg/day gave a progression-free survival hazard ratio of 0.46 (95% CI 0.31 to 0.69) — a 54% relative reduction in the progression hazard — with higher objective response and disease control rates. In EXAM (330 patients with documented radiographic progression), cabozantinib 140 mg/day gave a median progression-free survival of 11.2 months vs 4.0 months on placebo (hazard ratio 0.28; 95% CI 0.19 to 0.40 — a 72% relative reduction), with responses in 28% vs 0%. Neither trial demonstrated an overall-survival benefit in its primary report (ZETA survival was immature, hazard ratio 0.89 with a wide interval; EXAM's survival analysis is not reported in the primary paper). Toxicity is substantial: diarrhoea, rash, nausea and hypertension with vandetanib; with cabozantinib, dose reductions in 79% and discontinuation for adverse events in 16%. The benefit claim is delay of progression, not longer life.

cards.headline: ZETA: vandetanib prolongs progression-free survival in advanced medullary thyroid cancer (HR 0.46)
cards.summary: ZETA: vandetanib prolongs progression-free survival in advanced medullary thyroid cancer (HR 0.46)
cards.people: 331 patients with locally advanced or metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma (mean age 52 years; 90% sporadic; 95% metastatic), randomised 2:1 to vandetanib 300 mg/day (231) or placebo (100); median follow-up 24 months.
cards.result: Progression-free survival hazard ratio 0.46 (95% CI 0.31 to 0.69; P < .001) favouring vandetanib — a 54% relative reduction in the hazard of progression. Objective response rate, disease control rate and biochemical response all significantly favoured vandetanib. Overall survival was immature at cutoff (HR 0.89; 95% CI 0.48 to 1.65). Common adverse events on vandetanib vs placebo: diarrhoea 56% vs 26%, rash 45% vs 11%, nausea 33% vs 16%, hypertension 32% vs 5%.
cards.watchOut: Placebo patients could cross to open-label vandetanib on progression, which blurs any later survival comparison. The survival data were immature in this report; the claim this trial supports is delayed progression.
cards.source: Wells SA Jr et al. Vandetanib in patients with locally advanced or metastatic medullary thyroid cancer: a randomized, double-blind phase III trial (ZETA). J Clin Oncol. 2012;30(2):134-141. PMID: 22025146. Registry ID: NCT00410761. cards.headline: EXAM: cabozantinib prolongs progression-free survival in progressive metastatic medullary thyroid cancer (11.2 vs 4.0 months)
cards.summary: EXAM: cabozantinib prolongs progression-free survival in progressive metastatic medullary thyroid cancer (11.2 vs 4.0 months)
cards.people: 330 patients with documented radiographic progression of metastatic medullary thyroid cancer, randomised 2:1 to cabozantinib 140 mg/day or placebo.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival 11.2 months on cabozantinib vs 4.0 months on placebo (hazard ratio 0.28; 95% CI 0.19 to 0.40; P < .001) — a 72% relative reduction in the progression hazard, consistent across age, prior TKI treatment and RET mutation status. Response rate 28% vs 0%. Alive and progression-free at 1 year: 47.3% vs 7.2%. Dose reductions in 79% and dose holds in 65% of cabozantinib patients; adverse events led to discontinuation in 16% vs 8%.
cards.watchOut: The 140 mg dose used here is higher than the 60 mg dose later standard in other cancers, and the dose-reduction rate (79%) reflects that. Overall survival results are not reported in this primary paper, so no survival claim is made.
cards.source: Elisei R et al. Cabozantinib in progressive medullary thyroid cancer (EXAM). J Clin Oncol. 2013;31(29):3639-3646. PMID: 24002501. Registry ID: NCT00704730. cards.headline: Synthesis: two placebo-controlled trials agree — multikinase inhibitors delay progression in advanced medullary thyroid cancer; survival benefit unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: two placebo-controlled trials agree — multikinase inhibitors delay progression in advanced medullary thyroid cancer; survival benefit unproven
cards.people: Synthesis of ZETA (Wells 2012; vandetanib, 331 patients) and EXAM (Elisei 2013; cabozantinib, 330 patients), both double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials in advanced medullary thyroid cancer.
cards.result: Progression-free survival hazard ratios 0.46 (vandetanib) and 0.28 (cabozantinib) — large, concordant effects on progression. Response rates clearly favour treatment (28% vs 0% in EXAM). No overall-survival benefit was demonstrated in either primary report. Toxicity is considerable with both drugs, and cabozantinib at the EXAM dose required dose reduction in four of five patients.
cards.watchOut: Progression-free survival is a delay-of-progression claim, not a longer-life claim; crossover in ZETA and the absence of reported survival results in EXAM's primary paper leave the survival question open. First-line choice between these agents and the RET-selective inhibitor selpercatinib (in RET-mutant disease) is answered head-to-head on the selpercatinib shelf.

shelves.title: RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer: selpercatinib beats cabozantinib/vandetanib head-to-head — progression-free survival HR 0.28, and far better tolerated
shelves.question: In advanced RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer, is the selective RET inhibitor selpercatinib better than the multikinase inhibitors cabozantinib or vandetanib as first-line treatment?
shelves.mesh: Thyroid Neoplasms · Carcinoma, Neuroendocrine · Proto-Oncogene Proteins c-ret · Antineoplastic Agents · Disease Progression · Humans
shelves.balance: LIKELY (single trial — developer's personal ruling requested under the outstanding-single rule): in the one randomised phase 3 trial (LIBRETTO-531, 291 patients with progressive RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer), first-line selpercatinib beat physician's choice of cabozantinib or vandetanib on progression-free survival — hazard ratio 0.28 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.48), a 72% relative reduction in the hazard of progression or death; median not reached vs 16.8 months at a median follow-up of only 12 months, with 12-month progression-free survival 86.8% vs 65.7% in absolute terms. Overall response was 69.4% vs 38.8%. Selpercatinib was also easier to stay on: dose reductions 38.9% vs 77.3% and discontinuation for adverse events 4.7% vs 26.8%. Overall survival cannot be judged yet — follow-up is short and control patients could cross over to selpercatinib at progression. One trial only, an industry-funded interim analysis: the effect is large and the comparison is against active drugs, not placebo, but replication does not exist.

cards.headline: LIBRETTO-531: selpercatinib superior to cabozantinib or vandetanib in RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer (PFS HR 0.28)
cards.summary: LIBRETTO-531: selpercatinib superior to cabozantinib or vandetanib in RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer (PFS HR 0.28)
cards.people: 291 patients with advanced RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer and documented progression within 14 months before enrolment, randomised to first-line selpercatinib or physician's choice of cabozantinib or vandetanib; median follow-up 12 months; blinded independent central review of the primary end point.
cards.result: Progression-free survival: hazard ratio 0.28 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.48; P < .001) — a 72% relative reduction in the hazard of progression or death; median not reached on selpercatinib vs 16.8 months (95% CI 12.2 to 25.1) on control; 12-month progression-free survival 86.8% vs 65.7%. Treatment failure-free survival hazard ratio 0.25 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.42). Overall response 69.4% vs 38.8%. Dose reduction for adverse events 38.9% vs 77.3%; discontinuation 4.7% vs 26.8%.
cards.watchOut: Protocol-specified INTERIM efficacy analysis at a median follow-up of 12 months; crossover to selpercatinib was permitted at progression, so an overall-survival difference may never be cleanly measurable. Funded by the manufacturer (Loxo Oncology/Eli Lilly). Applies only to RET-mutant disease — the mutation must be documented.
cards.source: Hadoux J et al. Phase 3 Trial of Selpercatinib in Advanced RET-Mutant Medullary Thyroid Cancer (LIBRETTO-531). N Engl J Med. 2023;389(20):1851-1861. PMID: 37870969. shelves.title: Radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer after lenvatinib/sorafenib: cabozantinib prolongs progression-free survival (HR 0.22) — one interim trial analysis
shelves.question: In radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer that has progressed after lenvatinib or sorafenib, does cabozantinib improve outcomes compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Thyroid Neoplasms · Progression-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Drug Resistance, Neoplasm · Humans
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (single trial — developer's personal ruling requested): in the one randomised trial (COSMIC-311, 187 patients with radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer who had progressed on lenvatinib and/or sorafenib, a population with no standard option), cabozantinib 60 mg/day prolonged progression-free survival vs placebo — hazard ratio 0.22 (96% CI 0.13 to 0.36), a 78% relative reduction in the progression hazard; median not reached vs 1.9 months at a preplanned INTERIM analysis with median follow-up of 6.2 months. The co-primary objective-response end point formally missed its prespecified significance level (15% vs 0%; P = 0.028 against a required alpha of 0.01). Toxicity was heavy: grade 3-4 adverse events in 57% vs 26%, and serious treatment-related events in 16% vs 2%, though no treatment-related deaths. Placebo patients could cross over at progression, so overall survival will be hard to read. One interim analysis of one trial, against placebo, in a no-option population: a real progression benefit is probable, its size and durability not yet settled.

cards.headline: COSMIC-311: cabozantinib prolongs progression-free survival after VEGFR therapy in radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer (HR 0.22)
cards.summary: COSMIC-311: cabozantinib prolongs progression-free survival after VEGFR therapy in radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer (HR 0.22)
cards.people: 187 patients aged 16+ with radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer (papillary, follicular and variants), ECOG 0-1, previously treated with lenvatinib or sorafenib (up to two prior VEGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors) with progression during or after treatment; randomised 2:1 to cabozantinib 60 mg/day (125) or placebo (62) at 164 clinics in 25 countries; blinded independent radiology review.
cards.result: Progression-free survival (interim, intention-to-treat): hazard ratio 0.22 (96% CI 0.13 to 0.36; P < .0001) — a 78% relative reduction in the progression hazard; median not reached (96% CI 5.7 to not estimable) vs 1.9 months on placebo, at median follow-up 6.2 months. Objective response in the first 100 randomised patients: 15% vs 0% (P = 0.028), which did not meet the prespecified alpha of 0.01. Grade 3-4 adverse events 57% vs 26% (palmar-plantar erythrodysaesthesia 10% vs 0%, hypertension 9% vs 3%, fatigue 8% vs 0%); serious treatment-related adverse events 16% vs 2%; no treatment-related deaths.
cards.watchOut: Preplanned INTERIM progression-free survival analysis with short follow-up (median 6.2 months), and the response-rate co-primary end point missed its prespecified significance threshold — the honest summary is a large progression benefit whose response and survival value are unproven. Crossover at progression was allowed. First-line kinase-inhibitor evidence (lenvatinib, sorafenib) lives on shelf #741; this shelf is the after-they-fail question.
cards.source: Brose MS et al. Cabozantinib for radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer (COSMIC-311): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet Oncol. 2021;22(8):1126-1138. PMID: 34237250. Registry ID: NCT03690388. shelves.title: BRAF V600E anaplastic thyroid cancer: dabrafenib + trametinib responded in 69% (11 of 16) — single-arm evidence in a near-uniformly fatal cancer
shelves.question: In BRAF V600E-mutated anaplastic thyroid cancer, does dabrafenib plus trametinib produce meaningful tumour responses?
shelves.mesh: Thyroid Carcinoma, Anaplastic · Proto-Oncogene Proteins B-raf · Mutation · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Humans
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (single-arm evidence — Tier C, developer's personal ruling required): anaplastic thyroid cancer is among the most lethal solid tumours, historically killing most patients within months, and the BRAF V600E-mutant subset is the one place targeted therapy has changed the picture. In the ROAR basket trial's anaplastic cohort — 16 evaluable patients, all previously treated with radiation and/or surgery and six with prior systemic therapy — dabrafenib plus trametinib produced a confirmed overall response rate of 69% (11 of 16; 95% CI 41% to 89%), with seven responses ongoing at the report; 12-month estimates were 79% for progression-free survival and 80% for overall survival, against a historical expectation of roughly 20-40% alive at one year with conventional care. There is NO control group, the cohort is 16 patients, and response rate is the primary evidence — this is dramatic-signal evidence in an orphan disease, not proof of the size a randomised trial would give. Common adverse events across the basket's safety population were fatigue (38%), fever (37%) and nausea (35%). Benefit, if real at this scale, applies only to the BRAF V600E-mutant minority (about a quarter to a half of anaplastic cancers) — mutation testing is the gate.

cards.headline: ROAR (anaplastic cohort): dabrafenib + trametinib responses in 11 of 16 BRAF V600E-mutant anaplastic thyroid cancers
cards.summary: ROAR (anaplastic cohort): dabrafenib + trametinib responses in 11 of 16 BRAF V600E-mutant anaplastic thyroid cancers
cards.people: 16 evaluable patients with BRAF V600E-mutated locally advanced or metastatic anaplastic thyroid cancer in the phase II open-label ROAR basket trial; all had prior radiation and/or surgery, six had prior systemic therapy; median follow-up 47 weeks. Safety population: 100 patients across seven rare-tumour histologies in the basket.
cards.result: Confirmed overall response rate 69% (11 of 16; 95% CI 41% to 89%), with 7 responses ongoing. Median duration of response, progression-free survival and overall survival not reached; 12-month estimates: duration of response 90%, progression-free survival 79%, overall survival 80%. Common adverse events (basket safety population): fatigue 38%, pyrexia 37%, nausea 35%; no new safety signals.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm, 16 patients, no comparator: the 80% 12-month survival estimate is compared in the balance against historical experience, not against a randomised control, and the confidence interval is wide. The shelf's claim is a strong response signal in a disease with no effective standard therapy — the reason it sits at POSSIBLE rather than MAYBE is the size of the signal in a near-uniformly fatal cancer; the reason it is not higher is the design.
cards.source: Subbiah V et al. Dabrafenib and Trametinib Treatment in Patients With Locally Advanced or Metastatic BRAF V600-Mutant Anaplastic Thyroid Cancer. J Clin Oncol. 2018;36(1):7-13. single-arm phase ii cohort (basket trial) 16 evaluable patients with braf v600e-mutated locally advanced or metastatic anaplastic thyroid cancer in the phase ii open-label roar basket trial; all had prior radiation and/or surgery, six had prior systemic therapy; median follow-up 47 weeks. safety population: 100 patients across seven rare-tumour histologies in the basket. confirmed overall response rate 69% (11 of 16; 95% ci 41% to 89%), with 7 responses ongoing. median duration of response, progression-free survival and overall survival not reached; 12-month estimates: duration of response 90%, progression-free survival 79%, overall survival 80%. common adverse events (basket safety population): fatigue 38%, pyrexia 37%, nausea 35%; no new safety signals. single-arm, 16 patients, no comparator: the 80% 12-month survival estimate is compared in the balance against historical experience, not against a randomised control, and the confidence interval is wide. the shelf's claim is a strong response signal in a disease with no effective standard therapy — the reason it sits at possible rather than maybe is the size of the signal in a near-uniformly fatal cancer; the reason it is not higher is the design. subbiah v et al. dabrafenib and trametinib treatment in patients with locally advanced or metastatic braf v600-mutant anaplastic thyroid cancer. j clin oncol. 2018;36(1):7-13. pmid: 29072975. registry id: nct02034110. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · antineoplastic combined chemotherapy protocols · disease-free survival · fatigue · female · fever · humans · imidazoles · male · middle aged · mutation* · nausea · neoplasm metastasis · oximes · proto-oncogene proteins b-raf · pyridones · pyrimidinones · thyroid carcinoma, anaplastic · young adult

shelves.title: Subacute thyroiditis: one week of prednisone did the work of six — same efficacy and recurrence, lower blood pressure and parathyroid hormone at withdrawal
shelves.question: In subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis, does a short prednisone course relieve pain and inflammation as durably as a conventional six-week taper, with fewer steroid adverse effects?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Humans · Middle Aged · Prednisone/adverse effects · Prospective Studies · Single-Blind Method · Thyroiditis, Subacute/drug therapy* · Thyroxine · Triiodothyronine · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the short course. In the only randomised trial of treatment duration (Duan L et al., PMID: 33471681), 50 patients with moderate-to-severe subacute thyroiditis completed either 30 mg/day prednisone for 1 week followed by a week of a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug, or a conventional 6-week prednisone course: efficacy and recurrence rates did not differ significantly between groups at withdrawal (P = .65), thyroid function did not differ at weeks 6, 12 or 24, and the short-course group had lower parathyroid hormone (28.8 versus 38.9 pg/mL; P = .011) and lower systolic blood pressure (113.9 versus 122.4 mm Hg; P = .023) at discontinuation, consistent with less steroid exposure. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one week of prednisone appears to relieve moderate-to-severe subacute thyroiditis as durably as six weeks, with fewer steroid effects — on a single small single-blind trial.

cards.headline: Duan 2020 RCT: 1 week of prednisone (then a week of an anti-inflammatory) matched a 6-week course — no significant difference in efficacy or recurrence (P = .65)
cards.summary: Duan 2020 RCT: 1 week of prednisone (then a week of an anti-inflammatory) matched a 6-week course — no significant difference in efficacy or recurrence (P = .65)
cards.people: 96 patients aged 18–70 with subacute thyroiditis were screened at a single hospital (2013–2014); 52 with moderate-to-severe symptoms were randomised single-blind to prednisone 30 mg/day for 1 week followed by 1 week of a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug, or to conventional 6-week prednisone therapy, and 50 completed the 24-week study.
cards.result: Efficacy and recurrence rates were not significantly different between groups at treatment withdrawal (P = .65). At discontinuation, parathyroid hormone was lower in the short-course group (28.8 versus 38.9 pg/mL; P = .011) and systolic blood pressure was lower (113.9 versus 122.4 mm Hg; P = .023). There were no significant intergroup differences in other post-withdrawal adverse-effect parameters, and thyroid function did not differ at weeks 6, 12 and 24. The authors conclude short-term prednisone showed fewer glucocorticoid side effects with similar efficacy and recurrence, and may be an alternative strategy for moderate-to-severe symptoms.
cards.watchOut: Small (50 completers), single-centre and single-blind, and the abstract reports the efficacy/recurrence comparison only as a P value (.65) without the underlying rates — a null in 50 patients cannot exclude a clinically important difference in recurrence. The short arm also received a week of an anti-inflammatory drug after prednisone, so this is a short-course strategy, not prednisone alone for one week.
cards.source: Duan et al. Short-Term Versus 6-Week Prednisone In The Treatment Of Subacute Thyroiditis: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Endocrine practice : official journal of the American College of Endocrinology and the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists. 2020. PMID: 33471681. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one small trial says a week is enough — equal relief and recurrence, measurably less steroid footprint
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small trial says a week is enough — equal relief and recurrence, measurably less steroid footprint
cards.people: One randomised trial, 50 completers with moderate-to-severe subacute thyroiditis, followed for 24 weeks — the entire randomised record on prednisone duration for this condition.
cards.result: Efficacy and recurrence at withdrawal: no significant difference (P = .65). Steroid-exposure markers at discontinuation favoured the short course: parathyroid hormone 28.8 versus 38.9 pg/mL (P = .011); systolic blood pressure 113.9 versus 122.4 mm Hg (P = .023). Thyroid function at weeks 6, 12 and 24: no differences. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Subacute thyroiditis is self-limiting, so both arms were racing a disease that resolves on its own; the question the trial answers is symptom control with less steroid, not cure. Patients with mild symptoms (managed without steroids at all) and patients who relapse repeatedly are outside this evidence. Tier C is set because the shelf rests on one small trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Duan L et al. Endocrine practice. 2020 (PMID: 33471681).

shelves.title: Amiodarone thyrotoxicosis type 2: prednisone worked in 100% — perchlorate alone failed in 29% until prednisone was added, and amiodarone could continue
shelves.question: In amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis type 2, does prednisone restore euthyroidism faster than methimazole or combination therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Amiodarone/adverse effects · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents/adverse effects · Antithyroid Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Endocrine Disruptors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Feasibility Studies · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Perchlorates/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Recurrence · Thyroid Function Tests · Thyrotoxicosis/chemically induced/classification/therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for prednisone as the preferred treatment. In the randomised multicentre trial (Eskes SA et al., PMID: 22130792), 36 patients with amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis type 2 all continued amiodarone and received methimazole, and were randomised to prednisone alone, perchlorate alone, or both: initial therapy restored euthyroidism (thyroid-stimulating hormone at least 0.4 mU/liter) in 100% on prednisone, 71% on perchlorate alone and 100% on the combination (P = 0.03), and the 29% who failed on perchlorate alone became euthyroid only after prednisone was added. Times to euthyroidism did not differ significantly between groups, recurrent thyrotoxicosis occurred in 8.3%, and euthyroidism was ultimately reached in all patients despite continuing amiodarone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prednisone restores euthyroidism reliably in type 2 disease; perchlorate adds nothing and fails alone in nearly a third — but note every patient also received methimazole, so this is not prednisone versus methimazole as the question's wording might suggest.

cards.headline: Eskes 2012 RCT: prednisone restored euthyroidism in 100% versus 71% for perchlorate alone (P = 0.03) — and every perchlorate failure was rescued by adding prednisone
cards.summary: Eskes 2012 RCT: prednisone restored euthyroidism in 100% versus 71% for perchlorate alone (P = 0.03) — and every perchlorate failure was rescued by adding prednisone
cards.people: 36 patients with amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis type 2 randomised across 10 Dutch hospitals to prednisone 30 mg/day (n = 12), sodium perchlorate 500 mg twice daily (n = 14), or prednisone plus perchlorate (n = 10); all patients continued amiodarone and all also received methimazole 30 mg/day, with 2 years of follow-up.
cards.result: Initial therapy was efficacious (thyroid-stimulating hormone at least 0.4 mU/liter while continuing amiodarone) in 100% of the prednisone group, 71% of the perchlorate group and 100% of the combination group (P = 0.03); the 29% failures on perchlorate alone became euthyroid after prednisone was added. Time to reach a thyroid-stimulating hormone of 0.4 mU/liter or higher did not differ significantly (median 8 weeks [range 4–20] prednisone, 14 weeks [4–32] perchlorate, 12 weeks [4–28] combination), nor did time to free thyroxine of 25 pmol/liter or below (4, 12 and 8 weeks respectively). Recurrent thyrotoxicosis occurred in 8.3%. Euthyroidism was reached in all patients despite continuation of amiodarone.
cards.watchOut: Very small groups (10–14 per arm), so the time-to-euthyroidism comparisons are imprecise and the medians numerically favour prednisone without reaching significance. Crucially, all arms received methimazole 30 mg/day — the trial compares prednisone against perchlorate as the added agent on a methimazole background, not prednisone against methimazole head-to-head, and mixed type 1/type 2 cases in practice may behave differently from the classified type 2 patients enrolled.
cards.source: Eskes et al. Treatment of amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis type 2: a randomized clinical trial. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2012. PMID: 22130792. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: prednisone is the reliable arm — 100% initial success, with perchlorate alone failing in 29% until prednisone was added
cards.summary: Synthesis: prednisone is the reliable arm — 100% initial success, with perchlorate alone failing in 29% until prednisone was added
cards.people: One randomised multicentre trial, 36 patients with amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis type 2, all continuing amiodarone and receiving background methimazole, followed for 2 years.
cards.result: Initial efficacy: 100% (prednisone), 71% (perchlorate alone), 100% (combination); P = 0.03. Median time to thyroid-stimulating hormone at least 0.4 mU/liter: 8 versus 14 versus 12 weeks, not significantly different. Recurrence: 8.3%. Eventual euthyroidism on continued amiodarone: 100% of patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for prednisone as the preferred modality.
cards.watchOut: Type 2 disease is described in the record itself as self-limiting, so part of every arm's success is the disease settling; the trial's contribution is comparative reliability, not proof that treatment is always required. No randomised evidence here addresses stopping amiodarone, thyroidectomy, or type 1 disease. Tier C is set because the shelf rests on one 36-patient trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Eskes SA et al. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2012 (PMID: 22130792).

shelves.title: Thyroid cancer ablation: low-dose radioiodine with thyrotropin alfa matched high-dose treatment — 85.0% versus 88.9% success, with fewer harms and shorter stays
shelves.question: In low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer after thyroidectomy, does low-dose radioiodine ablation with thyrotropin alfa achieve remnant ablation as reliably as high-dose radioiodine or hormone withdrawal?
shelves.mesh: Ablation Techniques/adverse effects/psychology · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Combined Modality Therapy · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hypothyroidism/etiology · Iodine Radioisotopes/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Radiotherapy Dosage · Thyroid Hormones/blood/therapeutic use · Thyroid Neoplasms/drug therapy/radiotherapy/surgery · Thyroidectomy · Thyrotropin Alfa/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for the low-dose, thyrotropin alfa strategy. In HiLo (Mallick U et al., PMID: 22551128), 438 patients with differentiated thyroid cancer were randomised in a two-by-two design to low-dose (1.1 GBq) or high-dose (3.7 GBq) radioiodine, each after thyrotropin alfa or thyroid hormone withdrawal: ablation success at 6–9 months was 85.0% with low dose versus 88.9% with high dose, and 87.1% with thyrotropin alfa versus 86.7% with withdrawal, with all 95% confidence intervals for the differences within the ±10 percentage point noninferiority margin; low-dose plus thyrotropin alfa succeeded in 84.3% versus 87.6% for high-dose plus withdrawal. The low-dose strategy cost less harm: adverse events in 21% versus 33% (P = 0.007) and hospitalisation for at least 3 days in 13.0% versus 36.3% (P < 0.001). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): low-dose radioiodine with thyrotropin alfa ablates the remnant as reliably as high-dose treatment, with fewer adverse events and shorter stays.

cards.headline: HiLo 2012: ablation success 85.0% low-dose versus 88.9% high-dose radioiodine, and 87.1% with thyrotropin alfa versus 86.7% with hormone withdrawal — noninferior on both comparisons
cards.summary: HiLo 2012: ablation success 85.0% low-dose versus 88.9% high-dose radioiodine, and 87.1% with thyrotropin alfa versus 86.7% with hormone withdrawal — noninferior on both comparisons
cards.people: 438 patients aged 16–80 with differentiated thyroid cancer, tumour stage T1 to T3 with possible spread to nearby lymph nodes but no distant metastasis, randomised at 29 UK centres in a two-by-two factorial design to low-dose (1.1 GBq [30 mCi]) or high-dose (3.7 GBq [100 mCi]) radioiodine, each combined with thyrotropin alfa or thyroid hormone withdrawal before ablation; data were analysable for 421 patients, with ablation success assessed at 6 to 9 months.
cards.result: Ablation success rates were 85.0% (low-dose) versus 88.9% (high-dose) and 87.1% (thyrotropin alfa) versus 86.7% (thyroid hormone withdrawal); all 95% confidence intervals for the differences lay within ±10 percentage points, indicating noninferiority. Low-dose radioiodine plus thyrotropin alfa achieved 84.3%, versus 87.6% for high-dose plus withdrawal and 90.2% for high-dose plus thyrotropin alfa. More high-dose than low-dose patients were hospitalised for at least 3 days (36.3% versus 13.0%; P < 0.001). Adverse events occurred in 21% (low-dose) versus 33% (high-dose) (P = 0.007) and in 23% (thyrotropin alfa) versus 30% (withdrawal) (P = 0.11).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority was declared against a generous ±10 percentage point margin on a 6–9 month ablation-success endpoint — the trial was not powered for recurrence or survival, which take years to declare themselves in this cancer, and it enrolled T1–T3 patients without distant metastases, so it says nothing about high-risk or metastatic disease where higher activities may still be chosen.
cards.source: Mallick et al. Ablation with low-dose radioiodine and thyrotropin alfa in thyroid cancer. The New England journal of medicine. 2012. PMID: 22551128. Registry ID: NCT00415233. shelves.title: Watching a tiny thyroid cancer: 1,235 patients observed, no distant spread and no cancer deaths — growth in about 5% and nodal spread in about 2% by five years
shelves.question: In papillary thyroid microcarcinoma, does active surveillance avoid surgery without excess progression or metastasis compared with immediate surgery, in long-term cohort follow-up?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Carcinoma, Papillary/diagnostic imaging/pathology · Disease Progression · Female · Humans · Lymphatic Metastasis · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/surgery · Thyroid Gland/surgery · Thyroid Neoplasms/diagnostic imaging/pathology · Thyroidectomy · Ultrasonography
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for active surveillance in selected low-risk patients, with an age gradient. In the long-term Kuma Hospital cohort (Ito Y et al., PMID: 24001104), 1,235 patients with low-risk papillary microcarcinoma chose observation without immediate surgery and were followed for a mean 75 months: none developed distant metastasis and none died of thyroid cancer, progression was least frequent in patients aged 60 and over and most frequent in those under 40 (young age an independent predictor on multivariate analysis), and of 191 patients who later had surgery, none died of the cancer and only one recurred, in the residual thyroid. A systematic review and meta-analysis of active surveillance for small papillary thyroid cancer (Cho SJ et al., PMID: 31368412) pooled a 5-year size-enlargement proportion of 5.3% (95% CI 4.4% to 6.4%) and 5-year lymph-node metastasis of 1.6% (1.1% to 2.4%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): surveillance avoids surgery in most patients without excess metastasis or death in these cohorts — but there is no randomised comparison with immediate surgery, so the counterfactual rests on the cancers' indolent behaviour.

cards.headline: Ito 2014 cohort (1,235 patients, mean 75 months): no distant metastases and no thyroid-cancer deaths on observation — progression commonest under 40, rarest at 60 and over
cards.summary: Ito 2014 cohort (1,235 patients, mean 75 months): no distant metastases and no thyroid-cancer deaths on observation — progression commonest under 40, rarest at 60 and over
cards.people: 1,235 patients with low-risk papillary thyroid microcarcinoma diagnosed between 1993 and 2011 who chose observation without immediate surgery, followed periodically with ultrasound for 18–227 months (average 75 months), divided by age at the start of observation into young (under 40), middle-aged (40–59) and old (60 and over) groups; progression was defined as size enlargement, novel lymph-node metastasis, or progression to clinical disease (tumour reaching 12 mm or new nodal metastasis).
cards.result: The proportion of patients with progression was lowest in the old group and highest in the young group, and on multivariate analysis young age was an independent predictor of progression. None of the 1,235 patients showed distant metastasis or died of papillary thyroid cancer during observation. Only 51 patients (4%) received thyrotropin suppression, by physician preference, and all but one remained clinically stable. In total 191 patients underwent surgery after observation for various reasons; none showed recurrence except one in the residual thyroid, and none died of thyroid cancer after surgery.
cards.watchOut: There is no immediate-surgery comparison group in this record — patients chose observation, so selection (low-risk tumours, motivated patients, an expert centre with disciplined ultrasound follow-up) is built in, and the abstract reports the age gradient qualitatively without per-group progression percentages. Delayed surgery outcomes are reassuring but apply to the minority who crossed over, often for reasons other than progression.
cards.source: Ito et al. Patient age is significantly related to the progression of papillary microcarcinoma of the thyroid under observation. Thyroid : official journal of the American Thyroid Association. 2014. PMID: 24001104. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cho 2019 meta-analysis: on active surveillance, 5.3% had size enlargement of at least 3 mm and 1.6% developed lymph-node metastasis by 5 years
cards.summary: Cho 2019 meta-analysis: on active surveillance, 5.3% had size enlargement of at least 3 mm and 1.6% developed lymph-node metastasis by 5 years
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies of patients followed with active surveillance for papillary thyroid cancer, searched to 5 January 2019, with pooled proportions for size enlargement of 3 mm or more and for lymph-node metastasis at a 5-year follow-up period, calculated with an inverse-variance weighting model.
cards.result: The pooled proportion of size enlargement at 5 years was 5.3% (95% CI 4.4% to 6.4%), and the pooled proportion of lymph-node metastasis at 5 years was 1.6% (95% CI 1.1% to 2.4%). In many subjects who underwent delayed operations, the reasons for surgery were often other than size enlargement or lymph-node metastasis. The authors conclude active surveillance is effective for the management of small papillary thyroid cancer, with low proportions of enlargement or nodal metastasis at 5 years.
cards.watchOut: Pooled single-arm proportions from observational cohorts, mostly from a small number of experienced programmes — they describe what happens on surveillance, not what surgery would have prevented, and five years is early in the life of a cancer that can declare itself over decades. A substantial share of delayed operations happen for patient or clinician preference rather than progression, which is part of the real cost of the strategy.
cards.source: Cho et al. Active Surveillance for Small Papillary Thyroid Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Thyroid : official journal of the American Thyroid Association. 2019. PMID: 31368412. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: surveillance holds the line — about 1 in 20 tumours grows and about 1 in 60 spreads to nodes by five years, with no cancer deaths in 1,235 observed patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: surveillance holds the line — about 1 in 20 tumours grows and about 1 in 60 spreads to nodes by five years, with no cancer deaths in 1,235 observed patients
cards.people: One 1,235-patient prospective observation cohort with mean 75 months of follow-up (Ito 2014) and one meta-analysis of active-surveillance cohorts (Cho 2019).
cards.result: Distant metastasis on observation: none in 1,235 patients. Thyroid-cancer deaths on observation: none. Five-year size enlargement: pooled 5.3% (95% CI 4.4% to 6.4%). Five-year lymph-node metastasis: pooled 1.6% (1.1% to 2.4%). Progression risk is age-graded: highest under 40, lowest at 60 and over. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: No randomised trial of surveillance versus immediate surgery exists in these records, so 'without excess progression' is inferred from the absence of distant spread and death in selected cohorts, not measured against a surgical control. Younger patients — who have the longest horizon and the highest progression rates — are exactly where the inference is weakest. Tier C is set because all evidence is observational.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ito Y et al. Thyroid. 2014 (PMID: 24001104); Cho SJ et al. Thyroid. 2019 (PMID: 31368412).

shelves.title: Asymptomatic hyperparathyroidism: surgery builds bone (+3.5% at the spine) but randomised trials show no gain in how patients feel, fractures or stones
shelves.question: In asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism, does parathyroidectomy improve bone density and quality of life compared with medical observation?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Pressure/physiology · Bone Density · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hyperparathyroidism, Primary/psychology/surgery/therapy · Kidney Function Tests · Longitudinal Studies · Male · Middle Aged · Parathyroidectomy* · Prognosis · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the evidence splits by outcome. For bone: in the randomised trial (Bollerslev J et al., PMID: 17284629), areal bone mineral density increased in the 191 patients randomised to parathyroidectomy while it remained stable on medical observation, with calcium and parathyroid hormone normalising after surgery; a meta-analysis of four randomised trials (Anagnostis P et al., PMID: 33074457) quantified gains of 3.55% at the lumbar spine (95% CI 1.81% to 5.29%) and 3.44% at the total hip (1.39% to 5.49%) versus surveillance. For how patients feel and fare: the same trial found no clinically significant change in quality of life (SF-36) or psychological symptoms in either group despite patients starting below healthy controls, and no change in kidney function or blood pressure; the meta-analysis found no difference in fracture risk, nephrolithiasis or quality-of-life indices except general health. PROPOSED SPLIT: parathyroidectomy improves bone density and normalises calcium, but randomised evidence does not show it improves quality of life, fractures, kidney stones or kidney function in asymptomatic patients.

cards.headline: Bollerslev 2007 RCT: surgery raised bone density and normalised calcium — but quality of life and psychological symptoms did not improve in either group
cards.summary: Bollerslev 2007 RCT: surgery raised bone density and normalised calcium — but quality of life and psychological symptoms did not improve in either group
cards.people: 191 patients (26 men) with asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism, mean age 64.2 ± 7.4 years, randomised to parathyroidectomy (baseline serum calcium 2.70 ± 0.08 mmol/liter) or medical observation (2.69 ± 0.08 mmol/liter); baseline and 1-year (n = 119) and 2-year (n = 99) data are reported for those who had completed follow-up.
cards.result: At baseline, patients had significantly lower quality of life (SF-36) and more psychological symptoms than age- and sex-matched healthy subjects. The groups were similar at baseline and no clinically significant changes in these parameters were seen during observation. Calcium and parathyroid hormone normalised after surgery. Areal bone mineral density increased in the surgery group and remained stable in the observation group. No change in kidney function (creatinine) or blood pressure was observed longitudinally or between groups. The authors conclude no benefit of operative treatment over medical observation was found on quality-of-life measures so far.
cards.watchOut: Only 99 of 191 randomised patients contribute 2-year data in this report, quality-of-life instruments may be insensitive to the vague symptoms patients attribute to hyperparathyroidism, and two years cannot answer the fracture question. The bone-density result is reported qualitatively in the abstract (increased versus stable) without the size of the gain — the quantified estimate comes from the meta-analysis card.
cards.source: Bollerslev et al. Medical observation, compared with parathyroidectomy, for asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism: a prospective, randomized trial. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2007. PMID: 17284629. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Anagnostis 2021 meta-analysis of 4 RCTs: parathyroidectomy raised spine BMD by 3.55% and hip BMD by 3.44% — no difference in fractures, stones or quality of life
cards.summary: Anagnostis 2021 meta-analysis of 4 RCTs: parathyroidectomy raised spine BMD by 3.55% and hip BMD by 3.44% — no difference in fractures, stones or quality of life
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Anagnostis 2021)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials comparing parathyroidectomy with conservative management (active surveillance) in mild asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism, searched to 23 February 2020; four studies were included in the quantitative synthesis.
cards.result: There was no difference in fracture risk between parathyroidectomy and active surveillance. The surgery group showed higher bone mineral density (mean difference 3.55% at the lumbar spine, 95% CI 1.81% to 5.29%; and 3.44% at the total hip, 95% CI 1.39% to 5.49%; no difference at femoral neck or forearm) and lower calcium concentrations (mean difference −13.26%, 95% CI −19.43% to −7.10%). No difference was observed for nephrolithiasis or quality-of-life indices, except general health, which was higher in the surgery group. The authors conclude surgery increases bone density and reduces calcium, but superiority over surveillance for fractures, stones and quality of life cannot be supported by current data.
cards.watchOut: Four small trials with short horizons: the fracture comparison is underpowered rather than proven equal, and bone density is a surrogate — a 3.5% density gain is real but its conversion into fewer fractures in this mild population is assumed, not shown. Quality-of-life pooling mixes instruments and timepoints.
cards.source: Anagnostis et al. Efficacy of parathyroidectomy compared with active surveillance in patients with mild asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized-controlled studies. Journal of endocrinological investigation. 2021. PMID: 33074457. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — bones and calcium improve with surgery; symptoms, fractures, stones and kidneys do not measurably change
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — bones and calcium improve with surgery; symptoms, fractures, stones and kidneys do not measurably change
cards.people: One 191-patient randomised trial with 2-year reporting (Bollerslev 2007) within a four-trial meta-analysis of parathyroidectomy versus surveillance in mild asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism (Anagnostis 2021).
cards.result: Bone mineral density: +3.55% lumbar spine and +3.44% total hip versus surveillance (meta-analysis); increased versus stable in the anchor trial. Serum calcium: normalised after surgery; pooled mean difference −13.26%. Quality of life and psychological symptoms: no clinically significant benefit. Fractures, nephrolithiasis, kidney function, blood pressure: no demonstrated differences. PROPOSED SPLIT — benefit for bone density and calcium; no shown benefit for symptoms or hard outcomes.
cards.watchOut: A SPLIT stamp must not be read as 'surgery is pointless': patients who meet surgical criteria for other reasons (marked hypercalcaemia, stones, low bone density for age) sit outside this mild asymptomatic population, and surveillance commits patients to indefinite monitoring with crossover when criteria are met. Tier C is set because the trials are few, small and short for the outcomes that matter most.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bollerslev J et al. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2007 (PMID: 17284629); Anagnostis P et al. Journal of endocrinological investigation. 2021 (PMID: 33074457).

shelves.title: Cancer hypercalcaemia that bisphosphonates could not move: denosumab responded in 64% by day 10, with responses lasting a median 104 days
shelves.question: In hypercalcaemia of malignancy refractory to bisphosphonates, does denosumab lower corrected serum calcium compared with continuing standard care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Bone Density Conservation Agents/administration & dosage · Bone Resorption/drug therapy/etiology · Denosumab · Diphosphonates/administration & dosage · Female · Gastrointestinal Diseases/chemically induced · Humans · Hypercalcemia/drug therapy/etiology · Hypophosphatemia/chemically induced · Internationality · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms/complications · RANK Ligand/antagonists & inhibitors · Serum Albumin/metabolism · Therapeutics · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single-arm international study (Hu MI et al., PMID: 24915117), 33 patients whose albumin-corrected serum calcium remained above 12.5 mg/dL despite intravenous bisphosphonates given 7–30 days before screening received denosumab 120 mg on days 1, 8, 15 and 29 and then every 4 weeks: by day 10, 64% (21 patients) had responded (corrected calcium at most 11.5 mg/dL) and 12 patients (reported as 33% in the record) reached at most 10.8 mg/dL; over the study, 70% responded and 64% reached at most 10.8 mg/dL, with an estimated median response duration of 104 days. The commonest serious adverse events were worsening hypercalcaemia (15%) and dyspnoea (9%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): denosumab lowers calcium in about two thirds of bisphosphonate-refractory hypercalcaemia of malignancy, with responses lasting a median of about three months — on uncontrolled single-arm evidence.

cards.headline: Hu 2014 single-arm study: 64% responded by day 10 (corrected calcium at most 11.5 mg/dL) after bisphosphonates had failed; median response lasted 104 days
cards.summary: Hu 2014 single-arm study: 64% responded by day 10 (corrected calcium at most 11.5 mg/dL) after bisphosphonates had failed; median response lasted 104 days
cards.people: 33 patients with solid tumours or haematological malignancies and hypercalcaemia of malignancy whose albumin-corrected serum calcium was above 12.5 mg/dL (3.1 mmol/L) despite intravenous bisphosphonate treatment given more than 7 and at most 30 days before screening; denosumab 120 mg subcutaneously was given on days 1, 8, 15 and 29 and then every 4 weeks in an international single-arm study.
cards.result: By day 10, 21 patients (64%) reached a corrected calcium of at most 11.5 mg/dL (2.9 mmol/L) (the primary response endpoint) and 12 patients (33% as reported) reached at most 10.8 mg/dL (2.7 mmol/L). During the study, 23 patients (70%) reached at most 11.5 mg/dL and 21 patients (64%) reached at most 10.8 mg/dL. The estimated median duration of response was 104 days. The most common serious adverse events were hypercalcaemia worsening (5 patients, 15%) and dyspnoea (3 patients, 9%). The authors conclude denosumab lowered serum calcium in 64% of patients within 10 days and induced durable responses.
cards.watchOut: No control group: in bisphosphonate-refractory patients some calcium fall could reflect the delayed effect of the prior bisphosphonate, hydration and the cancer's course, and a 33-patient study in mixed advanced cancers cannot separate those. 'Response' is a calcium threshold, not a symptom or survival outcome, and 15% had worsening hypercalcaemia as a serious adverse event even on treatment.
cards.source: Hu et al. Denosumab for treatment of hypercalcemia of malignancy. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2014. PMID: 24915117. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Inoperable parathyroid carcinoma: cinacalcet cut calcium by at least 1 mg/dL in 62% — responders from 15.0 down to 11.2 mg/dL
shelves.question: In inoperable parathyroid carcinoma, does cinacalcet reduce serum calcium compared with pretreatment values in open-label treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Calcium/blood · Cinacalcet · Female · Humans · Hypercalcemia/blood/drug therapy · Hyperparathyroidism, Primary/blood/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Naphthalenes/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Parathyroid Hormone/blood · Parathyroid Neoplasms/blood/drug therapy · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the open-label single-arm study (Silverberg SJ et al., PMID: 17666472), 29 patients with inoperable parathyroid carcinoma, mean baseline calcium 14.1 ± 0.4 mg/dL and parathyroid hormone 697 ± 94 pg/mL, had cinacalcet titrated from 30 mg twice daily up to 90 mg four times daily over 16 weeks: 62% achieved the endpoint of at least a 1 mg/dL fall in serum calcium (mean decline to 12.4 ± 0.5 mg/dL), and among the 18 responders calcium fell from 15.0 ± 0.5 to 11.2 ± 0.3 mg/dL (P < 0.001), with the greatest reductions in those with the highest baseline values. Parathyroid hormone fell only 4.6%, not significantly, and adverse events included nausea, vomiting, headache and fracture. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cinacalcet lowers calcium in about two thirds of inoperable parathyroid carcinoma — meaningful palliation of the hypercalcaemia that drives this disease's morbidity, on uncontrolled evidence.

cards.headline: Silverberg 2007: 62% of inoperable parathyroid carcinoma patients cut calcium by at least 1 mg/dL on cinacalcet — responders fell from 15.0 to 11.2 mg/dL (P < 0.001)
cards.summary: Silverberg 2007: 62% of inoperable parathyroid carcinoma patients cut calcium by at least 1 mg/dL on cinacalcet — responders fell from 15.0 to 11.2 mg/dL (P < 0.001)
cards.people: 29 patients with parathyroid carcinoma enrolled in an open-label, single-arm study with titration and maintenance phases; cinacalcet was titrated (30 mg twice daily to 90 mg four times daily) for 16 weeks or until serum calcium was no more than 10.0 mg/dL. Mean baseline serum calcium was 14.1 ± 0.4 mg/dL and parathyroid hormone 697 ± 94 pg/mL. The endpoint was the proportion with at least a 1 mg/dL reduction in serum calcium at the end of titration.
cards.result: At the end of titration, serum calcium had fallen by at least 1 mg/dL in 62% of patients (mean decline to 12.4 ± 0.5 mg/dL). In the 18 responders, calcium fell from 15.0 ± 0.5 to 11.2 ± 0.3 mg/dL (P < 0.001), and the greatest reductions occurred in patients with the highest baseline calcium. Parathyroid hormone decreased non-significantly to 635 ± 73 pg/mL (−4.6%). Adverse events included nausea, vomiting, headache and fracture. The authors conclude cinacalcet effectively reduces hypercalcaemia in approximately two thirds of patients with inoperable parathyroid carcinoma.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and open-label in 29 patients with a rare cancer: regression to the mean contributes when the greatest falls occur in those with the highest starting values, and even responders averaged 11.2 mg/dL — improved, not normalised. The drug moved calcium far more than parathyroid hormone, and the record reports no tumour, survival or hospitalisation outcomes.
cards.source: Silverberg et al. Cinacalcet hydrochloride reduces the serum calcium concentration in inoperable parathyroid carcinoma. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2007. cards.summary: Synthesis: two thirds respond on calcium — the hormone barely moves, and normal calcium remains out of reach for most

cards.result: Calcium fall of at least 1 mg/dL: 62% of patients. Responder calcium: 15.0 to 11.2 mg/dL (P < 0.001). Whole-group mean at end of titration: 12.4 mg/dL from 14.1 mg/dL at baseline. shelves.title: Desmopressin in central diabetes insipidus: action lasts 4 hours at low dose, 11 hours at the top dose — a 13-patient pharmacology study, not a regimen trial
shelves.question: In central diabetes insipidus, how long does the antidiuretic action of desmopressin last by formulation and dose, and does that duration support overnight control without hyponatraemia?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Antidiuretic Agents/administration & dosage/pharmacokinetics/therapeutic use · Cross-Over Studies · Deamino Arginine Vasopressin/administration & dosage/pharmacokinetics/therapeutic use · Diabetes Insipidus, Neurogenic/drug therapy/physiopathology/urine · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Osmolar Concentration · Sodium/blood · Thirst/physiology · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Urine
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the pharmacology is clear and the clinical inference is thin. In the crossover dose study (Juul KV et al., PMID: 21626284), 13 patients with central diabetes insipidus received intravenous desmopressin in two three-way crossover designs: the duration of antidiuretic action was 4 hours at 125 ng, 8 hours at 250 ng and 11 hours at 500 ng, while the other dynamic measures showed no difference between 250 and 500 ng, indicating the upper plateau of the dose-response curve had been reached; no serious adverse events occurred and all treatment-emergent events were classified as unrelated or unlikely related. The authors calculate that 500 ng intravenously, corresponding to 160 μg orodispersible tablets twice daily, could achieve antidiuretic control. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): duration is dose-dependent and an 11-hour action at the top dose is long enough on paper to cover a night, but this 13-patient pharmacodynamic study measured urine output and osmolality — it did not measure overnight symptom control or hyponatraemia on any twice-daily regimen, so that part of the question is unanswered by the record.

cards.headline: Juul 2011 crossover study (13 patients): desmopressin action lasted 4, 8 and 11 hours at 125, 250 and 500 ng — with a plateau reached by 250–500 ng on other measures
cards.summary: Juul 2011 crossover study (13 patients): desmopressin action lasted 4, 8 and 11 hours at 125, 250 and 500 ng — with a plateau reached by 250–500 ng on other measures
cards.people: 13 patients with central diabetes insipidus studied with intravenous desmopressin in two 3-way crossover designs, at doses of 30, 60 and 125 ng and of 125, 250 and 500 ng; duration of action, minimum output rate, maximum osmolality and average osmolality during action were measured every 30 minutes for the first 2 hours and then hourly or two-hourly until urine output exceeded 2 ml/kg per 30 minutes.
cards.result: The duration of antidiuretic action was 4 hours (125 ng), 8 hours (250 ng) and 11 hours (500 ng), increasing from 250 to 500 ng; for the remaining secondary dynamic efficacy parameters no difference could be detected between 250 and 500 ng on descriptive statistics, indicating the upper plateau region of the dose-response curve had been reached. All treatment-emergent adverse events were classified as unrelated or unlikely related to trial medication, and no serious adverse events occurred. The authors state the data indicate antidiuretic control is possible with 500 ng intravenously, corresponding to 160 μg orodispersible tablets twice daily, whereas the current label recommends 60 to 120 μg three times daily for most patients.
cards.watchOut: Thirteen patients, intravenous dosing, and laboratory endpoints: duration was defined by urine output crossing a threshold under study conditions, not by patients sleeping through the night at home. The record contains no hyponatraemia outcome and no comparison of once-, twice- or three-times-daily regimens on symptoms — the twice-daily suggestion is an extrapolation from duration, explicitly framed by the authors as what the data 'indicate is possible'.
cards.source: Juul et al. Desmopressin duration of antidiuretic action in patients with central diabetes insipidus. Endocrine. 2011. PMID: 21626284. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Synthesis: action lengthens with dose up to about 11 hours — enough on paper for overnight cover, unproven as a clinical regimen
cards.people: One 13-patient intravenous crossover pharmacodynamic study in central diabetes insipidus — the entire anchor evidence for the duration question.
cards.result: Duration of antidiuretic action: 4 hours (125 ng), 8 hours (250 ng), 11 hours (500 ng). Dose-response plateau on other dynamic measures: reached between 250 and 500 ng. Serious adverse events: none. Overnight symptom control and hyponatraemia on twice-daily dosing: not measured. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Individual duration varies and oral, intranasal and orodispersible formulations differ in bioavailability from the intravenous doses studied — the 160 μg equivalence is the authors' conversion, not a tested tablet regimen.
