shelves.title: Late-blooming boys: letrozole and testosterone both induced puberty without psychosocial harm — sociability edged to letrozole, and waiting itself was never the comparator
shelves.question: In boys with constitutional delay of growth and puberty, does puberty-promoting treatment with letrozole or testosterone improve growth, psychosocial well-being and quality of life compared with watchful waiting?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Child · Puberty, Delayed/drug therapy/psychology* · Letrozole/therapeutic use · Testosterone/therapeutic use* · Aromatase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Puberty/drug effects/psychology* · Adolescent · Temperament/drug effects · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — and note first what the trials do not contain: no watchful-waiting arm. Both reports come from one randomised open-label trial comparing letrozole 2.5 mg/day with intramuscular testosterone 1 mg/kg monthly for 6 months in boys with constitutional delay of growth and puberty. On psychosocial outcomes (Kariola L et al., PMID: 41054004; 30 boys), boys with the condition were more withdrawn than local peers at baseline (p = 0.02), sociability was higher in the letrozole group than the testosterone group after treatment (−0.48, 95% CI −0.89 to −0.08; p = 0.019) and at 12 months (−0.72, 95% CI −1.12 to −0.32; p = 0.001), and neither treatment caused adverse psychosocial effects on the temperament measures assessed. On growth (Huttunen H et al., PMID: 34596269; 28 boys), serum testosterone best predicted growth velocity in both groups, and a meta-analysis of letrozole in this condition (Dutta D et al., PMID: 34477355; 7 trials) found predicted adult height improved versus placebo (mean difference 4.63 cm, 95% CI 3.90 to 5.36) but not versus testosterone (2.21 cm, −1.71 to 6.16). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): both treatments promote puberty without psychosocial harm in these small studies, letrozole may edge testosterone on sociability and testicular volume, and neither has been shown better than watchful waiting for well-being in a randomised comparison.

cards.headline: Kariola 2026 RCT: no adverse psychosocial effects from either treatment — sociability favoured letrozole over testosterone at 6 and 12 months
cards.summary: Kariola 2026 RCT: no adverse psychosocial effects from either treatment — sociability favoured letrozole over testosterone at 6 and 12 months
cards.people: 30 boys with constitutional delay of growth and puberty randomised open-label to letrozole 2.5 mg/day (n = 15) or intramuscular testosterone 1 mg/kg every 4 weeks (n = 15) for 6 months and followed to 12 months, with temperament (emotionality, activity, sociability) measured by a standardised questionnaire at 0, 6 and 12 months and compared with age- and postal-code-matched local peers and a national reference population.
cards.result: Compared with local peers, boys with constitutional delay were more withdrawn (p = 0.02) and experienced less anger (p = 0.02) and fear (p = 0.02); on emotionality they were less negatively emotional than both control groups (p = 0.04), and overall exhibited a generally docile temperament. Sociability was higher in the letrozole group than the testosterone group after the 6-month treatment period (difference −0.48, 95% CI −0.89 to −0.08; p = 0.019) and at 12-month follow-up (−0.72, 95% CI −1.12 to −0.32; p = 0.001). The authors conclude puberty-promoting treatments did not result in any adverse psychosocial effects on the temperament characteristics assessed.
cards.watchOut: Thirty boys, open-label, and a temperament questionnaire rather than direct measures of distress, bullying, school functioning or quality of life — and there is no untreated or watchful-waiting group, so the study cannot show that treating at all improves well-being compared with waiting, which is the comparison families usually ask about. The sociability difference is one scale among several tested.
cards.source: Kariola et al. Puberty-Promoting Treatment and Psychosocial Well-Being in Boys With Constitutional Delay of Puberty: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Clinical endocrinology. 2026. PMID: 41054004. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Huttunen 2022: growth velocity tracked serum testosterone in both arms — each nmol/L raised velocity 2.7 times more on testosterone than on letrozole, with an oestradiol threshold for optimal growth
cards.summary: Huttunen 2022: growth velocity tracked serum testosterone in both arms — each nmol/L raised velocity 2.7 times more on testosterone than on letrozole, with an oestradiol threshold for optimal growth
cards.people: Boys with constitutional delay of growth and puberty recruited to a randomised, controlled, open-label trial (2013–2017) comparing 6 months of low-dose intramuscular testosterone 1 mg/kg/month (n = 14) with oral letrozole 2.5 mg/day (n = 14), evaluated at 0, 3 and 6 months with morning blood samples; this report examines how sex steroids predict the growth response.
cards.result: In the testosterone group, serum testosterone correlated with serum oestradiol at baseline and at 3 months; in the letrozole group the two correlated only at baseline. The association between testosterone level and growth velocity differed between groups: each nmol/L increase in serum testosterone increased growth velocity 2.7 times more in the testosterone group. Serum testosterone was the best predictor of growth velocity in both groups; in the letrozole group, adding serum oestradiol significantly improved the growth estimate, and only boys with serum oestradiol above 10 pmol/L had a growth velocity above 8 cm/year. The authors identify serum testosterone 1 week after injection, and testosterone and oestradiol at 3 months on letrozole, as biomarkers of growth response.
cards.watchOut: A biomarker analysis of 28 boys over 6 months: it explains variation in short-term growth velocity within two active treatments and reports no final-height, psychosocial or untreated-control comparison. Growth velocity over 6 months is not adult height, and the oestradiol threshold (10 pmol/L) is a post hoc cut-point from a very small sample.

cards.headline: Dutta 2022 meta-analysis (7 RCTs): letrozole beat placebo on predicted adult height (+4.63 cm) but not testosterone, and beat both on testicular volume
cards.summary: Dutta 2022 meta-analysis (7 RCTs): letrozole beat placebo on predicted adult height (+4.63 cm) but not testosterone, and beat both on testicular volume
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of letrozole in constitutional delay in growth and puberty: 130 articles reviewed, 7 randomised trials meeting all criteria analysed, with primary outcomes of predicted adult height and pubertal progression after 12 months of use.
cards.result: Letrozole was superior to placebo for predicted adult height (mean difference 4.63 cm, 95% CI 3.90 to 5.36; p < 0.01; I² = 0%) but not to testosterone (mean difference 2.21 cm, 95% CI −1.71 to 6.16; p = 0.27; I² = 98%). Letrozole was superior to both placebo (mean difference 4.80 mL, 95% CI 0.57 to 9.03; p = 0.03) and testosterone (3.36 mL, 0.58 to 6.75; p = 0.02) for testicular volume at 12 months. Serum luteinising hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, testosterone and inhibin-B were significantly higher after 6 months of letrozole than with active or passive controls. No increased occurrence of adverse events, including spinal deformities, was noted with letrozole.
cards.watchOut: Predicted adult height is a projection from bone age, not measured adult height, and the letrozole-versus-testosterone height comparison is extremely heterogeneous (I² = 98%), so its null is unstable. Psychosocial outcomes — half of this shelf's question — do not appear in the meta-analysis at all.

cards.headline: Synthesis: both drugs promote puberty without psychosocial harm in small trials — but 'better than watchful waiting' has never been randomised
cards.summary: Synthesis: both drugs promote puberty without psychosocial harm in small trials — but 'better than watchful waiting' has never been randomised
cards.people: One randomised trial programme reported twice (30 boys for psychosocial outcomes, 28 for growth biomarkers; letrozole versus testosterone, no untreated arm) and one meta-analysis of 7 letrozole trials.
cards.result: Psychosocial: no adverse temperament effects from either treatment; sociability favoured letrozole (−0.48 at 6 months, −0.72 at 12 months). Growth: predicted adult height +4.63 cm for letrozole versus placebo (95% CI 3.90 to 5.36) but no significant advantage over testosterone; testicular volume favoured letrozole over both comparators. Adult height, quality of life and any randomised comparison with watchful waiting: not reported. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Constitutional delay resolves on its own — that is its definition — so every uncontrolled improvement over time is expected with or without treatment, and only the placebo-controlled height data in the meta-analysis escape that trap. Families choosing treatment are usually buying earlier puberty and relief of present distress, neither of which these records quantify against waiting. Tier C is set because the direct trial evidence is one small open-label programme.

shelves.title: Turner syndrome: low-dose oxandrolone added 2.3 cm of adult height — the conventional double dose added virilisation and bone-age acceleration instead
shelves.question: In girls with Turner syndrome already treated with growth hormone, does adding oxandrolone increase adult height compared with growth hormone alone, and at what virilisation cost?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Age Factors · Androgens/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Body Height/drug effects · Chi-Square Distribution · Child · Child, Preschool · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination/adverse effects · Female · Human Growth Hormone/therapeutic use · Humans · Netherlands · Oxandrolone/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Puberty/drug effects · Recombinant Proteins/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Turner Syndrome/drug therapy · Virilism/chemically induced
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the low dose only. In the Dutch dose-response trial (Menke LA et al., PMID: 20061421), 133 growth-hormone-treated girls with Turner syndrome received placebo or oxandrolone from age 8: adult height gain was 9.5 ± 4.7 cm on oxandrolone 0.03 mg/kg/day versus 7.2 ± 4.0 cm on placebo (P = 0.02), while the conventional 0.06 mg/kg/day dose gained 8.3 ± 4.7 cm, not significantly different from placebo (P = 0.3), partly because of accelerated bone maturation (P < 0.001). The Cochrane review (Mohamed S et al., PMID: 31684688; 6 trials, 498 participants) found adult height a mean 2.7 cm greater with oxandrolone plus growth hormone (95% CI 1.3 to 4.1; moderate-quality evidence). The costs are dose-dependent: breast development was slower on both oxandrolone doses, and virilisation was significantly more reported on 0.06 mg/kg/day than placebo (P < 0.001), which is why the trial authors discourage the conventional dose. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): low-dose oxandrolone adds roughly 2–3 cm of adult height, at the price of slower breast development and a virilisation risk that makes the higher dose a poor bargain.

cards.headline: Menke 2010 dose-response RCT: low-dose oxandrolone added +2.3 cm of adult height gain (9.5 versus 7.2 cm, P = 0.02) — the conventional dose did not significantly beat placebo
cards.summary: Menke 2010 dose-response RCT: low-dose oxandrolone added +2.3 cm of adult height gain (9.5 versus 7.2 cm, P = 0.02) — the conventional dose did not significantly beat placebo
cards.people: 133 girls with Turner syndrome at 10 Dutch centres, in age groups 2–7.99, 8–11.99 and 12–15.99 years, all treated with growth hormone (1.33 mg/m²/day) from baseline and randomised double-blind to placebo or oxandrolone at low dose (0.03 mg/kg/day) or conventional dose (0.06 mg/kg/day) from age 8, with oestrogens from age 12; adult height gain (adult height minus predicted adult height) was the primary outcome.
cards.result: Compared with growth hormone plus placebo, growth hormone plus oxandrolone 0.03 increased adult height gain in the intention-to-treat analysis (mean ± SD 9.5 ± 4.7 versus 7.2 ± 4.0 cm; P = 0.02) and in the per-protocol analysis (9.8 ± 4.9 versus 6.8 ± 4.4 cm; P = 0.02). Adult height gain on oxandrolone 0.06 was not significantly different from placebo (8.3 ± 4.7 versus 7.2 ± 4.0 cm; P = 0.3), partly due to accelerated bone maturation (P < 0.001). Breast development was slower on oxandrolone (0.03 dose, P = 0.02; 0.06 dose, P = 0.05), and more girls reported virilisation on oxandrolone 0.06 than on placebo (P < 0.001). The authors discourage the conventional dosage and describe the 0.03 dose as modestly increasing adult height gain with a fairly good safety profile except for decelerated breast development.
cards.watchOut: Adult height gain is measured against a predicted adult height, and prediction error in Turner syndrome is part of the outcome; the low-dose advantage (2.3 cm) sits within a wide spread of individual gains (± 4–5 cm). One trial, one country, and a growth-hormone dose and oestrogen schedule that may differ from current practice elsewhere.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2019 (6 trials, 498 girls): oxandrolone plus growth hormone gave +2.7 cm final adult height (95% CI 1.3 to 4.1), moderate-quality evidence
cards.summary: Cochrane 2019 (6 trials, 498 girls): oxandrolone plus growth hormone gave +2.7 cm final adult height (95% CI 1.3 to 4.1), moderate-quality evidence
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials in growth-hormone-treated girls up to 18 years with Turner syndrome: 6 trials, 498 participants (267 randomised to oxandrolone plus growth hormone, 231 to growth hormone only), conducted in 65 paediatric endocrinology facilities in the USA and Europe, with intervention durations of 3 to 7.6 years and mean starting ages of 9 to 12 years; searches to October 2018.
cards.result: Final adult height was a mean 2.7 cm greater with oxandrolone plus growth hormone than with growth hormone alone (mean difference 2.7 cm, 95% CI 1.3 to 4.1; P < 0.001; 5 trials, 270 participants; moderate-quality evidence), with a 95% prediction interval of 0.3 to 5.1 cm. For adverse events, in the main analysis of two low-risk-of-bias trials there was no evidence of a difference between groups (relative risk 1.81, 95% CI 0.83 to 3.96; P = 0.14; 170 participants; low-quality evidence); the record's adverse-event counts as printed are internally inconsistent, and the reported events were mainly signs of virilisation such as deepening of the voice. Evidence was downgraded mainly for imprecision; only one included trial was at low risk of bias in all domains.
cards.watchOut: The pooled 2.7 cm mixes oxandrolone doses, including the conventional dose the Dutch trial found unhelpful and more virilising, so the pooled figure flatters the high dose and understates the dose question. The review's printed adverse-event percentages do not match its printed counts (6 of 86 is not 18.6%), so this card reports the relative risk and counts without repeating the mismatched percentage — virilisation risk is better read from the Menke trial's dose-specific result.
cards.source: Mohamed et al. Oxandrolone for growth hormone-treated girls aged up to 18 years with Turner syndrome. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2019. PMID: 31684688. cards.headline: Synthesis: about 2–3 cm of extra adult height from low-dose oxandrolone — bought with slower breast development, and virilisation if the dose creeps up
cards.summary: Synthesis: about 2–3 cm of extra adult height from low-dose oxandrolone — bought with slower breast development, and virilisation if the dose creeps up
cards.people: One 133-patient randomised dose-response trial with adult-height outcomes (Menke 2010) and one Cochrane review of 6 trials and 498 participants (Mohamed 2019).
cards.result: Adult height: +2.3 cm gain for oxandrolone 0.03 mg/kg/day versus placebo in the trial (P = 0.02); pooled mean difference +2.7 cm (95% CI 1.3 to 4.1) across doses in the review. Conventional dose 0.06 mg/kg/day: no significant height advantage (P = 0.3), accelerated bone maturation (P < 0.001), significantly more virilisation (P < 0.001). Breast development: slower on both doses. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for the low dose.
cards.watchOut: Height is the only outcome with solid data: neither record shows that 2–3 cm changes quality of life, and the trade-offs (breast timing, voice and other virilising effects, years of an extra daily drug) are borne by the girl herself, which is why the dose distinction matters more than the pooled average. shelves.title: Mifepristone in Cushing's syndrome: HbA1c fell 7.43% to 6.29% and 60% met the glucose response in SEISMIC — but the trial had no control group, so the effect size is a before-and-after number
shelves.question: In Cushing's syndrome with diabetes or hypertension, does the glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist mifepristone improve glycaemic control and blood pressure in open-label treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antihypertensive Agents/therapeutic use · Blood Glucose/drug effects/metabolism · Blood Pressure/drug effects/physiology · Body Composition/drug effects/physiology · Body Weight/drug effects/physiology · Cushing Syndrome/complications/drug therapy*/metabolism* · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications/drug therapy/metabolism · Female · Glucose Intolerance/complications/drug therapy/metabolism · Hormone Antagonists/administration & dosage*/adverse effects · Humans · Hydrocortisone/blood · Hypertension/complications/drug therapy/metabolism · Male · Middle Aged · Mifepristone/administration & dosage*/adverse effects · Quality of Life · Quinolines/blood · Receptors, Glucocorticoid/antagonists & inhibitors* · Urea/analogs & derivatives/blood
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the entire evidence base for this shelf is one open-label, uncontrolled trial of 50 patients (Fleseriu M et al., SEISMIC, PMID: 22466348). In the diabetes/impaired-glucose-tolerance cohort, 60% met the glucose-area-under-the-curve response definition, HbA1c fell from 7.43% to 6.29%, and fasting glucose fell from 149.0 to 104.7 mg/dl; in the hypertension-only cohort, 38% met the diastolic blood-pressure response definition; weight fell by a mean 5.7% and 87% of patients were judged clinically improved overall. Those are large before-and-after changes in a disease where spontaneous improvement is uncommon, which is why the signal is credible — but with no control group, regression to the mean, co-interventions and assessor expectation cannot be separated from drug effect, and the adverse-effect list (fatigue, nausea, headache, low potassium, oedema, endometrial thickening in women) comes from the same uncontrolled exposure. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): mifepristone probably improves glycaemic control and blood pressure in Cushing's syndrome with diabetes or hypertension, but a single open-label trial cannot size the effect or the harm balance.

cards.headline: Fleseriu 2012 (SEISMIC): open-label mifepristone in 50 patients with Cushing's syndrome — 60% glucose response in the diabetes cohort, HbA1c 7.43% to 6.29%, 38% blood-pressure response in the hypertension cohort
cards.summary: Fleseriu 2012 (SEISMIC): open-label mifepristone in 50 patients with Cushing's syndrome — 60% glucose response in the diabetes cohort, HbA1c 7.43% to 6.29%, 38% blood-pressure response in the hypertension cohort
cards.people: 50 adults with endogenous Cushing's syndrome after failed multimodality therapy, treated at 14 US academic medical centres and three private research centres: a cohort with type 2 diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance (C-DM) and a cohort with hypertension alone (C-HT). Mifepristone was given at 300–1200 mg daily for 24 weeks, with no control group.
cards.result: In the C-DM cohort, an area-under-the-curve glucose response on the 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test was seen in 60% of patients (P < 0.0001); mean HbA1c decreased from 7.43 ± 1.52% to 6.29 ± 0.99% (P < 0.001) and fasting plasma glucose from 149.0 ± 75.7 mg/dl to 104.7 ± 37.5 mg/dl (P < 0.03). In the C-HT cohort, a diastolic blood-pressure response was seen in 38% of patients (P < 0.05). Mean weight change was −5.7 ± 7.4% (P < 0.001), with waist circumference decreases of −6.78 ± 5.8 cm in women and −8.44 ± 5.9 cm in men. Overall, 87% (P < 0.0001) had significant improvement in clinical status, and insulin resistance, depression, cognition and quality of life also improved. Common adverse events were fatigue, nausea, headache, low potassium, arthralgia, vomiting, oedema, and endometrial thickening in women.
cards.watchOut: No control group and no blinding: every number here is a before-and-after change in patients who had already failed other therapy, so the trial cannot separate drug effect from regression to the mean, intensified usual care, or expectation. Because mifepristone blocks the cortisol receptor rather than lowering cortisol, cortisol levels cannot be used to monitor effect or over-treatment — a practical hazard the design does not address. Fifty patients and 24 weeks cannot characterise uncommon harms such as adrenal insufficiency or endometrial effects.

blood-pressure response in the hypertension cohort in cushing's syndrome with diabetes or hypertension, does the glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist mifepristone improve glycaemic control and blood pressure in open-label treatment? open-label single-arm trial (seismic, fleseriu 2012) 50 adults with endogenous cushing's syndrome after failed multimodality therapy, treated at 14 us academic medical centres and three private research centres: a cohort with type 2 diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance (c-dm) and a cohort with hypertension alone (c-ht). mifepristone was given at 300–1200 mg daily for 24 weeks, with no control group. in the c-dm cohort, an area-under-the-curve glucose response on the 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test was seen in 60% of patients (p < 0.0001); mean hba1c decreased from 7.43 ± 1.52% to 6.29 ± 0.99% (p < 0.001) and fasting plasma glucose from 149.0 ± 75.7 mg/dl to 104.7 ± 37.5 mg/dl (p < 0.03). in the c-ht cohort, a diastolic blood-pressure response was seen in 38% of patients (p < 0.05). mean weight change was −5.7 ± 7.4% (p < 0.001), with waist circumference decreases of −6.78 ± 5.8 cm in women and −8.44 ± 5.9 cm in men. overall, 87% (p < 0.0001) had significant improvement in clinical status, and insulin resistance, depression, cognition and quality of life also improved. common adverse events were fatigue, nausea, headache, low potassium, arthralgia, vomiting, oedema, and endometrial thickening in women. no control group and no blinding: every number here is a before-and-after change in patients who had already failed other therapy, so the trial cannot separate drug effect from regression to the mean, intensified usual care, or expectation. because mifepristone blocks the cortisol receptor rather than lowering cortisol, cortisol levels cannot be used to monitor effect or over-treatment — a practical hazard the design does not address. fifty patients and 24 weeks cannot characterise uncommon harms such as adrenal insufficiency or endometrial effects. fleseriu m et al. mifepristone, a glucocorticoid receptor antagonist, produces clinical and metabolic benefits in patients with cushing's syndrome. the journal of cards.headline: Synthesis: one open-label trial, large metabolic improvements, no comparator — the benefit is plausible and probably real, its size is unmeasured
cards.summary: Synthesis: one open-label trial, large metabolic improvements, no comparator — the benefit is plausible and probably real, its size is unmeasured
cards.people: 50 adults with endogenous Cushing's syndrome and diabetes/impaired glucose tolerance or hypertension, treated open-label with mifepristone for 24 weeks (SEISMIC) — the entire carded evidence base for this question.
cards.result: Glycaemia: 60% glucose-AUC response; HbA1c 7.43% to 6.29%; fasting glucose 149.0 to 104.7 mg/dl. Blood pressure: 38% diastolic response in the hypertension-only cohort. Weight: −5.7% mean. Clinical status: 87% improved. Harms reported: fatigue, nausea, headache, hypokalaemia, arthralgia, vomiting, oedema, endometrial thickening. No randomised or controlled comparison exists in this record. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the HbA1c or weight changes as if they were placebo-subtracted effects — they are not. This shelf also does not compare mifepristone with cortisol-synthesis inhibitors (the pasireotide/osilodrostat question homes at shelf #749): receptor blockade and synthesis inhibition have never been compared head-to-head in the carded record. Tier C is set because the evidence is a single open-label trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Fleseriu M et al. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2012 (PMID: 22466348).

shelves.title: Steroid cover for radioiodine in Graves' disease: progression of eye disease cut to near zero when ophthalmopathy is already present (pooled OR 0.14) — no benefit shown in patients without eye disease
shelves.question: In Graves' disease treated with radioiodine, do prophylactic glucocorticoids prevent new or worsening orbitopathy versus no prophylaxis?
shelves.mesh: Chi-Square Distribution · Disease Progression · Drug Administration Schedule · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Graves Ophthalmopathy/diagnosis/therapy · Humans · Iodine Radioisotopes/therapeutic use · Odds Ratio · Patient Selection · Radiopharmaceuticals/therapeutic use · Risk Assessment · Risk Factors · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends entirely on whether the eyes are already involved. The systematic review and meta-analysis (8 trials, 850 patients) found that in patients with preexisting Graves' ophthalmopathy, standard-dose prednisone (0.4–0.5 mg/kg tapered over 3 months) was very effective at preventing progression after radioiodine (odds ratio 0.14, 95% CI 0.06–0.35), and low-dose prednisone also looked effective on indirect comparisons (odds ratio 0.20, 95% CI 0.07–0.60). In patients without preexisting ophthalmopathy, steroid prophylaxis had no beneficial effect (odds ratio 1.87, 95% CI 0.81–4.3). The anchor randomised trial shows the same split in absolute terms: after radioiodine alone, ophthalmopathy developed or worsened in 23 of 150 patients (15%), whereas among 145 patients given radioiodine plus a 3-month prednisone course, no patient had progression and 50 of 75 (67%) with baseline ophthalmopathy improved. Steroid prophylaxis did not change whether the hyperthyroidism resolved (odds ratio 1.05, 95% CI 0.69–1.58), and glucocorticoid side effects were common but mild. PROPOSED SPLIT: give steroid cover to patients with existing ophthalmopathy or high progression risk; it is not supported for patients with no eye involvement.

cards.headline: Shiber 2014 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 8 trials, 850 patients): standard-dose prednisone OR 0.14 for progression with preexisting ophthalmopathy; OR 1.87 (not significant) without it
cards.summary: Shiber 2014 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 8 trials, 850 patients): standard-dose prednisone OR 0.14 for progression with preexisting ophthalmopathy; OR 1.87 (not significant) without it
cards.people: Eight randomised and retrospective controlled trials (850 patients) of glucocorticoid regimens versus placebo, no treatment, or other glucocorticoid regimens for preventing Graves' ophthalmopathy progression after radioactive iodine treatment for Graves' hyperthyroidism.
cards.result: In patients with preexisting ophthalmopathy, standard-dose prednisone (0.4–0.5 mg/kg tapered over 3 months) was very effective for prevention of progression (odds ratio 0.14, 95% CI 0.06–0.35; p<0.01) in mild-to-moderate disease. Low-dose prednisone (0.2–0.3 mg/kg for 4–6 weeks), evaluated by indirect comparison against matched controls, also showed excellent efficacy versus no treatment or placebo (odds ratio 0.20, 95% CI 0.07–0.60; p=0.004) with no significant difference from standard dose (odds ratio 1.7, 95% CI 0.52–5.52). In patients without preexisting ophthalmopathy, steroid prophylaxis had no beneficial effect (odds ratio 1.87, 95% CI 0.81–4.3), though data in patients with risk factors were insufficient. Glucocorticoid prophylaxis had no impact on hyperthyroidism resolution (odds ratio 1.05, 95% CI 0.69–1.58), and side effects were common but mild.
cards.watchOut: The low-dose estimate leans on indirect comparisons because the low-dose trials lacked proper control groups with preexisting ophthalmopathy — so 'low dose works as well' is weaker than the headline odds ratio suggests. The review mixes randomised and retrospective controlled trials, and 'common but mild' side effects are asserted at the review level rather than pooled precisely.
cards.source: Shiber S et al. Glucocorticoid regimens for prevention of Graves' ophthalmopathy progression following radioiodine treatment: systematic review and meta-analysis. Thyroid. 2014. cards.headline: Bartalena 1998: ophthalmopathy developed or worsened in 23 of 150 (15%) after radioiodine alone — in none of 145 given radioiodine plus prednisone
cards.summary: Bartalena 1998: ophthalmopathy developed or worsened in 23 of 150 (15%) after radioiodine alone — in none of 145 given radioiodine plus prednisone
cards.people: 443 patients with Graves' hyperthyroidism and slight or no ophthalmopathy, randomly assigned to radioiodine alone (n=150), radioiodine followed by a 3-month course of prednisone (n=145), or methimazole for 18 months (n=148), evaluated every 1–2 months for 12 months, with hypothyroidism and persistent hyperthyroidism promptly corrected.
cards.result: Among the 150 patients treated with radioiodine alone, ophthalmopathy developed or worsened in 23 (15%) two to six months after treatment; the change was transient in 15 but persisted in 8 (5%), who subsequently required treatment for their eye disease, and none of the patients with baseline ophthalmopathy in this group improved. Among the 145 patients treated with radioiodine and prednisone, 50 (67%) of the 75 with ophthalmopathy at baseline had improvement, and no patient had progression. Among the 148 methimazole patients, 3 (2%) with baseline ophthalmopathy improved and 4 (3%) had worsening. The effects of radioiodine on thyroid function were similar in the two radioiodine groups.
cards.watchOut: A 1998 trial from a single Italian research group, conducted before modern risk stratification (smoking status, antibody levels, and baseline activity scores now refine who gets cover); its prednisone course was a fixed 3-month regimen, and the trial's population had slight or no ophthalmopathy at entry, so it speaks most directly to mild disease.
cards.source: Bartalena L et al. Relation between therapy for hyperthyroidism and the course of Graves' ophthalmopathy. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1998. PMID: 9420337. cards.headline: Synthesis: cover the eyes that are already involved; the trial and the meta-analysis tell the same story in relative and absolute terms
cards.summary: Synthesis: cover the eyes that are already involved; the trial and the meta-analysis tell the same story in relative and absolute terms
cards.people: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 controlled trials (850 patients) plus its anchor randomised trial (443 patients) of glucocorticoid prophylaxis around radioiodine treatment for Graves' disease.
cards.result: With preexisting ophthalmopathy: progression odds ratio 0.14 (95% CI 0.06–0.35) for standard-dose prednisone; in the anchor trial, progression in 0 of 145 with prednisone versus 23 of 150 (15%) without. Without preexisting ophthalmopathy: odds ratio 1.87 (95% CI 0.81–4.3), no benefit shown. Hyperthyroidism resolution: odds ratio 1.05 (0.69–1.58), unaffected. PROPOSED SPLIT stamp, not Tier C: randomised and pooled evidence agree, split by baseline eye involvement.
cards.watchOut: The open clinical question is the middle group — no ophthalmopathy but high-risk features such as smoking or high antibody titres — where the review found insufficient data; practice there is extrapolation, and this shelf should not be read as settling it.
cards.source: Synthesis of Shiber S et al. Thyroid. 2014 (PMID: 25068172); Bartalena L et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1998 (PMID: 9420337).

shelves.title: Antithyroid drugs in early pregnancy: birth defects in 9.1% after methimazole and 8.0% after propylthiouracil versus 5.7% unexposed — different defect patterns, and switching drugs in early pregnancy did not remove the risk (10.1%)
shelves.question: In pregnancy, how do propylthiouracil and methimazole compare on congenital malformations, and does switching drugs in early pregnancy remove the risk?
shelves.mesh: Abnormalities, Drug-Induced/epidemiology · Adult · Antithyroid Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Carbimazole/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Denmark/epidemiology · Female · Humans · Hyperthyroidism/drug therapy · Infant, Newborn · Male · Methimazole/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications/drug therapy · Pregnancy Trimester, First · Prevalence · Propylthiouracil/administration & dosage/adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — both drugs carry risk; they differ in pattern, not in safety. In the Danish nationwide cohort of 817,093 children, birth defects diagnosed before age 2 occurred in 9.1% of children exposed to methimazole/carbimazole in early pregnancy, 8.0% exposed to propylthiouracil, and 10.1% exposed to both (switched in early pregnancy), versus 5.7% in never-exposed children and 5.4% in children whose mothers used antithyroid drugs but not in pregnancy. Adjusted odds ratios were 1.66 (95% CI 1.35–2.04) for methimazole/carbimazole, 1.41 (1.03–1.92) for propylthiouracil, and 1.82 (1.08–3.07) for switching — so switching in early pregnancy did not remove the excess. The defect spectra differed: methimazole/carbimazole was linked to a characteristic group (choanal atresia, oesophageal atresia, omphalocele, omphalomesenteric duct anomalies, aplasia cutis; combined adjusted odds ratio 21.8, 95% CI 13.4–35.4), while propylthiouracil was associated with face/neck and urinary malformations. The extended 2019 cohort (1,243,353 children) corroborated the rates — 9.6% after methimazole/carbimazole and 8.3% after propylthiouracil versus 6.7% unexposed — and found maternal thyroid dysfunction itself was not a major risk factor. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): early-pregnancy exposure to either antithyroid drug is associated with more birth defects than no exposure, with methimazole's pattern more severe, and switching does not abolish the risk.

cards.headline: Andersen 2013: birth defects in 9.1% (methimazole/carbimazole), 8.0% (PTU), 10.1% (switched) versus 5.7% unexposed; adjusted ORs 1.66, 1.41 and 1.82
cards.summary: Andersen 2013: birth defects in 9.1% (methimazole/carbimazole), 8.0% (PTU), 10.1% (switched) versus 5.7% unexposed; adjusted ORs 1.66, 1.41 and 1.82
cards.people: 817,093 children live-born in Denmark from 1996 to 2008, grouped by maternal antithyroid drug use in early pregnancy: propylthiouracil (n=564), methimazole/carbimazole (n=1,097), both drugs — shifted in early pregnancy (n=159), antithyroid drug use but not in pregnancy (n=3,543), and never exposed (n=811,730); the outcome was a birth-defect diagnosis before 2 years of age, analysed by multivariable logistic regression.
cards.result: Birth-defect prevalence was 8.0% after propylthiouracil, 9.1% after methimazole/carbimazole, 10.1% after shifting between them in early pregnancy, 5.4% with antithyroid use outside pregnancy, and 5.7% in nonexposed children (P<.001). Adjusted odds ratios versus nonexposed were 1.66 (95% CI 1.35–2.04) for methimazole/carbimazole, 1.41 (1.03–1.92) for propylthiouracil, and 1.82 (1.08–3.07) for shifting. Both drugs were associated with urinary-system malformation, and propylthiouracil with face and neck malformations; choanal atresia, oesophageal atresia, omphalocele, omphalomesenteric duct anomalies and aplasia cutis were common in methimazole/carbimazole-exposed children (combined adjusted odds ratio 21.8, 95% CI 13.4–35.4).
cards.watchOut: Observational register data: women are prescribed one drug or switched for reasons (disease severity, era, tolerance) that registers only partly capture, and the adjusted odds ratios for overall defects (1.41–1.82) are modest — the persuasive elements are the absolute-rate differences, the drug-specific defect patterns, and the very large odds ratio for the characteristic methimazole embryopathy group, not any single summary ratio.
cards.source: Andersen SL et al. Birth defects after early pregnancy use of antithyroid drugs: a Danish nationwide study. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2013. PMID: 24151287. cards.headline: Andersen 2019 (extended cohort, 1.24 million children): defects in 9.6% after methimazole/carbimazole and 8.3% after PTU versus 6.7% unexposed — maternal thyroid dysfunction itself not a major factor
cards.summary: Andersen 2019 (extended cohort, 1.24 million children): defects in 9.6% after methimazole/carbimazole and 8.3% after PTU versus 6.7% unexposed — maternal thyroid dysfunction itself not a major factor
cards.type: Nationwide register-based cohort study with nested birth cohorts (Andersen 2019)
cards.people: 1,243,353 children in the Danish Nationwide Register-Based Cohort (1997–2016), of whom 2,718 (0.2%) were exposed to antithyroid drugs in early pregnancy, plus the Danish National Birth Cohort (8,830 children, with stored early-pregnancy maternal blood) and the North Denmark Region Pregnancy Cohort (14,483 children) used to test whether maternal thyroid function itself explained the association; outcome was birth defects diagnosed before 2 years of age.
cards.result: The frequency of birth defects was 6.7% (95% CI 6.7–6.8) in nonexposed children, and higher after exposure to methimazole/carbimazole (9.6%, 95% CI 8.2–11.2) and propylthiouracil (8.3%, 95% CI 6.7–10.3). The frequency of maternal thyroid dysfunction in early pregnancy was similar in random cohort members and in birth-defect cases in both blood-sample cohorts (12.4% versus 12.6%, P=0.8; and 15.1% versus 15.4%, P=0.8).
cards.watchOut: A corroborating cohort from the same national registers and research group — it extends the years and adds the thyroid-function analysis, but it is not an independent population, and exposure misclassification (a redeemed prescription is not proof of ingestion during the organogenesis window) applies to both studies.
cards.source: Andersen SL et al. Maternal Thyroid Function, Use of Antithyroid Drugs in Early Pregnancy, and Birth Defects. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2019. PMID: 31408173. cards.people: Two Danish nationwide register cohorts (817,093 children, 1996–2008; and 1,243,353 children, 1997–2016) of early-pregnancy antithyroid drug exposure and birth defects diagnosed before age 2, the second adding stored-blood cohorts to separate drug effect from maternal thyroid dysfunction.
cards.result: Birth defects: methimazole/carbimazole 9.1% and 9.6% across the two cohorts; propylthiouracil 8.0% and 8.3%; unexposed 5.7% and 6.7%; switched in early pregnancy 10.1% (adjusted OR 1.82, 95% CI 1.08–3.07). Characteristic methimazole embryopathy defects: combined adjusted OR 21.8 (13.4–35.4). Maternal thyroid dysfunction itself: no material association. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm), Tier C: observational evidence carrying a harm claim.
cards.watchOut: Untreated hyperthyroidism in pregnancy is itself dangerous, so these data argue for planning — preconception definitive therapy or the lowest effective dose with drug choice by trimester — not for stopping treatment; the cohorts compare exposed versus unexposed children, not treated versus untreated hyperthyroid mothers head-to-head.

shelves.title: Liquid levothyroxine when tablets are not absorbed: in 24 patients whose proton-pump inhibitors blocked tablet absorption, switching to the oral solution at the same dose brought TSH from 5.4 to 1.7 mU/L
shelves.question: In hypothyroid patients with impaired levothyroxine absorption, does liquid levothyroxine normalise TSH more reliably than tablets?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Cohort Studies · Drug Interactions · Female · Humans · Intestinal Absorption/drug effects · Male · Middle Aged · Pharmaceutical Solutions · Prospective Studies · Proton Pump Inhibitors/adverse effects · Tablets · Thyrotropin/blood · Thyroxine/administration & dosage/pharmacokinetics
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a neat pharmacological story tested only in a small uncontrolled switch study. Twenty-four adults whose tablet levothyroxine absorption was impaired by proton-pump inhibitors were switched to the oral solution at the same daily dose. Mean TSH fell from 5.4 ± 4.3 mU/L on tablets to 1.7 ± 1.0 on the solution in the replacement group, and from 2.1 ± 2.7 to 0.1 ± 0.3 in the group needing TSH suppression (both P<.0001). In the suppression group, no pre-switch measurement (0 of 22) reached the target TSH of at most 0.10 mU/L, versus 26 of 35 measurements (74.3%) after switching. There was no parallel control group, no randomisation, and no blinding — patients switched because tablets were failing, so regression to the mean and intensified follow-up are built into the design. The mechanism is plausible (the solution does not need gastric dissolution), and the within-patient consistency is striking, but 24 patients in one centre is the whole of this card's evidence. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): liquid levothyroxine appears to restore TSH control when proton-pump inhibitors impair tablet absorption, on small uncontrolled evidence.

cards.headline: Vita 2014: TSH 5.4 → 1.7 mU/L (replacement) and 2.1 → 0.1 mU/L (suppression) after switching 24 patients from tablets to oral solution at the same dose
cards.summary: Vita 2014: TSH 5.4 → 1.7 mU/L (replacement) and 2.1 → 0.1 mU/L (suppression) after switching 24 patients from tablets to oral solution at the same dose
cards.people: 24 consecutive adults (18 women, 6 men) at a tertiary university hospital clinic taking levothyroxine for replacement (n=14) or suppressive purposes (n=10), all with absorption of tablet levothyroxine impaired by proton-pump inhibitor therapy, switched from tablet to oral solution levothyroxine at the same daily dose and followed for a mean of 23.7 ± 11.9 weeks.
cards.result: Serum TSH was lower with the oral solution than with the tablet formulation in both groups (replacement group, 1.7 ± 1.0 mU/L versus 5.4 ± 4.3, P<.0001; suppression group, 0.1 ± 0.3 versus 2.1 ± 2.7, P<.0001). In the replacement group, the rate of TSH values at or below 4.12 mU/L was 29 of 30 measurements (96.7%) after switching versus 17 of 36 (47.2%) before, and at or below 2.5 mU/L, 24 of 30 (80.0%) versus 9 of 36 (25.0%) (P<.0001). In the suppression group, TSH values at or below 0.10 mU/L were 26 of 35 measurements (74.3%) after switching versus 0 of 22 (0%) before (P<.0001).
cards.watchOut: An uncontrolled before–after switch in patients selected precisely because their TSH was uncontrolled: some improvement would be expected from closer monitoring alone, the denominators are measurements rather than patients, and the study answers only the proton-pump-inhibitor scenario — not coffee, food timing, coeliac disease, or bariatric anatomy, where the formulation question also arises.
cards.source: Vita R et al. Switching levothyroxine from the tablet to the oral solution formulation corrects the impaired absorption of levothyroxine induced by proton-pump inhibitors. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2014. PMID: 25259910. cards.headline: Synthesis: within-patient TSH control restored in a small selected cohort — enough to try the switch, not enough to promise it
cards.summary: Synthesis: within-patient TSH control restored in a small selected cohort — enough to try the switch, not enough to promise it
cards.people: One prospective observational switch cohort (24 adults) with proton-pump-inhibitor-impaired tablet levothyroxine absorption, switched to the same dose in oral solution and followed for about 24 weeks.
cards.result: Mean TSH: 5.4 → 1.7 mU/L (replacement) and 2.1 → 0.1 mU/L (suppression), both P<.0001. Target-range TSH measurements rose from 47.2% to 96.7% (replacement, ≤4.12 mU/L) and from 0% to 74.3% (suppression, ≤0.10 mU/L). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C: a single small uncontrolled observational study carries this shelf.
cards.watchOut: The practical alternative explanations — stopping or retiming the proton-pump inhibitor, or separating tablet dosing from food and other drugs — were not compared; the solution's advantage over simply fixing tablet administration is untested in this record.

shelves.title: Block-and-replace versus dose titration in Graves' disease: relapse in 51% versus 54% across 12 trials — no stability or remission advantage, and more rashes and treatment withdrawals
shelves.question: In Graves' hyperthyroidism, does block-and-replace therapy produce more stable control or higher remission than dose titration with antithyroid drugs?
shelves.mesh: Antithyroid Agents/administration & dosage · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Graves Disease/drug therapy · Humans · Hyperthyroidism/drug therapy · Male · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Thyroxine/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on remission; block-and-replace simply costs more side effects. The Cochrane review (26 randomised trials, 3,388 participants) pooled 12 trials of block-replace versus titration regimens: relapse rates were 51% in the block-replace group and 54% in the titration group (odds ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.68–1.08), a difference compatible with no effect. Adverse effects ran the other way: rashes in 10% versus 6%, and withdrawal due to side effects in 16% versus 9%, both significantly more frequent with block-replace — unsurprising, since the regimen uses higher antithyroid doses plus levothyroxine. On duration, the review found 12 months of titration superior to 6 months for relapse, with no benefit in extending treatment beyond 18 months. No trial in the review measured hypothyroidism incidence, weight change, quality of life, ophthalmopathy progression, or costs. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): block-and-replace does not improve remission over dose titration in Graves' disease and causes more adverse effects.

cards.headline: Abraham 2010 (Cochrane): relapse 51% (block-replace) versus 54% (titration), OR 0.86 (0.68–1.08); rashes 10% versus 6%, withdrawals 16% versus 9%
cards.summary: Abraham 2010 (Cochrane): relapse 51% (block-replace) versus 54% (titration), OR 0.86 (0.68–1.08); rashes 10% versus 6%, withdrawals 16% versus 9%
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Abraham 2010)
cards.people: 26 randomised trials involving 3,388 participants with Graves' hyperthyroidism, comparing antithyroid drug doses, regimens (block-replace versus titration) and treatment durations; 12 trials addressed the block-replace versus titration comparison specifically.
cards.result: Relapse rates were similar between block-replace and titration: 51% in the block-replace group and 54% in the titration group (odds ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.68–1.08). Adverse effects were significantly higher with block-replace: rashes in 10% versus 6%, and participants withdrawing due to side effects in 16% versus 9%. On treatment duration with the titration regimen, 12 months was superior to 6 months for relapse, but there was no benefit in extending treatment beyond 18 months. None of the included studies investigated the incidence of hypothyroidism, changes in weight, health-related quality of life, ophthalmopathy progression, or economic outcomes, and the overall quality of the trials, as reported, was poor.
cards.watchOut: The underlying trials were small and poorly reported, with relapse defined and timed differently across decades of practice; the pooled null is consistent but not precise enough to exclude a small benefit (the confidence interval reaches an odds ratio of 0.68). The side-effect excess, driven by the higher antithyroid doses block-replace requires, is the more robust finding.
cards.source: Abraham P et al. Antithyroid drug regimen for treating Graves' hyperthyroidism. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2010. PMID: 20091544. shelves.title: Gene-expression classifier for indeterminate thyroid nodules: a 'benign' result was right 94–95% of the time in the validation study — but the test still called half of all benign nodules suspicious
shelves.question: In indeterminate thyroid nodules, does gene-expression classifier testing reduce unnecessary diagnostic surgery versus standard management?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Algorithms · Biomarkers, Tumor/genetics · Biopsy, Fine-Needle · Diagnosis, Differential · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gene Expression · Gene Expression Profiling/methods · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Oligonucleotide Array Sequence Analysis · Prospective Studies · RNA, Messenger/analysis · Sensitivity and Specificity · Thyroid Gland/pathology · Thyroid Nodule/diagnosis/genetics/pathology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — as a rule-out test, with a specific arithmetic patients should hear. In the prospective multicentre validation study, 265 cytologically indeterminate nodules with surgical histology were tested: 85 were malignant, and the classifier identified 78 of the 85 as suspicious (sensitivity 92%, 95% CI 84–97), with specificity of 52% (95% CI 44–59). The negative predictive value of a benign classifier result — the number that matters for a decision to observe rather than operate — was 95% for atypia of undetermined significance, 94% for follicular neoplasm, and 85% for suspicious cytology. The flip side: with specificity of 52%, roughly half of benign nodules are still labelled suspicious and head to surgery anyway, so the test spares an operation mainly for the minority whose result comes back benign. Of the 7 false-negative aspirates, 6 had a paucity of thyroid follicular cells, flagging sampling as the failure mode. The study was funded by the test's manufacturer, Veracyte, and it validates accuracy against surgical histology — it does not itself randomise patients to testing versus standard management or measure how many operations are actually avoided in practice. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a benign gene-expression classifier result identifies indeterminate nodules that can reasonably be observed, on a single manufacturer-funded validation study.

cards.headline: Alexander 2012: sensitivity 92%, specificity 52%; negative predictive value 95% (atypia), 94% (follicular neoplasm), 85% (suspicious cytology) among 265 indeterminate nodules
cards.summary: Alexander 2012: sensitivity 92%, specificity 52%; negative predictive value 95% (atypia), 94% (follicular neoplasm), 85% (suspicious cytology) among 265 indeterminate nodules
cards.people: A 19-month prospective study at 49 clinical sites enrolling 3,789 patients with 4,812 fine-needle aspirates from thyroid nodules at least 1 cm; 577 aspirates were cytologically indeterminate, 413 had corresponding histopathology from excised lesions, and 265 indeterminate nodules meeting inclusion criteria formed the classifier analysis set, with central blinded histopathological review as the reference standard. The classifier measures expression of 167 genes.
cards.result: Of the 265 indeterminate nodules, 85 were malignant. The gene-expression classifier correctly identified 78 of the 85 as suspicious (sensitivity 92%, 95% CI 84–97), with a specificity of 52% (95% CI 44–59). Negative predictive values were 95% for 'atypia (or follicular lesion) of undetermined clinical significance', 94% for 'follicular neoplasm or lesion suspicious for follicular neoplasm', and 85% for 'suspicious cytologic findings'. Analysis of the 7 aspirates with false-negative results revealed that 6 had a paucity of thyroid follicular cells, suggesting insufficient sampling of the nodule.
cards.watchOut: Accuracy is not outcome: this study does not show that using the test reduces operations, costs, or missed cancers in routine practice — those require management studies. Verification bias is built in (only nodules that went to surgery have histology), the malignancy prevalence in this surgical set (85 of 265) is higher than in all-comers with indeterminate cytology, which flatters the predictive values, and the study was funded by Veracyte, the test's manufacturer.
cards.source: Alexander EK et al. Preoperative diagnosis of benign thyroid nodules with indeterminate cytology. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22731672. cards.headline: Synthesis: a good rule-out test for the nodules it calls benign, an unchanged pathway for everyone else
cards.summary: Synthesis: a good rule-out test for the nodules it calls benign, an unchanged pathway for everyone else
cards.people: One prospective multicentre validation study (265 indeterminate nodules with surgical histology, drawn from 4,812 aspirates at 49 sites) of the 167-gene expression classifier against blinded central histopathology.
cards.result: Sensitivity 92% (95% CI 84–97); specificity 52% (95% CI 44–59); negative predictive value 95% (atypia of undetermined significance), 94% (follicular neoplasm), 85% (suspicious cytology). False negatives: 7, of which 6 had scant follicular cells. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single validation study, manufacturer-funded, carries this shelf.

shelves.title: Ethanol instillation for recurrent benign thyroid cysts: cure in 82% versus 48% with saline flushing in a double-blind trial — with moderate-to-severe pain in a fifth of patients
shelves.question: In benign recurrent thyroid cysts, does percutaneous ethanol injection achieve lasting volume reduction versus aspiration or saline injection?
shelves.mesh: Cysts/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy/surgery · Double-Blind Method · Drainage · Ethanol/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Injections · Instillation, Drug · Male · Middle Aged · Sodium Chloride/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Thyroid Diseases/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy/surgery · Treatment Outcome · Ultrasonography
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small, well-blinded trial with a clear result. Sixty-six patients with benign thyroid cysts that had already recurred after aspiration were randomised to aspiration plus ethanol flushing or aspiration plus saline flushing, repeated up to three times if the cyst returned. Cure — cyst volume at most 1 ml at 6 months — was achieved in 27 of 33 patients (82%, 95% CI 65–93) with ethanol versus 16 of 33 (48%, 95% CI 31–66) with saline (P=0.006), and cure after a single session in 64% versus 18% (P=0.002). Success fell with more previous aspirations and with larger baseline cyst volume. The cost was pain: 7 patients (21%) in the ethanol group had moderate-to-severe pain (median duration 5 minutes) and one had transient dysphonia; laryngoscopy was normal in all patients. Follow-up was 6 months, so 'lasting' beyond that horizon is unproven here, and the trial predates modern cyst-ablation comparisons. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ethanol instillation roughly doubles the cure rate of recurrent benign thyroid cysts over aspiration with saline, in one small double-blind trial.

cards.headline: Bennedbæk & Hegedüs 2003: cure in 27 of 33 (82%) with ethanol versus 16 of 33 (48%) with saline (p=0.006); single-session cure 64% versus 18%
cards.summary: Bennedbæk & Hegedüs 2003: cure in 27 of 33 (82%) with ethanol versus 16 of 33 (48%) with saline (p=0.006); single-session cure 64% versus 18%
cards.people: 66 consecutive patients with recurrent, benign (on ultrasound-guided biopsy) thyroid cysts of at least 2 ml, randomised to subtotal cyst aspiration followed by flushing with 99% ethanol and complete emptying (n=33), or the same procedure with isotonic saline (n=33), all ultrasound-guided; treatment was repeated on recurrence (cyst volume above 1 ml) at monthly evaluations, up to a maximum of three treatments, with 6 months of follow-up. Age, sex, number of previous aspirations, pretreatment cyst volume and serum TSH did not differ between groups.
cards.result: Cure (cyst volume at most 1 ml at the end of follow-up) was obtained in 27 of 33 patients (82%; 95% CI 65–93) treated with ethanol and 16 of 33 (48%; 95% CI 31–66) treated with saline (P=0.006). In the ethanol group, 21 of 33 patients (64%) were cured after one session only, compared with 6 of 33 (18%) in the saline group (P=0.002). The number of previous aspirations (P=0.005) and baseline cyst volume (P=0.005) influenced outcome, with success falling as both rose. Seven patients (21%) treated with ethanol had moderate-to-severe pain (median duration 5 minutes; 95% CI 2–10) and one had transient dysphonia; indirect laryngoscopy before and after the last session was normal in all patients.
cards.watchOut: Sixty-six patients, one centre, 6 months of follow-up: recurrence after 6 months — the clinically decisive horizon for a cyst that has already recurred at least once — is unmeasured, and the comparison is against saline flushing, not against surgery, radiofrequency ablation, or simple repeat aspiration alone.

shelves.title: Alendronate in mild primary hyperparathyroidism: lumbar spine density up 6.85% over two years in a 44-patient trial — the distal radius, the site this disease hits hardest, did not improve
shelves.question: In mild primary hyperparathyroidism, does alendronate improve bone mineral density versus placebo over two years?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Alendronate/therapeutic use · Alkaline Phosphatase/antagonists & inhibitors/blood · Biomarkers/analysis · Bone Density/drug effects · Bone Remodeling/drug effects · Bone and Bones/enzymology · Collagen/antagonists & inhibitors/urine · Collagen Type I · Double-Blind Method · Female · Femur Neck/metabolism · Hip Joint/metabolism · Humans · Hyperparathyroidism/drug therapy/metabolism · Lumbosacral Region · Male · Middle Aged · Peptides/antagonists & inhibitors/urine · Placebos · Radius/metabolism · Spine/metabolism
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for spine and hip density, in a very small trial with a crossover design. Forty-four patients with asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism who did not meet surgical guidelines or refused surgery were randomised to alendronate 10 mg daily or placebo, with the placebo group crossing to alendronate at 12 months. Lumbar spine bone mineral density rose 6.85% over 2 years on alendronate (P<0.001 versus baseline); total hip density rose 4.01% at 12 months (P<0.001) and held; femoral neck density gained 3.67% at 24 months (P=0.038). The placebo group showed no significant change at any site at 12 months, and after crossing over gained 4.1% at the spine and 1.7% at the hip in its year on treatment — an internal replication. The exception matters: the distal one-third radius, the cortical site primary hyperparathyroidism characteristically erodes, showed no significant change at 12 or 24 months. Bone turnover markers fell sharply (urinary NTX down 66% by 3 months), while serum calcium, PTH and urinary calcium did not change — alendronate treats the bone consequence, not the parathyroid disease, and no fracture outcomes were measured. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): alendronate improves spine and hip bone density in primary hyperparathyroidism over two years, without improving the distal radius and without touching calcium or PTH.

cards.headline: Khan 2004: spine BMD +6.85% at 2 years and hip +4.01% at 12 months on alendronate; placebo unchanged at 12 months, then gained after crossover — radius unchanged throughout
cards.summary: Khan 2004: spine BMD +6.85% at 2 years and hip +4.01% at 12 months on alendronate; placebo unchanged at 12 months, then gained after crossover — radius unchanged throughout
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial with crossover (Khan 2004)
cards.people: 44 patients with asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism who did not meet surgical guidelines or had refused surgery, randomised (stratified by sex) to alendronate 10 mg daily or placebo; at 12 months the placebo group crossed over to active treatment, so all patients were on alendronate in year 2. Bone mineral density at the lumbar spine, femoral neck, total hip and distal one-third radius was measured every 6 months; calcium, phosphate, PTH and bone turnover markers every 3 months.
cards.result: Alendronate over 2 years was associated with a significant 6.85% increase in lumbar spine BMD versus baseline (P<0.001). Total hip BMD increased significantly at 12 months by 4.01% (P<0.001) and remained stable over the next 12 months. Femoral neck BMD gained 3.67% at 24 months (P=0.038). Distal one-third radius BMD showed no statistically significant change at 12 or 24 months. The placebo group showed no significant change at 12 months at any site; after crossover it gained 4.1% at the lumbar spine (P=0.003) and 1.7% at the total hip (P=0.009) in its year on alendronate. Urinary NTX fell 66% by 3 months on alendronate (P<0.001) and bone-specific alkaline phosphatase by about half, while serum calcium (total and ionised), PTH and urinary calcium did not change.
cards.watchOut: Forty-four patients, and the headline comparisons are against baseline rather than a parallel placebo group beyond month 12 (by design, everyone was treated in year 2). BMD is a surrogate: no fractures were recorded as an outcome, and the null result at the cortical radius — the site of greatest parathyroid bone loss — limits how far 'bone protection' can be claimed.
cards.source: Khan AA et al. Alendronate in primary hyperparathyroidism: a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2004. shelves.title: Vitamin D repletion in primary hyperparathyroidism: PTH fell 17% and spine density rose 2.5% on 2,800 IU daily — with no rise in blood or urine calcium in a 46-patient trial
shelves.question: In primary hyperparathyroidism with vitamin D insufficiency, does cholecalciferol repletion lower parathyroid hormone without raising serum calcium?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Bone Density/drug effects · Calcium/blood · Cholecalciferol/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Hyperparathyroidism/blood/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Parathyroid Hormone/blood · Phosphates/blood · Placebos · Vitamin D/analogs & derivatives/blood
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the feared harm did not appear, and the hormone moved the right way. In this double-blind trial, 46 patients with primary hyperparathyroidism received cholecalciferol 70 µg (2,800 IU) daily or placebo for 52 weeks, spanning their parathyroidectomy at week 26. Vitamin D levels rose from 50 to 94 nmol/L on treatment while falling from 57 to 52 nmol/L on placebo (P<.001). Before surgery, PTH was 17% lower on vitamin D than on placebo (P=.01), lumbar spine bone density was 2.5% higher (P=.01), and the bone-resorption marker C-terminal β-CrossLaps was 22% lower (P<.005); postoperatively, PTH remained lower in the cholecalciferol group (P=.04). The safety point of the question: plasma creatinine and plasma and urinary calcium did not differ between groups at any stage. The trial was small and single-centre, PTH and density are surrogates, and all patients proceeded to parathyroidectomy — so this supports repletion as safe preparation, not as an alternative to surgery. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): high-dose cholecalciferol safely repletes vitamin D in primary hyperparathyroidism, lowering PTH modestly without raising calcium, in one small trial.

cards.headline: Rolighed 2014: 25(OH)D 50 → 94 nmol/L on cholecalciferol; PTH −17% pre-operatively (p=.01); calcium and urinary calcium no different from placebo
cards.summary: Rolighed 2014: 25(OH)D 50 → 94 nmol/L on cholecalciferol; PTH −17% pre-operatively (p=.01); calcium and urinary calcium no different from placebo
cards.people: 46 patients with primary hyperparathyroidism (mean age 58 years, range 29–77; 35 women, 76%) at a single centre, randomised to cholecalciferol 70 µg (2,800 IU) daily or identical placebo for 52 weeks — 26 weeks before parathyroidectomy and 26 weeks after — with PTH, calcium homeostasis and bone metabolism as the evaluated outcomes.
cards.result: Preoperatively, 25-hydroxyvitamin D rose from 50 to 94 nmol/L in the treatment group and fell from 57 to 52 nmol/L on placebo (P<.001). Compared with placebo, vitamin D decreased PTH significantly by 17% before parathyroidectomy (P=.01), increased lumbar spine bone mineral density by 2.5% (P=.01), and decreased C-terminal β-CrossLaps by 22% (P<.005). The trabecular bone score did not change with treatment but improved after surgery. Postoperatively, PTH remained lower in the cholecalciferol group (P=.04). Plasma creatinine and plasma and urinary calcium did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: Forty-six patients at one centre, all heading to surgery: the trial can show that a year of high-dose repletion did not destabilise calcium in monitored patients, but it cannot exclude rare hypercalcaemic harm, and its PTH and density effects are surrogates measured around an operation that itself transforms both.
cards.source: Rolighed L et al. Vitamin D treatment in primary hyperparathyroidism: a randomized placebo controlled trial. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2014. PMID: 24423366. shelves.title: Starting lenvatinib lower (18 mg versus 24 mg) in radioiodine-refractory thyroid cancer: response rate fell from 57.3% to 40.3% — and severe toxicity did not fall with it (57.1% versus 61.3%)
shelves.question: In radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer, does a lower starting dose of lenvatinib (18 mg) preserve efficacy with less toxicity than 24 mg?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Chemoradiotherapy/adverse effects/methods · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Iodine Radioisotopes/therapeutic use · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Phenylurea Compounds/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Progression-Free Survival · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Quinolines/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Radiation Tolerance · Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors · Thyroid Neoplasms/mortality/pathology/therapy · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — starting lower trades away responses and buys no safety. Study 211 randomised patients with radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer double-blind to a starting dose of lenvatinib 18 mg or the approved 24 mg daily. The objective response rate at week 24 was 40.3% (95% CI 29.3–51.2) on 18 mg versus 57.3% (95% CI 46.1–68.5) on 24 mg (odds ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.26–0.96), so the lower dose failed its noninferiority criterion by a clinically meaningful margin. The hoped-for compensation never arrived: grade 3 or worse treatment-emergent adverse events at week 24 occurred in 57.1% on 18 mg versus 61.3% on 24 mg (difference −4.2%, 95% CI −19.8 to 11.4), and the companion quality-of-life analysis found no significant differences between arms on EQ-5D or FACT-G scores. The trial's logic is now the standard one for this drug: start at 24 mg and reduce for toxicity in the individual patient, rather than pre-emptively underdosing everyone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): a lower lenvatinib starting dose (18 mg) reduces tumour responses without reducing severe toxicity or improving quality of life, compared with starting at 24 mg.

cards.headline: Brose 2022 (Study 211): response at week 24 in 40.3% on 18 mg versus 57.3% on 24 mg (OR 0.50) — grade ≥3 adverse events 57.1% versus 61.3%
cards.summary: Brose 2022 (Study 211): response at week 24 in 40.3% on 18 mg versus 57.3% on 24 mg (OR 0.50) — grade ≥3 adverse events 57.1% versus 61.3%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind dose-comparison phase 2 trial (Brose 2022, Study 211)
cards.people: Patients with radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer randomised double-blind to lenvatinib starting doses of 18 mg/day or 24 mg/day (152 patients in the trial's quality-of-life population: 77 on 18 mg and 75 on 24 mg). The primary efficacy endpoint was objective response rate at week 24 (noninferiority odds-ratio margin 0.4); the primary safety endpoint was the frequency of grade 3 or worse treatment-emergent adverse events at week 24; tumours were assessed by RECIST v1.1.
cards.result: The week-24 objective response rate was 57.3% (95% CI 46.1–68.5) in the 24 mg arm and 40.3% (95% CI 29.3–51.2) in the 18 mg arm, an odds ratio (18/24 mg) of 0.50 (95% CI 0.26–0.96) — noninferiority was not demonstrated, and the authors describe the difference as clinically meaningful. Grade ≥3 treatment-emergent adverse events at week 24 occurred in 61.3% on 24 mg and 57.1% on 18 mg, a difference of −4.2% (95% CI −19.8 to 11.4). The authors conclude the results support the approved 24 mg starting dose, with dose adjustment as necessary.
cards.watchOut: Response rate at 24 weeks is an early endpoint — the trial was not powered to compare progression-free or overall survival between doses, and patients on the lower dose could still have dose escalations and reductions managed clinically, so this tests a starting-dose strategy, not a lifetime dose. The safety confidence interval (−19.8 to 11.4) is wide enough to hide a modest toxicity difference in either direction.
cards.source: Brose MS et al. A Randomized Study of Lenvatinib 18 mg vs 24 mg in Patients With Radioiodine-Refractory Differentiated Thyroid Cancer. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2022. PMID: 34664662. Registry ID: NCT02702388. cards.headline: Taylor 2023 (Study 211 quality of life): no significant EQ-5D or FACT-G differences between the 18 mg and 24 mg arms
cards.summary: Taylor 2023 (Study 211 quality of life): no significant EQ-5D or FACT-G differences between the 18 mg and 24 mg arms
cards.type: Randomised trial secondary analysis (Taylor 2023, Study 211 HRQoL)
cards.people: The 152 patients of Study 211 (77 randomised to lenvatinib 18 mg/day and 75 to 24 mg/day) with health-related quality of life assessed at baseline, every 8 weeks to week 24, then every 16 weeks and at the off-treatment visit, using the EQ-5D-3L and FACT-G instruments.
cards.result: Baseline scores and overall changes from baseline were comparable between arms: least-squares mean differences (18 mg versus 24 mg) were −0.42 (95% CI −4.88 to 4.03) for EQ-5D-VAS and 0.47 (95% CI −3.45 to 4.39) for FACT-G total. Time to first deterioration did not significantly favour either arm (EQ-5D-VAS hazard ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.61–1.40; FACT-G total 0.73, 95% CI 0.48–1.12), and time to definitive deterioration likewise showed no significant advantage for the lower dose. The authors conclude these data further support the approved 24 mg starting dose.
cards.watchOut: Quality-of-life completion falls as patients leave treatment, so later time points over-represent patients tolerating therapy in both arms; a null here means 'no demonstrated quality-of-life gain from starting lower', measured under that attrition, not proof the lived experience is identical.
cards.source: Taylor MH et al. Health-related quality-of-life analyses from a multicenter, randomized, double-blind phase 2 study of patients with differentiated thyroid cancer treated with lenvatinib 18 or 24 mg/day. Cancer Medicine. 2023. PMID: 36464853. Registry ID: NCT02702388. cards.headline: Synthesis: the lower starting dose fails on its own terms — fewer responses, same severe toxicity, same quality of life
cards.summary: Synthesis: the lower starting dose fails on its own terms — fewer responses, same severe toxicity, same quality of life
cards.people: One randomised double-blind phase 2 dose-comparison trial (Study 211, 152 patients) of lenvatinib starting doses 18 mg versus 24 mg daily in radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer, with its prespecified quality-of-life analysis.
cards.result: Week-24 response: 40.3% (18 mg) versus 57.3% (24 mg); odds ratio 0.50 (95% CI 0.26–0.96); noninferiority not met. Grade ≥3 adverse events: 57.1% versus 61.3% (difference −4.2%, 95% CI −19.8 to 11.4). Quality of life (EQ-5D, FACT-G): no significant differences. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm), Tier C: a single dose-comparison trial carries this shelf, and the claim is about a treatment strategy's harm (lost responses) rather than a drug toxicity.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here argues against dose reduction after toxicity appears on 24 mg — that is how the drug is normally managed and is a different question from the starting-dose strategy this trial randomised.
cards.source: Synthesis of Brose MS et al. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2022 (PMID: 34664662); Taylor MH et al. Cancer Medicine. 2023 (PMID: 36464853).

shelves.title: Selenium in TPO-antibody-positive pregnancy: postpartum thyroid dysfunction in 28.6% versus 48.6% on placebo in the one randomised trial — permanent hypothyroidism also halved, but the trial stands alone
shelves.question: In women with thyroid-peroxidase antibodies, does selenium supplementation during pregnancy prevent postpartum thyroiditis?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Autoantibodies/blood · Dietary Supplements · Female · Humans · Iodide Peroxidase/immunology · Parity · Placebos · Postpartum Period/drug effects/physiology · Pregnancy/blood/immunology · Prospective Studies · Selenomethionine/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Thyroid Function Tests · Thyrotropin/blood · White People
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on one trial's evidence. In the single randomised placebo-controlled trial, pregnant women positive for thyroid peroxidase antibodies who took selenomethionine 200 micrograms daily during pregnancy and after delivery developed postpartum thyroid dysfunction in 28.6% of cases versus 48.6% on placebo (P<0.01), and permanent hypothyroidism in 11.7% versus 20.3% (P<0.01) (Negro R et al., PMID: 17284630). The absolute differences — about 20 percentage points for postpartum dysfunction and about 9 points for permanent hypothyroidism — are large, but they come from one centre's trial of 151 antibody-positive women, the abstract reports no adverse-event rates, and no second randomised trial in this session's records confirms the result. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): selenium during and after pregnancy reduced postpartum thyroid dysfunction and later permanent hypothyroidism in the one randomised trial; confirmation is still missing, so this is Tier C.

cards.headline: Negro 2007: postpartum thyroid dysfunction in 28.6% on selenium versus 48.6% on placebo (P<0.01); permanent hypothyroidism 11.7% versus 20.3% (P<0.01)
cards.summary: Negro 2007: postpartum thyroid dysfunction in 28.6% on selenium versus 48.6% on placebo (P<0.01); permanent hypothyroidism 11.7% versus 20.3% (P<0.01)
cards.people: Euthyroid pregnant women screened in an Italian obstetrics/endocrinology service: of 2,143 participants, 7.9% were thyroid-peroxidase-antibody positive; 77 antibody-positive women received selenomethionine 200 µg/day and 74 received placebo during pregnancy and the postpartum period, with 81 antibody-negative women as a control group.
cards.result: Postpartum thyroid dysfunction occurred in 28.6% of the selenium group versus 48.6% of the placebo group (P<0.01), an absolute difference of about 20 percentage points. Permanent hypothyroidism occurred in 11.7% versus 20.3% (P<0.01), an absolute difference of about 9 percentage points. The authors concluded that selenium reduced thyroid inflammatory activity and the incidence of hypothyroidism.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one centre, 151 antibody-positive women. The abstract reports no adverse-event or safety rates for selenium in pregnancy, and the placebo group's very high event rate (48.6%) reflects a selected antibody-positive population — the absolute benefit will be smaller wherever baseline risk is lower.
cards.source: Negro R et al. The influence of selenium supplementation on postpartum thyroid status in pregnant women with thyroid peroxidase autoantibodies. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2007. PMID: 17284630. cards.headline: Synthesis: a large effect in a single small trial — promising, unconfirmed, and without reported safety rates
cards.summary: Synthesis: a large effect in a single small trial — promising, unconfirmed, and without reported safety rates
cards.people: One randomised placebo-controlled trial of 151 thyroid-peroxidase-antibody-positive pregnant women (77 selenium, 74 placebo), with treatment continued into the postpartum period.
cards.result: Postpartum thyroid dysfunction 28.6% versus 48.6%; permanent hypothyroidism 11.7% versus 20.3% — both favouring selenomethionine 200 µg/day. No second randomised trial and no adverse-event rates are available in the records fetched for this shelf. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single-trial benefit claim.
cards.watchOut: Selenium has a narrow therapeutic window in general use, and this record cannot weigh that: the trial abstract is silent on harms. The stamp grades the benefit evidence only, and it should fall if a larger confirmatory trial does not reproduce the effect.
cards.source: Synthesis of Negro R et al. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2007 (PMID: 17284630).
