shelves.title: Levothyroxine suppression for benign nodules: ≥50% shrinkage in 16% versus 10% in the Cochrane pooling — a small edge bought with hyperthyroid symptoms in 25% versus 7%
shelves.question: In benign nodular goitre, does levothyroxine suppression shrink nodules or prevent growth versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Catheter Ablation/methods · Ethanol/therapeutic use · High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound Ablation/methods · Humans · Laser Therapy/methods · Microwaves/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sclerotherapy/methods · Thyroid Nodule/pathology/therapy · Thyroxine/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the shrinkage edge is small and the price is real. The Cochrane review found levothyroxine, versus no treatment or placebo, gave a nodule volume reduction of 50% or more in 16% of participants versus 10% after 6 to 24 months (risk ratio 1.57, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.38; 958 participants, 10 studies, moderate-quality evidence) (Bandeira-Echtler E et al., PMID: 24941398). The largest double-blind trial inside that evidence base found the same pattern for solitary nodules: a clinically relevant volume reduction in 26.6% on levothyroxine versus 16.9% on placebo (P=0.04) (Wémeau JL et al., PMID: 12414852). Against that, signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism appeared in 25% of levothyroxine-treated versus 7% of placebo-treated participants in the trials that reported them. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): suppression shrinks a minority of nodules a little more often than placebo, with hyperthyroid symptoms in a quarter of treated patients in the reporting trials.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2014: ≥50% nodule volume reduction in 16% on levothyroxine versus 10% on placebo/no treatment (RR 1.57, 95% CI 1.04–2.38) — hyperthyroid symptoms 25% versus 7%
cards.summary: Cochrane 2014: ≥50% nodule volume reduction in 16% on levothyroxine versus 10% on placebo/no treatment (RR 1.57, 95% CI 1.04–2.38) — hyperthyroid symptoms 25% versus 7%
cards.people: 31 randomised studies of 2,952 outpatients with benign thyroid nodules across all therapies reviewed; the levothyroxine comparison pooled 958 participants in 10 studies with 6 to 24 months of follow-up (levothyroxine treatment across the review ran up to five years).
cards.result: Levothyroxine versus no treatment or placebo was associated with a nodule volume reduction of 50% or more in 16% compared with 10% of participants (risk ratio 1.57, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.38; P=0.03; moderate-quality evidence). Signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism were observed in 25% of levothyroxine-treated versus 7% of placebo-treated participants at 12 to 18 months (269 participants, 3 trials, low-quality evidence). No study evaluated all-cause mortality or health-related quality of life, and pressure symptoms or cosmetic complaints were not investigated in the levothyroxine studies.
cards.watchOut: The evidence was low-to-moderate quality with high risk of performance and detection bias for subjective outcomes in most trials, and the endpoint is nodule volume — a surrogate. A 6-percentage-point absolute gain in shrinkage against an 18-point absolute excess of hyperthyroid symptoms is the honest trade this record offers.
cards.source: Bandeira-Echtler E et al. Levothyroxine or minimally invasive therapies for benign thyroid nodules. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014. PMID: 24941398. cards.headline: Wémeau 2002 (French Thyroid Research Group): ≥50% volume reduction in 26.6% on levothyroxine versus 16.9% on placebo (P=0.04) over 18 months
cards.summary: Wémeau 2002 (French Thyroid Research Group): ≥50% volume reduction in 26.6% on levothyroxine versus 16.9% on placebo (P=0.04) over 18 months
cards.people: 123 patients with a single palpable benign thyroid nodule in a French multicentre trial, randomised to levothyroxine (dose adjusted to keep serum TSH below 0.3 mIU/litre) or placebo for 18 months, with clinical and ultrasound assessment at 3, 6, 12 and 18 months.
cards.result: Mean nodule size on palpation changed by −3.5 ± 7 mm on levothyroxine versus +0.5 ± 6 mm on placebo (P=0.006), and ultrasound volume by −0.36 ± 1.71 ml versus +0.62 ± 3.67 ml (P=0.01). The proportion with a clinically relevant volume reduction (≥50%) was 26.6% versus 16.9% (P=0.04), and a reduced number of infraclinical additional nodules was seen in 9.4% versus 0% (P=0.04).
cards.watchOut: A single-nodule, palpable-nodule population treated to a suppressed TSH below 0.3 mIU/litre — deeper suppression than many clinicians would now accept for a benign condition, in a trial whose absolute shrinkage advantage was about 10 percentage points.
cards.source: Wémeau JL et al. Effects of thyroid-stimulating hormone suppression with levothyroxine in reducing the volume of solitary thyroid nodules and improving extranodular nonpalpable changes: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial by the French Thyroid Research Group. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2002. PMID: 12414852. cards.headline: Synthesis: shrinkage is real but small, symptoms are common, and no trial measured what patients feel
cards.summary: Synthesis: shrinkage is real but small, symptoms are common, and no trial measured what patients feel
cards.people: A Cochrane pooling of 10 levothyroxine trials (958 participants) plus its largest double-blind component trial (123 patients with solitary nodules, 18 months).
cards.result: ≥50% shrinkage: 16% versus 10% pooled (RR 1.57); 26.6% versus 16.9% in the solitary-nodule trial. Hyperthyroid signs and symptoms: 25% versus 7% where reported. Mortality, quality of life, pressure symptoms and cosmetic outcomes: not measured in the levothyroxine trials. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C: the pooled effect is small, the evidence quality low-to-moderate, and the harm signal sits on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Nodule volume is a surrogate; spontaneous shrinkage on placebo (10–17% reaching ≥50%) is a large part of the story, which is why the stamp stays at MAYBE (weak evidence) despite a statistically significant pooled result.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bandeira-Echtler E et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014 (PMID: 24941398); Wémeau JL et al. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2002 (PMID: 12414852).

shelves.title: Denosumab in primary hyperparathyroidism (DENOCINA): spine bone density up 6.9% versus placebo in one year in a 45-patient proof-of-concept trial — bone, not calcium, is what it treats
shelves.question: In primary hyperparathyroidism in patients unfit for or declining surgery, does denosumab improve bone mineral density versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Bone Density/drug effects · Bone Remodeling/drug effects · Cinacalcet/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Denosumab/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hyperparathyroidism, Primary/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for bone density, in one small trial. In DENOCINA, patients with primary hyperparathyroidism randomised to denosumab (with placebo tablets) gained bone mineral density over one year compared with placebo at the lumbar spine (6.9%, 95% CI 4.2 to 9.6), total hip (4.1%, 95% CI 2.5 to 5.8) and femoral neck (3.8%, 95% CI 1.4 to 6.3); the combination arm with cinacalcet gained similarly (5.4%, 5.0% and 4.5% respectively) (Leere JS et al., PMID: 32333877). Six non-fatal serious adverse events occurred across the arms (2 combination, 1 denosumab, 3 placebo), overall adverse-event prevalence did not differ between groups, and there were no fatal events. The trial enrolled patients selected for low bone density (T-score −1.0 to −3.5), not specifically patients unfit for surgery, and it measured density and turnover — not fractures or calcium control. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): denosumab improves bone mineral density over one year in primary hyperparathyroidism; fracture and calcium outcomes are untested, and the single small trial makes this Tier C.

cards.headline: Leere 2020 (DENOCINA): spine BMD +6.9% on denosumab and +5.4% on denosumab plus cinacalcet versus placebo at 1 year (p<0.0001); hip and femoral neck also improved
cards.summary: Leere 2020 (DENOCINA): spine BMD +6.9% on denosumab and +5.4% on denosumab plus cinacalcet versus placebo at 1 year (p<0.0001); hip and femoral neck also improved
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Leere 2020, DENOCINA)
cards.people: Adults with primary hyperparathyroidism at a single Danish centre (Aalborg University Hospital) with a T-score between −1.0 and −3.5 at the lumbar spine, femoral neck or total hip, randomised 1:1:1 to cinacalcet 30 mg/day plus denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months (n=14), denosumab plus placebo (n=16), or placebo plus placebo injection (n=15) for 1 year; dropout was limited to one patient in the combination group.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, bone mineral density improved in both denosumab groups: lumbar spine 5.4% (95% CI 2.7 to 8.1) for the combination and 6.9% (95% CI 4.2 to 9.6) for denosumab alone (p<0.0001); total hip 5.0% (3.0 to 6.9) and 4.1% (2.5 to 5.8) (p<0.0001); femoral neck 4.5% (1.9 to 7.9; p=0.0008) and 3.8% (1.4 to 6.3; p=0.0022). Distal forearm changes were borderline significant. Six non-fatal serious adverse events occurred (combination 2, denosumab 1, placebo 3); overall adverse-event prevalence did not differ between groups and no fatal adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: A proof-of-concept trial of 45 patients at one centre, powered for density, not fractures. Eligibility turned on low bone density rather than surgical unfitness, so the shelf's 'unfit for or declining surgery' population is an extrapolation; and denosumab does not treat the hypercalcaemia of primary hyperparathyroidism — the record's benefit is skeletal only.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one small trial, a clear density gain, and the two questions that matter — fractures and calcium — untouched
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small trial, a clear density gain, and the two questions that matter — fractures and calcium — untouched
cards.people: One randomised double-blind trial, 45 patients with primary hyperparathyroidism and low bone density, treated for 1 year.
cards.result: Bone density gains versus placebo at one year: lumbar spine 6.9% (denosumab) and 5.4% (combination); total hip 4.1% and 5.0%; femoral neck 3.8% and 4.5%. Serious adverse events: 6 non-fatal across all arms, none fatal. Fractures, kidney outcomes and calcium control were not endpoints the record reports. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: single-trial benefit claim on a surrogate endpoint.
cards.watchOut: Bone density is a surrogate with a good track record for antiresorptives generally, but primary hyperparathyroidism bone disease has its own pattern (cortical sites such as the forearm fared worst here), and stopping denosumab carries a rebound concern this one-year record cannot address.

shelves.title: Pralsetinib in RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer (ARROW): tumours responded in 60% of previously treated and 71% of treatment-naive patients — single-arm evidence, with hypertension in 17% at grade 3 or worse
shelves.question: In advanced RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer, does pralsetinib produce durable tumour responses in previously treated and treatment-naive patients?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antineoplastic Agents/therapeutic use · Carcinoma, Neuroendocrine/drug therapy/genetics/pathology · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mutation · Neoplasm Metastasis · Prognosis · Proto-Oncogene Proteins c-ret/genetics · Pyrazoles/therapeutic use · Pyridines/therapeutic use · Pyrimidines/therapeutic use · Survival Rate · Thyroid Neoplasms/drug therapy/genetics/pathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — deep responses, but from a single-arm study with no comparator. In ARROW, pralsetinib 400 mg daily produced overall responses in 33 of 55 patients (60%, 95% CI 46 to 73) with previously treated RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer and 15 of 21 (71%, 95% CI 48 to 89) with treatment-naive disease (Subbiah V et al., PMID: 34118198). The updated analysis of the same study, with more patients and longer follow-up, found responses in 55.7% of previously treated and 77.4% of treatment-naive patients, with median duration of response and progression-free survival both 25.8 months in the previously treated group (Subbiah V et al., PMID: 38009200). The price in the updated safety population was substantial: 97.1% reported a treatment-related adverse event, 52.6% needed a dose reduction, and grade 3 or worse treatment-related hypertension occurred in 17% in the primary report. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): response rates of this size in a cancer with few options are unlikely to be spontaneous, but without a randomised comparator the survival benefit is unproven — Tier C.

cards.headline: Subbiah 2021 (ARROW primary): responses in 60% of previously treated and 71% of treatment-naive RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer; grade ≥3 hypertension in 17%
cards.summary: Subbiah 2021 (ARROW primary): responses in 60% of previously treated and 71% of treatment-naive RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer; grade ≥3 hypertension in 17%
cards.people: Patients aged 18 or older with RET-altered locally advanced or metastatic thyroid cancer at 71 sites in 13 countries; 122 patients with RET-mutant medullary and 20 with RET fusion-positive thyroid cancer were enrolled, and efficacy was assessed in those with measurable disease who received pralsetinib 400 mg once daily by the July 11, 2019 cutoff.
cards.result: Overall response rates were 15 of 21 (71%, 95% CI 48 to 89) in treatment-naive RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer, 33 of 55 (60%, 95% CI 46 to 73) in patients previously treated with cabozantinib or vandetanib, and 8 of 9 (89%, 95% CI 52 to 100) in previously treated RET fusion-positive thyroid cancer; all responses were confirmed. Among 142 patients with RET-altered thyroid cancer, common grade 3 or worse treatment-related adverse events were hypertension (17%), neutropenia (13%), lymphopenia (12%) and anaemia (10%); serious treatment-related events occurred in 15%, discontinuation for treatment-related events in 4%, and one patient (1%) died of a treatment-related event.
cards.watchOut: No control arm: response rate in a single-arm study cannot show that patients live longer or feel better, and cross-trial comparison with older multikinase inhibitors is unreliable because the populations differ. Enrolment of the fusion-positive cohort was still ongoing at this interim analysis.
cards.source: Subbiah V et al. Pralsetinib for patients with advanced or metastatic RET-altered thyroid cancer (ARROW): a multi-cohort, open-label, registrational, phase 1/2 study. The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology. 2021. PMID: 34118198. Registry ID: NCT03037385. cards.headline: Subbiah 2024 (ARROW update, same study): responses 55.7% previously treated and 77.4% treatment-naive; median response duration 25.8 months in the previously treated group — not an independent confirmation
cards.summary: Subbiah 2024 (ARROW update, same study): responses 55.7% previously treated and 77.4% treatment-naive; median response duration 25.8 months in the previously treated group — not an independent confirmation
cards.type: Updated analysis of the same single-arm study (Subbiah 2024, ARROW)
cards.people: The measurable-disease population as of October 18, 2021 comprised 61 patients with RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer previously treated with cabozantinib and/or vandetanib, 62 treatment-naive patients with RET-mutant medullary cancer, and 22 patients with previously treated RET fusion-positive thyroid cancer; the safety population was 175 patients with RET-altered thyroid cancer.
cards.result: Overall response rates were 55.7% (95% CI 42.4 to 68.5) after previous cabozantinib/vandetanib, 77.4% (95% CI 65.0 to 87.1) in treatment-naive medullary cancer, and 90.9% (95% CI 70.8 to 98.9) in previously treated fusion-positive disease. Median duration of response and median progression-free survival were both 25.8 months in the previously treated medullary group and were not reached in the treatment-naive group. Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 97.1% of the safety population, led to dose reduction in 52.6% and discontinuation in 5.7%, and caused one death (0.6%).
cards.watchOut: This is a later, larger cut of the same ARROW study as the first card — it lengthens follow-up but adds no comparator and no independent replication. More than half of patients needed a dose reduction, so the 400 mg starting dose's tolerability is part of the result, not a footnote.

cards.summary: Synthesis: responses too large and durable to dismiss, survival unproven, tolerability demanding

cards.result: Response rates: 60% and 71% (primary) and 55.7% and 77.4% (updated) for previously treated and treatment-naive RET-mutant medullary cancer respectively; median duration of response 25.8 months in previously treated patients at the update. shelves.title: Total thyroidectomy versus lobectomy in low-risk papillary cancer: 5-year recurrence-free survival 95% versus 96% in the pooled cohorts — no survival advantage for taking the whole gland
shelves.question: In low-risk papillary thyroid cancer, does total thyroidectomy improve outcomes versus lobectomy?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Thyroidectomy/methods · Thyroid Cancer, Papillary/surgery/mortality · Thyroid Neoplasms/surgery/mortality/pathology · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · United States · Risk Assessment
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — more surgery did not buy better cancer outcomes in the observational record. A 2025 meta-analysis of 10 studies (17,082 patients) found 5-year recurrence-free survival in intermediate-risk papillary cancer of 96% after lobectomy and 95% after total thyroidectomy (hazard ratio 1.19, 95% CI 0.69 to 2.04), raw recurrence of 3% versus 4% across low-to-intermediate-risk cohorts, and no mortality benefit for total thyroidectomy in any risk group (Wong RSH et al., PMID: 40891682). An earlier systematic review of 13 studies of 1.0–4.0 cm tumours reached the same conclusion on disease-specific survival, while noting that four of six studies reporting disease-free survival found a small statistically significant edge for total thyroidectomy of uncertain clinical significance (Gartland RM et al., PMID: 29855833). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for low-risk papillary cancer, total thyroidectomy has not been shown to improve recurrence or survival over lobectomy — Tier C, because every study behind this is observational and confounding by indication runs against the bigger operation.

cards.headline: Wong 2025 meta-analysis: 5-year recurrence-free survival 96% lobectomy versus 95% total thyroidectomy (HR 1.19, 95% CI 0.69–2.04); recurrence 3% versus 4%; no mortality benefit
cards.summary: Wong 2025 meta-analysis: 5-year recurrence-free survival 96% lobectomy versus 95% total thyroidectomy (HR 1.19, 95% CI 0.69–2.04); recurrence 3% versus 4%; no mortality benefit
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Wong 2025)
cards.people: 10 studies totalling 17,082 patients with papillary thyroid cancer managed under the 2015 American Thyroid Association risk framework, published 2015–2025; the recurrence-free-survival pooling covered 3,881 intermediate-risk patients and the disease-specific-survival review 3,081 patients.
cards.result: Five-year recurrence-free survival in intermediate-risk disease was 96% (95% CI 89 to 99) after lobectomy and 95% (95% CI 91 to 97) after total thyroidectomy (hazard ratio 1.19, 95% CI 0.69 to 2.04; P=0.2096). Raw recurrence across low-to-intermediate-risk cohorts (n=1,119) was 3% after lobectomy and 4% after total thyroidectomy. The systematic review of disease-specific survival found no mortality benefit for total thyroidectomy across all risk groups.
cards.watchOut: All observational: surgeons choose total thyroidectomy for worse-looking cancers, which biases the comparison against it — yet it still shows no advantage. Heterogeneity was high for several pooled estimates (I² up to 92.7% for the total-thyroidectomy recurrence pool), and the record reports cancer outcomes, not the surgical harms (nerve injury, hypoparathyroidism, lifelong hormone replacement) that complete the comparison.
cards.source: Wong RSH et al. Lobectomy Versus Total Thyroidectomy Across 2015 American Thyroid Association Low-to-Intermediate-Risk Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma. cards.headline: Gartland 2018 review: no clinically significant disease-specific survival gain from total thyroidectomy for 1.0–4.0 cm tumours; a small disease-free-survival edge in 4 of 6 studies, clinical significance disputed
cards.summary: Gartland 2018 review: no clinically significant disease-specific survival gain from total thyroidectomy for 1.0–4.0 cm tumours; a small disease-free-survival edge in 4 of 6 studies, clinical significance disputed
cards.people: 13 relevant studies of papillary thyroid cancer measuring 1.0–4.0 cm (1990–2018), including eight national cancer registry database studies, one multi-institutional thyroid-cancer database, three large institutional series and one meta-analysis.
cards.result: The assembled data demonstrate that total thyroidectomy does not confer a clinically significant improvement in disease-specific survival compared with lobectomy for tumours of 1.0–4.0 cm. Four of six studies reporting disease-free survival found a small but statistically significant improvement with total thyroidectomy, whose clinical significance the authors argue is doubtful. The authors conclude that most data support comparable oncologic outcomes for lobectomy and total thyroidectomy in this size range, with tumour characteristics, patient risk factors and preferences deciding individual cases.
cards.watchOut: A narrative systematic review without pooled effect sizes in its abstract — it corroborates direction, not magnitude. Registry studies dominate, with the same confounding by indication as the meta-analysis above.
cards.source: Gartland RM et al. Impact of Extent of Surgery on Tumor Recurrence and Survival for Papillary Thyroid Cancer Patients. Annals of Surgical Oncology. 2018. PMID: 29855833. cards.headline: Synthesis: two reviews, one answer — survival and recurrence do not reward the bigger operation in low-risk disease
cards.summary: Synthesis: two reviews, one answer — survival and recurrence do not reward the bigger operation in low-risk disease
cards.people: A 2025 meta-analysis (10 studies, 17,082 patients) and a 2018 systematic review (13 studies) of lobectomy versus total thyroidectomy for low-risk and 1.0–4.0 cm papillary thyroid cancer; no randomised trial exists in these records.
cards.result: Recurrence-free survival 96% versus 95% at 5 years; raw recurrence 3% versus 4%; disease-specific survival: no clinically significant difference in either review. A small disease-free-survival advantage for total thyroidectomy in some component studies is the only signal favouring more surgery, and its own reviewers doubt its clinical significance. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C: observational evidence throughout.
cards.watchOut: 'No difference shown' in confounded observational data is weaker than a randomised non-inferiority result; patients whose tumours have adverse features were preferentially given total thyroidectomy, so the true comparison in strictly low-risk disease could differ in either direction.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wong RSH et al. Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery. 2025 (PMID: 40891682); Gartland RM et al. Annals of Surgical Oncology. 2018 (PMID: 29855833).

shelves.title: Rituximab for Graves' orbitopathy: two randomised trials, two answers — 100% improved versus intravenous steroid in Italy, 31% versus 25% on placebo at Mayo
shelves.question: In moderate-to-severe Graves' orbitopathy, does rituximab improve disease activity versus intravenous methylprednisolone or placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Murine-Derived/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Graves Ophthalmopathy/diagnosis/drug therapy · Humans · Immunologic Factors/therapeutic use · Male · Methylprednisolone/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Rituximab · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two randomised trials disagree, and the split follows the comparator. Against intravenous methylprednisolone, rituximab won clearly: at 24 weeks 100% of rituximab patients had improved versus 69% after intravenous methylprednisolone, disease reactivation occurred in five steroid patients and in no rituximab patient, and fewer rehabilitative operations followed (5 in 15 versus 12 in 16 patients) (Salvi M et al., PMID: 25494967). Against placebo, rituximab won nothing: clinical activity score improvement at 24 weeks in 31% on rituximab versus 25% on placebo (P=0.75), no difference in any secondary endpoint, and more moderate or severe adverse events on rituximab (Stan MN et al., PMID: 25343233). PROPOSED SPLIT: rituximab beat an active steroid comparator in one small trial and matched placebo in another — whether it works at all is unresolved, which is why this shelf is Tier C.

cards.headline: Salvi 2015: improvement at 24 weeks in 100% on rituximab versus 69% on intravenous methylprednisolone (P<0.001); reactivation in 0 versus 5 patients; operations 5 versus 12
cards.summary: Salvi 2015: improvement at 24 weeks in 100% on rituximab versus 69% on intravenous methylprednisolone (P<0.001); reactivation in 0 versus 5 patients; operations 5 versus 12
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial versus active comparator (Salvi 2015)
cards.people: 32 patients with active moderate-to-severe Graves' orbitopathy randomised to intravenous methylprednisolone (cumulative 7.5 g) or rituximab (2,000 mg or a single 500 mg dose); the primary endpoint was a fall in clinical activity score of at least 2 points or to below 3 at week 24, with follow-up for surgery to 76 weeks.
cards.result: The clinical activity score fell with both treatments but more after rituximab at weeks 16, 20 and 24 (P<0.04, P<0.02, P<0.006). At 24 weeks 100% of rituximab patients had improved compared with 69% after intravenous methylprednisolone (P<0.001), with no difference between the 2,000 mg and 500 mg rituximab doses. Disease reactivation was never observed after rituximab but occurred in five patients after methylprednisolone. Eye motility at 52 weeks favoured rituximab (right eye P=0.014; left eye P=0.026), and rehabilitative surgical procedures during follow-up numbered 5 in 15 rituximab patients versus 12 in 16 steroid patients (P=0.049). Registry ID: EudraCT 2007-003910-33, as printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-two patients, no placebo arm: because steroids themselves are active, this trial shows rituximab is better than this steroid regimen in this population — it cannot show how much of the rituximab arm's improvement was the drug rather than the natural history of the disease, which is exactly what the placebo-controlled trial tested.
cards.source: Salvi M et al. Efficacy of B-cell targeted therapy with rituximab in patients with active moderate to severe Graves' orbitopathy: a randomized controlled study. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2015. PMID: 25494967. Registry ID: EudraCT 2007-003910-33. cards.headline: Stan 2015 (Mayo): clinical activity improvement at 24 weeks in 31% on rituximab versus 25% on placebo (P=0.75) — no endpoint differed, and moderate/severe adverse events clustered on rituximab
cards.summary: Stan 2015 (Mayo): clinical activity improvement at 24 weeks in 31% on rituximab versus 25% on placebo (P=0.75) — no endpoint differed, and moderate/severe adverse events clustered on rituximab
cards.people: 25 patients with active moderate-to-severe Graves' orbitopathy at a large US academic centre, randomised to two rituximab infusions of 1,000 mg or two saline infusions two weeks apart; 21 completed the study to the primary endpoint at 24 weeks, with follow-up to 52 weeks.
cards.result: No differences were found in the proportions showing clinical activity score improvement at 24 weeks (31% rituximab versus 25% placebo, P=0.75) or in the fall in score from baseline at 24 weeks (mean 1.2 points on rituximab versus 1.5 on placebo, P=0.73) or 52 weeks, and no secondary endpoint (proptosis, lid fissure, diplopia, lagophthalmos, disease severity, orbital volumes, quality of life) differed at either time point. Four adverse events occurred in 3 of 12 placebo patients and 11 events in 8 of 13 rituximab patients; five of the six moderate or severe events occurred in the rituximab group.
cards.watchOut: Even smaller than its Italian counterpart, and its population differed (longer-standing disease is the usual explanation offered for the discrepancy) — but as the only placebo-controlled test it is the trial that decides whether rituximab has any effect beyond natural history, and it found none.
cards.source: Stan MN et al. Randomized controlled trial of rituximab in patients with Graves' orbitopathy. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2015. PMID: 25343233. cards.headline: Synthesis: a split verdict — superiority over steroids in one trial, equivalence with placebo in the other
cards.summary: Synthesis: a split verdict — superiority over steroids in one trial, equivalence with placebo in the other
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind trials totalling 57 patients with active moderate-to-severe Graves' orbitopathy: one versus intravenous methylprednisolone (n=32), one versus placebo (n=25).
cards.result: Versus steroid: improvement 100% versus 69%, reactivation 0 versus 5, later operations 5 versus 12 — all favouring rituximab. Versus placebo: improvement 31% versus 25%, every secondary endpoint null, adverse events more frequent on rituximab. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: two small discordant randomised trials; neither result can be discarded, and the difference in comparators is the most economical explanation.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are small enough that chance and population differences (disease duration, prior treatment) could each explain the gap. A clinician reading only the positive trial would overstate rituximab; reading only the negative one would discard a possibly real advantage over steroids in early active disease.
cards.source: Synthesis of Salvi M et al. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2015 (PMID: 25494967); Stan MN et al. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2015 (PMID: 25343233).

shelves.title: Routine calcitonin screening in nodular thyroid disease: medullary cancer in about 1 in 250 patients screened, found earlier, with complete remission in 59% versus 2.7% in a pre-screening era cohort — no randomised test
shelves.question: In nodular thyroid disease, does routine calcitonin screening detect medullary carcinoma earlier and change outcomes versus no screening?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Biomarkers, Tumor/blood · Calcitonin/blood · Carcinoma, Medullary/blood/diagnosis/surgery · Chemistry, Clinical/standards · Child · Cohort Studies · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm, Residual/blood/diagnosis · Pentagastrin · Predictive Value of Tests · Preoperative Care/standards · Reproducibility of Results · Sensitivity and Specificity · Thyroid Neoplasms/blood/diagnosis/surgery · Thyroid Nodule/blood/diagnosis/surgery
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — screening finds the cancer early; whether it saves lives is inferred, not trialled. In 5,817 consecutive patients with nodular thyroid disease, systematic calcitonin measurement identified 15 medullary cancers (and 7 cases of C-cell hyperplasia); every patient with a basal calcitonin above 100 pg/ml had medullary cancer, though the positive predictive value at the 20 pg/ml threshold was only 23.1%, so stimulation testing was needed to sort most positives (Costante G et al., PMID: 17119000). In a 10,864-patient screening experience, medullary cancer prevalence was 0.40% (44 patients, about 1 in 250), cancers were diagnosed at an earlier stage than in a pre-screening historical group (P=0.004), and complete remission at the end of follow-up was 59% versus 2.7% (P=0.0001) (Elisei R et al., PMID: 14715844). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): routine calcitonin measurement detects medullary cancer earlier and at a more curable stage — Tier C, because the outcome comparison is against a historical era, not a randomised or concurrent control.

cards.headline: Costante 2007: screening 5,817 patients found 15 medullary cancers — predictive value 100% above 100 pg/ml but only 23.1% at ≥20 pg/ml, so most positives need stimulation testing
cards.summary: Costante 2007: screening 5,817 patients found 15 medullary cancers — predictive value 100% above 100 pg/ml but only 23.1% at ≥20 pg/ml, so most positives need stimulation testing
cards.people: 5,817 consecutive patients with nodular thyroid disease (excluding multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2) at an Italian national-health-system hospital; basal serum calcitonin was measured in all, with pentagastrin stimulation when basal values were 20–100 pg/ml, and surgery when basal or stimulated levels exceeded 100 pg/ml.
cards.result: Fifteen cases of medullary thyroid carcinoma and seven of C-cell hyperplasia were identified. Medullary cancer was diagnosed in all patients with basal calcitonin above 100 pg/ml; of four patients at 50–100 pg/ml, two had medullary cancer and two C-cell hyperplasia; of ten at 20–50 pg/ml, four had medullary cancer, four C-cell hyperplasia and two no malignancy. Positive predictive values for medullary cancer were 23.1% at ≥20 pg/ml, 100% above 100 pg/ml, 25% at 50–100 pg/ml and 8.3% at 20–50 pg/ml; the pentagastrin test's predictive value was 40% in the entire series.
cards.watchOut: A diagnostic-accuracy study, not an outcomes trial: it shows screening finds cancers, at the cost of working up many false positives (roughly three of four positives at the low threshold were not medullary cancer). Whether finding them this way changes survival is tested only by the historical comparison in the second card.
cards.source: Costante G et al. Predictive value of serum calcitonin levels for preoperative diagnosis of medullary thyroid carcinoma in a cohort of 5817 consecutive patients with thyroid nodules. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2007. PMID: 17119000. cards.headline: Elisei 2004: screening 10,864 patients found medullary cancer in 0.40%, at earlier stage (P=0.004), with complete remission in 59% versus 2.7% in the pre-screening era (P=0.0001)
cards.summary: Elisei 2004: screening 10,864 patients found medullary cancer in 0.40%, at earlier stage (P=0.004), with complete remission in 59% versus 2.7% in the pre-screening era (P=0.0001)
cards.people: 10,864 patients with nodular thyroid disorders seen in 1991–1998 after routine calcitonin measurement was introduced (group 1), compared with a historical group diagnosed in 1970–1990 before calcitonin screening (group 2).
cards.result: The prevalence of medullary cancer found by calcitonin screening in group 1 was 0.40% (44 patients — nearly 1 in 250 patients with nodules). A positive calcitonin test had higher diagnostic sensitivity and specificity than fine-needle aspiration cytology. Screening allowed diagnosis at an earlier stage than in group 2 (P=0.004); post-surgical normalisation of calcitonin (undetectable) was more frequent in group 1, and at the end of follow-up complete remission was observed in 59% of group 1 versus 2.7% of group 2 (P=0.0001).
cards.watchOut: The comparison is across eras: surgery, imaging and follow-up all improved between 1970–1990 and 1991–1998, and lead-time bias inflates remission in any screen-detected group. The 59% versus 2.7% gap is therefore an upper bound on screening's true effect, not an estimate of it — which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE and Tier C rather than stronger.
cards.source: Elisei R et al. Impact of routine measurement of serum calcitonin on the diagnosis and outcome of medullary thyroid cancer: experience in 10,864 patients with nodular thyroid disorders. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2004. PMID: 14715844. cards.headline: Synthesis: screening unquestionably finds medullary cancer early; the outcome dividend rests on a historical comparison
cards.summary: Synthesis: screening unquestionably finds medullary cancer early; the outcome dividend rests on a historical comparison
cards.people: Two Italian screening cohorts totalling 16,681 patients with nodular thyroid disease (5,817 diagnostic-accuracy; 10,864 with a pre-screening historical comparator).
cards.result: Yield: 15 medullary cancers in 5,817 screened (predictive value 100% only above 100 pg/ml) and 44 in 10,864 (0.40%). Outcomes: earlier stage at diagnosis (P=0.004) and complete remission 59% versus 2.7% against the historical era. No randomised or concurrent comparison exists in these records. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: observational evidence with era confounding on the outcome claim.
cards.watchOut: Universal screening also commits health systems to stimulating tests, operations for C-cell hyperplasia of uncertain significance, and lifelong follow-up of false positives — costs the yield figures alone do not capture.

shelves.title: When to take levothyroxine: with breakfast, TSH rose to 2.93 versus 1.06 fasting in one crossover trial — but a second trial found bedtime and pre-meal dosing non-inferior, and coffee alone cuts absorption by about a third
shelves.question: In hypothyroidism, does levothyroxine absorption timing with food and interacting drugs (iron, calcium, coffee) change TSH control?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Cross-Over Studies · Drug Administration Schedule · Fasting · Female · Hormone Replacement Therapy · Humans · Hypothyroidism/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Thyroid Hormones/blood · Thyroid Neoplasms/surgery · Thyrotropin/blood/drug effects · Thyroxine/administration & dosage · Time Factors
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the food effect is consistent, the clock effect is not. In a three-period crossover trial, mean TSH was 1.06 mIU/litre when levothyroxine was taken fasting, 2.93 when taken with breakfast, and 2.19 at bedtime — both non-fasting regimens significantly higher and more variable (Bach-Huynh TG et al., PMID: 19584184). A second crossover trial, testing half an hour before breakfast against an hour before the main meal and against bedtime (at least 2 hours after dinner), found all three timings non-inferior with no significant TSH difference between any regimen (Skelin M et al., PMID: 30043093). The interacting-drinks evidence is mechanistic but direct: swallowing levothyroxine with coffee lowered the incremental rise in serum thyroxine by 36% in patients and 29% in volunteers and delayed its peak by about 40 minutes (Benvenga S et al., PMID: 18341376). PROPOSED SPLIT: taking levothyroxine with breakfast worsens TSH control in the trial that isolated breakfast; bedtime dosing split the two trials; coffee demonstrably impairs absorption — Tier C for small crossover evidence throughout.

cards.headline: Bach-Huynh 2009 crossover: TSH 1.06 fasting versus 2.93 with breakfast and 2.19 at bedtime (both significantly higher and more variable)
cards.summary: Bach-Huynh 2009 crossover: TSH 1.06 fasting versus 2.93 with breakfast and 2.19 at bedtime (both significantly higher and more variable)
cards.people: 65 patients completing the study at a US academic centre, treated with levothyroxine for hypothyroidism or thyroid cancer, each rotated through three 8-week regimens in randomised sequence: fasting ingestion, ingestion with breakfast, and ingestion at bedtime.
cards.result: Mean serum TSH was 1.06 ± 1.23 mIU/litre in the fasting state. Taken with breakfast, TSH was significantly higher at 2.93 ± 3.29 mIU/litre; taken at bedtime it was also significantly higher at 2.19 ± 2.66 mIU/litre. The authors concluded that non-fasting regimens are associated with higher and more variable TSH concentrations, and that fasting ingestion keeps TSH within the narrowest target range.
cards.watchOut: TSH is a surrogate for the clinical outcomes of hypothyroidism, and the bedtime regimen in this trial was not standardised against the evening meal the way the later trial standardised it (at least 2 hours after dinner) — a plausible reason the two trials disagree about bedtime.
cards.source: Bach-Huynh TG et al. Timing of levothyroxine administration affects serum thyrotropin concentration. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2009. PMID: 19584184. cards.headline: Skelin 2018 crossover: pre-breakfast, pre-main-meal and bedtime dosing all non-inferior — no significant TSH, free T4 or free T3 difference between any timings
cards.summary: Skelin 2018 crossover: pre-breakfast, pre-main-meal and bedtime dosing all non-inferior — no significant TSH, free T4 or free T3 difference between any timings
cards.people: 84 patients with primary hypothyroidism on a stable levothyroxine dose, rotated in crossover fashion through three regimens of at least 8 weeks each: half an hour before breakfast; an hour before the main meal of the day; and at bedtime, at least 2 hours after dinner.
cards.result: The three timings were non-inferior to the standard regimen and to each other. Median TSH differences from baseline were −0.017 (95% CI −0.400 to 0.192) for pre-breakfast, −0.325 (95% CI −0.562 to 0.023) for pre-main-meal and −0.260 (95% CI −0.475 to 0.000) for bedtime dosing, with no statistically significant differences in TSH, free T4 or free T3 between any timing regimens, and no differences in any lipid parameter.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority in 84 stable patients over 8-week periods does not exclude the breakfast effect the other trial found, because this trial never tested taking the tablet with food — its 'bedtime' arm kept a 2-hour gap from dinner. The two trials test overlapping but different questions, which is the substance of the split.
cards.source: Skelin M et al. Effect of timing of levothyroxine administration on the treatment of hypothyroidism: a three-period crossover randomized study. Endocrine. 2018. PMID: 30043093. cards.headline: Benvenga 2008: coffee swallowed with levothyroxine cut the serum thyroxine rise by 36% in patients and 29% in volunteers and delayed the peak by 38–43 minutes
cards.summary: Benvenga 2008: coffee swallowed with levothyroxine cut the serum thyroxine rise by 36% in patients and 29% in volunteers and delayed the peak by 38–43 minutes
cards.type: Absorption study series — case histories with in vivo and in vitro tests (Benvenga 2008)
cards.people: Eight women whose TSH was inappropriately high or non-suppressed when levothyroxine was swallowed with coffee/espresso, six of whom consented to formal absorption testing, plus nine volunteers; each test swallowed two 100 µg thyroxine tablets with water, with coffee, or with water followed 60 minutes later by coffee.
cards.result: Compared with water, coffee lowered the average incremental rise of serum thyroxine by 36% in patients and 29% in volunteers, the peak incremental rise by 30% and 19%, and the area under the curve by 36% and 27%, and delayed the time of maximal rise by 38 and 43 minutes respectively. Results with water followed by coffee an hour later resembled water alone. In vitro, coffee sequestered thyroxine more weakly than known interferers such as bran, aluminium hydroxide and sucralfate.
cards.watchOut: A pharmacokinetic study in 15 tested people, not a TSH-outcomes trial: it proves coffee impairs absorption when swallowed together, and the size of the effect on long-term TSH control is inferred. It does, however, test exactly the iron/calcium/coffee class of interaction the shelf asks about, with bran the stronger interferer in the same experiments.
cards.source: Benvenga S et al. Altered intestinal absorption of L-thyroxine caused by coffee. Thyroid. 2008. PMID: 18341376. cards.headline: Synthesis: keep the tablet away from breakfast and coffee; bedtime is defensible if it is kept away from dinner
cards.summary: Synthesis: keep the tablet away from breakfast and coffee; bedtime is defensible if it is kept away from dinner
cards.people: Two randomised crossover trials (65 and 84 patients) on timing, plus a 15-person absorption study series on coffee.
cards.result: With breakfast: TSH 2.93 versus 1.06 fasting in the trial that tested it. Bedtime: TSH 2.19 versus 1.06 in one trial, non-inferior (median difference −0.260) in the trial that kept bedtime at least 2 hours after food. Coffee taken with the tablet: thyroxine absorption down by roughly a third, peak delayed by about 40 minutes. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: the consistent rule across all three records is separation from food and coffee; the disagreement is only about which separated timing is best.
cards.watchOut: All endpoints are TSH or absorption surrogates over weeks, in small crossover samples. No record here tests iron or calcium co-ingestion against TSH outcomes directly — that part of the question rests on the same sequestration mechanism the coffee study demonstrated in vitro, and is flagged as a declared gap.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bach-Huynh TG et al. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2009 (PMID: 19584184); Skelin M et al. Endocrine. 2018 (PMID: 30043093); Benvenga S et al. Thyroid. 2008 (PMID: 18341376).

shelves.title: TSH suppression in differentiated thyroid cancer — a split picture: fewer major events in old mixed-risk data (RR 0.73), no benefit in low-risk disease, and observational harm signals for atrial fibrillation (HR 1.58) and postmenopausal bone loss
shelves.question: In differentiated thyroid cancer, does more intensive TSH suppression improve recurrence-free survival, and at what cost in atrial fibrillation and bone loss?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Carcinoma, Papillary/therapy · Carcinoma, Papillary, Follicular/therapy · Humans · Thyroid Hormones · Thyroid Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality · Thyrotropin/blood · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the benefit and the harm sit in different patients and different outcomes, and the evidence is observational-heavy throughout (labelled as such). Benefit component, POSSIBLE (benefit): an older meta-analysis of thyroid hormone suppression therapy found fewer major adverse clinical events (disease progression, recurrence and death) with suppression (RR 0.73; 95% CI 0.60 to 0.88) across a cumulative cohort of 4,174 patients (McGriff 2002, PMID: 12553495) — but in low-risk small cancers after lobectomy, a propensity-matched cohort of 446 patients found no disease-free-survival benefit from suppression at all (Park 2017, PMID: 28699428). Harm component, POSSIBLE (harm, observational only): a 2023 meta-analysis of 195,879 differentiated thyroid cancer patients on long-term suppression found higher risks of atrial fibrillation (HR 1.58) and stroke (HR 1.14) (Yu 2023, PMID: 37295414), and a 2021 meta-analysis found lower lumbar-spine bone mineral density in postmenopausal women on suppression (Ku 2021, PMID: 34302730). No randomised trial of suppression intensity is carded on this shelf. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for major-event reduction in the older mixed-risk data, no demonstrated benefit in low-risk disease, and POSSIBLE (harm, observational only) for atrial fibrillation and postmenopausal bone loss.

cards.headline: McGriff 2002: suppression therapy was associated with fewer major adverse events (RR 0.73) across 4,174 thyroid cancer patients — in a meta-analysis whose own authors call the primary studies imperfect
cards.summary: McGriff 2002: suppression therapy was associated with fewer major adverse events (RR 0.73) across 4,174 thyroid cancer patients — in a meta-analysis whose own authors call the primary studies imperfect
cards.type: Meta-analysis of observational and uncontrolled studies (McGriff 2002)
cards.people: Quantitative research synthesis of 28 clinical trials published 1934–2001 in papillary and/or follicular thyroid cancer, of which only 10 were amenable to meta-analysis; the cumulative cohort comprised 4,174 patients, of whom 2,880 (69%) received thyroid hormone suppression therapy (THST).
cards.result: Meta-analysis showed patients who received THST had a decreased risk of major adverse clinical events — disease progression, recurrence and death (RR = 0.73; CI = 0.60–0.88; P < 0.05). On a Likert-scale assessment, 15 of 17 interpretable studies showed either a 'likely' or 'questionable' beneficial effect of THST, and Hill-criteria assessment suggested a probable association. The authors conclude THST appears justified after initial therapy, while stating that most primary studies were imperfect and that no randomised validation exists. This is a 27% relative reduction in major adverse clinical events; the record gives no absolute event rates.
cards.watchOut: Pre-2002, largely non-randomised evidence spanning 1934–2001: patients chosen for suppression differed from those who were not, and only 10 of 28 identified studies could be pooled — confounding by indication can manufacture exactly this kind of association.
cards.source: McGriff NJ et al. Effects of thyroid hormone suppression therapy on adverse clinical outcomes in thyroid cancer. Annals of Medicine. 2002. PMID: 12553495. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Park 2017: in low-risk small thyroid cancer after lobectomy, suppression did not improve disease-free survival — recurrence was 2.7% and identical between groups over 8.6 years
cards.summary: Park 2017: in low-risk small thyroid cancer after lobectomy, suppression did not improve disease-free survival — recurrence was 2.7% and identical between groups over 8.6 years
cards.people: Retrospective propensity score-matched cohort of 446 patients with differentiated thyroid cancer who underwent lobectomy from 2002 to 2008, with or without thyrotropin suppressive therapy (TST); about 74% of the TST group and 11% of the no-TST group had suppressed serum TSH (below 2 mIU/L); median follow-up 8.6 years.
cards.result: Disease recurred in 10 patients (2.7%) during follow-up, with no significant difference in disease-free survival between the TST and no-TST groups (p = 0.63), and no difference when groups were compared by serum TSH level (p = 0.57). Excellent treatment response was similar (65.2% TST versus 64.4% no-TST); incomplete biochemical response was noted in 17.2% of the TST group and 9.4% of the no-TST group. The authors conclude TST showed no clinical benefit in low-risk patients after lobectomy and that levothyroxine is not necessary for such patients without hypothyroidism.
cards.watchOut: Observational and confined to low-risk small cancers after lobectomy, where recurrence is rare (2.7%) — it cannot exclude a benefit in higher-risk disease, which is where suppression is most often aimed.
cards.source: Park S et al. Thyrotropin Suppressive Therapy for Low-Risk Small Thyroid Cancer: A Propensity Score-Matched Cohort Study. Thyroid. 2017. PMID: 28699428. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Yu 2023: long-term TSH suppression in 195,879 thyroid cancer patients was associated with more atrial fibrillation (HR 1.58), more stroke (HR 1.14) and higher all-cause mortality (HR 2.04)
cards.summary: Yu 2023: long-term TSH suppression in 195,879 thyroid cancer patients was associated with more atrial fibrillation (HR 1.58), more stroke (HR 1.14) and higher all-cause mortality (HR 2.04)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Yu 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of cardiovascular outcomes in differentiated thyroid cancer patients on long-term TSH suppression; 195,879 patients with median follow-up of 8.6 years (range 5 to 18.8 years).
cards.result: Differentiated thyroid cancer patients were at higher risk of atrial fibrillation (HR 1.58; 95% CI 1.40 to 1.77), stroke (HR 1.14; 95% CI 1.09 to 1.20) and all-cause mortality (HR 2.04; 95% CI 1.02 to 4.07). There was no difference in risk of heart failure, ischaemic heart disease or cardiovascular mortality. The authors conclude the degree of TSH suppression must be titrated to accommodate the risk of cancer recurrence against cardiovascular morbidity.
cards.watchOut: Observational comparisons — in much of this literature the comparator is people without thyroid cancer rather than cancer patients on gentler suppression, so the hazard ratios mix the effects of the cancer, its treatment and suppression itself; the all-cause mortality estimate is imprecise (95% CI 1.02 to 4.07).
cards.source: Yu J et al. Cardiovascular Outcomes of Differentiated Thyroid Cancer Patients on Long Term TSH Suppression: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Hormone and Metabolic Research. 2023. cards.headline: Ku 2021: TSH suppression was associated with lower lumbar-spine bone density in postmenopausal women — but not in premenopausal women or men
cards.summary: Ku 2021: TSH suppression was associated with lower lumbar-spine bone density in postmenopausal women — but not in premenopausal women or men
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Ku 2021)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies of TSH suppression therapy and bone mineral density (BMD) after total thyroidectomy for differentiated thyroid cancer; 17 studies with 739 patients and 1,085 controls were included in the quantitative analysis, covering lumbar spine, femoral neck and total hip.
cards.result: In postmenopausal women, TSH suppression therapy showed a significant decrease in lumbar-spine BMD (weighted mean difference −0.03; 95% CI −0.05 to −0.02), with a similar trend at the total hip. In premenopausal women, suppression was significantly associated with higher lumbar-spine BMD (0.04; 95% CI 0.02 to 0.06) and femoral-neck BMD (0.02; 95% CI 0.01 to 0.04). In men there was no significant association at any site. The authors conclude postmenopausal women on TSH suppression are at risk for lower BMD and need attention to long-term skeletal safety. The record reports BMD differences, not fracture rates.
cards.watchOut: Bone density is a surrogate — no fracture outcomes are reported in this record — and the premenopausal 'higher BMD' finding runs against the harm direction, underlining that these are confounded observational comparisons, not randomised contrasts of suppression intensity.

cards.headline: Synthesis: suppression's event benefit comes from old, mixed-risk, non-randomised data and disappears in low-risk disease, while atrial fibrillation and postmenopausal bone loss track with long-term suppression — a split verdict
cards.summary: Synthesis: suppression's event benefit comes from old, mixed-risk, non-randomised data and disappears in low-risk disease, while atrial fibrillation and postmenopausal bone loss track with long-term suppression — a split verdict
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis of pre-2002 studies (4,174 patients), one propensity-matched cohort in low-risk disease (446 patients), and two observational meta-analyses of harm (195,879 patients for cardiovascular outcomes; 17 studies, 739 patients and 1,085 controls, for bone density). No randomised trial of suppression intensity is carded.
cards.result: Suppression was associated with fewer major adverse clinical events overall (RR 0.73; McGriff 2002) but with no disease-free-survival benefit in low-risk small cancers (Park 2017). On the harm side, long-term suppression was associated with atrial fibrillation (HR 1.58) and stroke (HR 1.14) (Yu 2023) and with lower lumbar-spine bone density in postmenopausal women only (Ku 2021). PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for major-event reduction in the older mixed-risk data with no demonstrated benefit in low-risk disease; POSSIBLE (harm, observational only) for atrial fibrillation and postmenopausal bone loss.
cards.watchOut: Nothing on this shelf randomises suppression intensity: every contrast is between patients clinicians chose to suppress and those they did not, so both the benefit and the harm estimates carry confounding by indication in opposite directions.
cards.source: Synthesis of McGriff NJ et al. Annals of Medicine. 2002 (PMID: 12553495); Park S et al. Thyroid. 2017 (PMID: 28699428); Yu J et al. Hormone and Metabolic Research. 2023 (PMID: 37295414); Ku EJ et al. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2021 (PMID: 34302730).

shelves.title: Encaleret in autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia type 1 — promising but tiny evidence: calcium corrected and urinary calcium reduced over 24 weeks in N = 13 (open-label, no controls), with an N = 5 proof-of-concept study behind it and conventional therapy's renal harms as the rationale
shelves.question: In autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia type 1, does the calcilytic encaleret normalise serum calcium and reduce urinary calcium versus conventional therapy?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Calcium/metabolism · Calcium-Regulating Hormones and Agents/therapeutic use · Genes, Dominant/genetics · Humans · Hypercalciuria/drug therapy · Hypercalciuria/genetics · Hypocalcemia/drug therapy · Hypocalcemia/genetics · Hypoparathyroidism/congenital · Hypoparathyroidism/drug therapy · Hypoparathyroidism/genetics · Mutation · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the human evidence for calcilytics in autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia type 1 (ADH1) totals 18 treated patients across two uncontrolled studies, with the study numbers printed on the face of this shelf. In the encaleret phase 2b study (N = 13 adults with ADH1), encaleret corrected hypocalcaemia and reduced hypercalciuria during inpatient dose-ranging and a 24-week outpatient period, with calcitriol and calcium supplements withheld, no serious adverse events and no discontinuations (Gafni 2023, PMID: 37754292; the report is a journal letter whose PubMed record carries no abstract, and its laboratory values are reported in its figure rather than as numbers in the text). An earlier calcilytic, NPSP795, raised plasma parathyroid hormone up to 129% above baseline in a 3-day proof-of-concept study (N = 5 adults; Roberts 2019, PMID: 31063613). The need is real: in the ADH1 systematic review, 75% of 57 patients assessed on conventional calcium and active vitamin D therapy had at least one renal or related complication, and starting conventional therapy increased the incidence of hypercalciuria by 91% in the 27 patients with before-and-after urine measures (Roszko 2022, PMID: 35879818). There is no randomised or controlled comparison of encaleret against conventional therapy. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — based on a very small total N = 18 across two uncontrolled calcilytic studies.

cards.headline: Gafni 2023 (N = 13, printed on the face): encaleret corrected hypocalcaemia and reduced hypercalciuria over 24 weeks in 13 adults with ADH1, with no serious adverse events — an open-label phase 2b letter with no control group
cards.summary: Gafni 2023 (N = 13, printed on the face): encaleret corrected hypocalcaemia and reduced hypercalciuria over 24 weeks in 13 adults with ADH1, with no serious adverse events — an open-label phase 2b letter with no control group
cards.type: Open-label phase 2b study reported as a journal letter (Gafni 2023) — N = 13
cards.people: 13 adults with autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia type 1 (ADH1) caused by nine different CASR variants, all non-Hispanic White, treated with the investigational oral calcilytic encaleret in an open-label phase 2b study (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04581629, as printed in the letter's full text): one or two 5-day inpatient dose-ranging periods followed by a 24-week outpatient period, encaleret twice daily (dose range required to maintain eucalcaemia 5 to 190 mg twice daily), with calcitriol and supplemental calcium withheld during treatment. N = 13 is printed here under the reference-floor rule for small studies.
cards.result: Encaleret corrected hypocalcemia and reduced hypercalciuria during the inpatient periods and the 24-week outpatient period; mean blood levels of intact parathyroid hormone, magnesium and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D increased, while phosphorus levels and tubular reabsorption of phosphate decreased. Individual doses were mostly stable with minimal adjustments. Renal function and preexisting renal calcifications did not worsen, bone-turnover markers rose (remaining normal in 9 of 13 participants) and short-term effects on bone density were negligible. No serious adverse events were reported; treatment-related adverse events were limited to infrequent mild, transient, asymptomatic hypophosphatemia, hypercalcemia, or both, and there were no treatment discontinuations or study withdrawals. The letter reports laboratory values graphically (its Figure 1) rather than as numbers in the text, so no mean calcium or urinary-calcium values are printed on this card.
cards.watchOut: No abstract exists in the PubMed record (publication type: Letter) and no control group exists in the study: 13 patients, open-label, 24 weeks, with the numeric laboratory results presented only in a figure — this is hypothesis-confirming early evidence, not a demonstrated advantage over conventional therapy.
cards.source: Gafni RI et al. Efficacy and Safety of Encaleret in Autosomal Dominant Hypocalcemia Type 1. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 37754292. Registry ID: NCT04581629. cards.headline: Roberts 2019 (N = 5, printed on the face): the earlier calcilytic NPSP795 raised parathyroid hormone up to 129% above baseline over 3 days in 5 adults with ADH1 — proof of concept only
cards.summary: Roberts 2019 (N = 5, printed on the face): the earlier calcilytic NPSP795 raised parathyroid hormone up to 129% above baseline over 3 days in 5 adults with ADH1 — proof of concept only
cards.people: Five adults with ADH1 due to four distinct CASR (reported as CAR) mutations, who received escalating doses of the calcilytic compound NPSP795 (SHP635) on 3 consecutive days, with pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, efficacy and safety assessed, and parallel in vitro testing of each subject's mutant calcium-sensing receptor. N = 5 is printed here under the reference-floor rule for studies under 10 humans.
cards.result: NPSP795 increased plasma parathyroid hormone levels in a concentration-dependent manner, up to 129% above baseline (p = 0.013) at the highest exposure levels. Fractional excretion of calcium trended down but not significantly. Blood ionized calcium levels remained stable during infusion despite fasting, no calcitriol supplementation and little calcium supplementation. NPSP795 was generally safe and well tolerated, with significant variability in clinical response across genotypes; in vitro responses did not correlate with clinical parameters. The authors present this as proof of concept that calcilytics could be an effective treatment for ADH1.
cards.watchOut: Five patients and 3 days of dosing of a different, earlier calcilytic — it supports the drug class mechanism (raising parathyroid hormone) and says nothing about sustained calcium control, urinary calcium over time, or renal outcomes.
cards.source: Roberts MS et al. Treatment of Autosomal Dominant Hypocalcemia Type 1 With the Calcilytic NPSP795 (SHP635). Journal of Bone and Mineral Research. 2019. PMID: 31063613. cards.headline: Roszko 2022: on conventional therapy, 75% of assessed ADH1 patients had at least one complication, and starting calcium plus active vitamin D increased hypercalciuria incidence by 91% — the problem calcilytics aim to solve
cards.summary: Roszko 2022: on conventional therapy, 75% of assessed ADH1 patients had at least one complication, and starting calcium plus active vitamin D increased hypercalciuria incidence by 91% — the problem calcilytics aim to solve
cards.type: Systematic review of published cases and series (Roszko 2022)
cards.people: Systematic literature review of published ADH1 reports from 1994 to 2021: 113 unique CASR variants; clinical data available in 191 patients; blood and urine chemistries at diagnosis in 91 patients; complications assessed in 57 patients on conventional therapy; urine calcium measures before and after starting conventional therapy in 27 patients.
cards.result: At diagnosis, hypocalcemia was present in 99%, hyperphosphatemia in 59%, low parathyroid hormone in 57% and hypercalciuria in 34%; seizures were the most frequent presentation (39%), and 41% had severe symptoms. Among 57 patients on conventional therapy assessed for complications (nephrocalcinosis, nephrolithiasis, renal impairment, brain calcifications), 75% had at least one complication, and hypercalciuria was associated with those complications (OR 9.3; 95% CI 2.4 to 37.2). In the 27 patients with urine calcium measures before and after starting conventional therapy, the incidence of hypercalciuria increased by 91% (p < 0.05) after therapy initiation. Blood calcium was lower in severely symptomatic patients (6.8 ± 0.7 versus 7.6 ± 0.7 mg/dL).
cards.watchOut: A review of published case reports and series, not a cohort with a denominator: complication rates in published cases overstate typical risk, and the before-and-after hypercalciuria comparison rests on 27 patients — it frames the rationale for calcilytics but is not comparative evidence for encaleret.
cards.source: Roszko KL et al. Autosomal Dominant Hypocalcemia Type 1: A Systematic Review. Journal of Bone and Mineral Research. 2022. PMID: 35879818. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: calcilytics do what their mechanism predicts in ADH1 — raise parathyroid hormone, correct calcium, lower urinary calcium — but the entire treated human evidence base is 18 patients in uncontrolled studies
cards.summary: Synthesis: calcilytics do what their mechanism predicts in ADH1 — raise parathyroid hormone, correct calcium, lower urinary calcium — but the entire treated human evidence base is 18 patients in uncontrolled studies
cards.people: The carded evidence: one open-label phase 2b encaleret study (N = 13), one 3-day proof-of-concept study of an earlier calcilytic (N = 5), and one systematic review of the ADH1 literature (191 patients with clinical data) describing the harms of conventional therapy. No randomised or controlled trial is carded.
cards.result: Encaleret corrected hypocalcemia and reduced hypercalciuria over 24 weeks with no serious adverse events in 13 adults (Gafni 2023), and NPSP795 raised parathyroid hormone up to 129% above baseline in 5 adults (Roberts 2019) — consistent, mechanism-concordant, and uncontrolled. The clinical rationale is strong because conventional therapy itself worsens hypercalciuria and most assessed patients on it had a complication (Roszko 2022). Whether encaleret beats conventional therapy on calcium control, symptoms or renal outcomes is untested in any controlled comparison. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — based on a very small total N = 18 across two uncontrolled calcilytic studies.
cards.watchOut: Rare-disease evidence this small can be overturned by a single larger study; the phase 3 programme referenced in the slate (CALIBRATE) had no indexed results record this session, so nothing on this shelf should be read as settled efficacy.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gafni RI et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2023 (PMID: 37754292); Roberts MS et al. Journal of Bone and Mineral Research. 2019 (PMID: 31063613); Roszko KL et al. Journal of Bone and Mineral Research. 2022 (PMID: 35879818).

shelves.title: Generic vs brand-name levothyroxine: TSH in range at near-identical rates in large cohorts (75.4% vs 76.9% in new users) — generic is as effective for maintaining TSH, on observational evidence
shelves.question: In adults with hypothyroidism, is generic levothyroxine as effective as brand-name levothyroxine for maintaining TSH in range?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Comparative Effectiveness Research · Databases, Factual · Drug Prescriptions · Drugs, Generic · Female · Humans · Longitudinal Studies · Male · Medicare · Middle Aged · Propensity Score · Retrospective Studies · Thyroid Diseases · Thyrotropin · Thyroxine · Treatment Outcome · United States
shelves.balance: Essentially yes, on the evidence carded. In the largest head-to-head cohort of new users (Brito 2020, PMID: 32997127; 4,570 propensity-matched patients), normal thyrotropin within 3 months was achieved by 75.4% on generic vs 76.9% on brand-name levothyroxine (P = .23, no significant difference), with similar maintenance of normal levels thereafter. A much larger matched cohort of persistent users (Wang 2022, PMID: 34905150; 18,382 per group) found a statistically significant but very small difference the other way: 78.5% in range on brand vs 77.2% on generic (P = .002) — 1.3 percentage points. The classic randomised crossover bioequivalence trial (Dong 1997, PMID: 9103344; 22 women) found the tested generic and brand products bioequivalent, with relative bioequivalence of 0.95 to 1.07. The clinical-outcome evidence is observational, which caps the stamp. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (generic is as effective) — observational only for the TSH outcome: generic and brand-name levothyroxine maintain TSH in range at near-identical rates.

cards.headline: Brito 2020: normal thyrotropin within 3 months in 75.4% starting generic vs 76.9% starting brand-name levothyroxine (P = .23, no difference) in 4,570 matched new users
cards.summary: Brito 2020: normal thyrotropin within 3 months in 75.4% starting generic vs 76.9% starting brand-name levothyroxine (P = .23, no difference) in 4,570 matched new users
cards.people: Adults with thyrotropin 4.5 to 19.9 mIU/L initiating levothyroxine in a US claims-and-laboratory database (17,598 patients in total; 15,299 generic and 2,299 brand-name initiators), with a 1:1 propensity-matched cohort of 4,570 patients analysed for the primary comparisons.
cards.result: In the matched cohort, the proportion with normal thyrotropin levels within 3 months was similar for generic vs brand-name levothyroxine (75.4%; 95% CI, 71.9% to 79.0% vs 76.9%; 95% CI, 73.4% to 80.6%; P = .23), as was the proportion with markedly abnormal levels, under 0.1 or over 10 mIU/L (4.1% vs 3.9%; P = .65). Among 1,034 matched patients who achieved a normal value, the proportion maintaining normal levels over the next 3 months was also similar (82.6% vs 83.8%; P = .62). The authors conclude generic levothyroxine as initial therapy for mild thyroid dysfunction is as effective as brand-name.
cards.watchOut: Observational and confined to initiation in mild dysfunction (thyrotropin 4.5–19.9 mIU/L): it does not test switching stable patients between products, where the narrow-therapeutic-index concern is usually raised, nor pregnancy or post-thyroidectomy replacement.
cards.source: Brito JP et al. Comparative Effectiveness of Generic vs Brand-Name Levothyroxine in Achieving Normal Thyrotropin Levels. JAMA Network Open. 2020. PMID: 32997127. retrospective propensity-matched cohort study (brito 2020) adults with thyrotropin 4.5 to 19.9 miu/l initiating levothyroxine in a us claims-and-laboratory database (17,598 patients in total; 15,299 generic and 2,299 brand-name initiators), with a 1:1 propensity-matched cohort of 4,570 patients analysed for the primary comparisons. in the matched cohort, the proportion with normal thyrotropin levels within 3 months was similar for generic vs brand-name levothyroxine (75.4%; 95% ci, 71.9% to 79.0% vs 76.9%; 95% ci, 73.4% to 80.6%; p = .23), as was the proportion with markedly abnormal levels, under 0.1 or over 10 miu/l (4.1% vs 3.9%; p = .65). among 1,034 matched patients who achieved a normal value, the proportion maintaining normal levels over the next 3 months was also similar (82.6% vs 83.8%; p = .62). the authors conclude generic levothyroxine as initial therapy for mild thyroid dysfunction is as effective as brand-name. observational and confined to initiation in mild dysfunction (thyrotropin 4.5–19.9 miu/l): it does not test switching stable patients between products, where the narrow-therapeutic-index concern is usually raised, nor pregnancy or post-thyroidectomy replacement. brito jp et al. comparative effectiveness of generic vs brand-name levothyroxine in achieving normal thyrotropin levels. jama network open. 2020. pmid: 32997127. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · comparative effectiveness research · databases, factual · drug prescriptions · drugs, generic · female · humans · longitudinal studies · male · medicare · middle aged · propensity score · retrospective studies · thyroid diseases · thyrotropin · thyroxine · treatment outcome · united states

cards.headline: Wang 2022: in 36,764 matched persistent users, TSH in range was 78.5% on brand vs 77.2% on generic (P = .002) — a statistically significant difference of 1.3 percentage points
cards.summary: Wang 2022: in 36,764 matched persistent users, TSH in range was 78.5% on brand vs 77.2% on generic (P = .002) — a statistically significant difference of 1.3 percentage points
cards.people: Patients with hypothyroidism in a US managed-care database who were persistent users of brand-name levothyroxine (Synthroid, named in the record) or of generic levothyroxine, propensity-matched 1:1 to 18,382 patients per cohort, with at least one TSH result during 12-month follow-up; the reference range was 0.3–4.12 mIU/L.
cards.result: At follow-up, significantly more patients receiving the brand product were in the TSH reference range than on generic (78.5% vs 77.2%, P = .002) — an absolute difference of 1.3 percentage points. Healthcare utilisation and costs were broadly similar between cohorts; irrespective of product, patients with TSH in range had significantly lower hypothyroidism-related costs than those out of range. The authors conclude the brand product was associated with better TSH target achievement in this population.
cards.watchOut: With 36,764 patients, a 1.3-point difference clears statistical significance without being clinically large, and persistent-user designs favour the product patients were already stable on; residual confounding by why patients were kept on brand cannot be excluded. The brand product is named here only because the record names the tested product.
cards.source: Wang L et al. Comparative Effectiveness of Persistent Use of a Name-Brand Levothyroxine (Synthroid®) vs. Persistent Use of Generic Levothyroxine on TSH Goal Achievement: A Retrospective Study Among Patients with Hypothyroidism in a Managed Care Setting. cards.headline: Dong 1997: in a randomised 4-way crossover of 22 women, two generic levothyroxine products and two brand products were bioequivalent (relative bioequivalence 0.95 to 1.07)
cards.summary: Dong 1997: in a randomised 4-way crossover of 22 women, two generic levothyroxine products and two brand products were bioequivalent (relative bioequivalence 0.95 to 1.07)
cards.people: 22 women with hypothyroidism who were clinically and chemically euthyroid on levothyroxine 0.1 or 0.15 mg, each receiving all 4 products (two brand-name and two generic preparations, named in the record) for 6-week periods in randomised sequence without washout. Randomised N = 22, printed here because it is small.
cards.result: No significant differences between the 4 products were found in area under the curve or peak concentrations of total thyroxine, total triiodothyronine, or free thyroxine index. The FDA criterion for bioequivalence (90% confidence intervals within 0.8–1.25) was met for all pairs of products (P < .05), with demonstrated relative bioequivalence of 0.95 to 1.07 — tighter than the criterion. The authors conclude the preparations studied are bioequivalent by FDA criteria and interchangeable in the majority of patients, while noting further work is needed for all existing preparations.
cards.watchOut: Bioequivalence was judged on thyroxine pharmacokinetics in 22 already-euthyroid women, not on long-term TSH control after switching, and the specific 1997 products are not today's formulations; it supports, but cannot by itself settle, present-day interchangeability.
cards.source: Dong BJ et al. Bioequivalence of generic and brand-name levothyroxine products in the treatment of hypothyroidism. JAMA. 1997. PMID: 9103344. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: generic levothyroxine maintains TSH in range at near-identical rates to brand-name in large cohorts, and the tested products were bioequivalent in a randomised crossover
cards.summary: Synthesis: generic levothyroxine maintains TSH in range at near-identical rates to brand-name in large cohorts, and the tested products were bioequivalent in a randomised crossover
cards.people: The carded evidence: two large retrospective propensity-matched cohorts (4,570 matched new users; 36,764 matched persistent users) and one small randomised crossover bioequivalence trial (N = 22). Total participants exceed 40,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the crossover's small N is printed on its card.
cards.result: Normal thyrotropin within 3 months: 75.4% generic vs 76.9% brand (P = .23) (Brito 2020). TSH in range at 12 months among persistent users: 77.2% generic vs 78.5% brand (P = .002), a 1.3-point difference (Wang 2022). Bioequivalence of tested products: 0.95 to 1.07 (Dong 1997). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (generic is as effective) — observational only for the TSH outcome.
cards.watchOut: None of the carded evidence tests the common clinical worry — repeated pharmacy-level switching among different generic manufacturers in a stable patient — and guidelines' advice to recheck TSH after any product change is not contradicted by anything on this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Brito JP et al. JAMA Network Open. 2020 (PMID: 32997127); Wang L et al. Advances in Therapy. 2022 (PMID: 34905150); Dong BJ et al. JAMA. 1997 (PMID: 9103344).
