shelves.title: Levothyroxine starting dose after total thyroidectomy: weight-based dosing does not achieve euthyroidism faster — only about a third of patients are euthyroid at first follow-up on any scheme
shelves.question: After total thyroidectomy for benign disease, does weight-based levothyroxine dosing achieve euthyroidism faster than fixed low-dose starting?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Thyroidectomy · Thyroxine · Hormone Replacement Therapy · Hypothyroidism · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug
shelves.balance: No faster or more reliable achievement is shown — on any scheme, only about a third of patients are euthyroid at the first follow-up. A systematic review and meta-analysis of dosing strategies after total thyroidectomy (Chiardi 2025, PMID: 40682434; 11 studies, 2,577 patients) found a pooled first-follow-up euthyroidism rate of 33.9%, with weight-based (dose/kg) methods at 29% and fixed or algorithm-based approaches at 40%, without statistical significance — no strategy consistently outperformed the others (the treatment made no difference between strategies). In the benign-disease cohort behind the leading dosing-scheme comparison (Zaborek 2019, PMID: 30413325; 598 patients), standard weight-based dosing at 1.6 µg/kg/day predicted the eventual euthyroid dose correctly in only 51.3% of patients, and an external validation in benign thyroidectomy (Valenzuela 2021, PMID: 33845415) found weight-based accuracy of 53.8% with overdosing errors in 32.1%. The carded studies compare prediction accuracy and first-follow-up rates rather than time-to-euthyroidism directly, and none shows weight-based dosing beating a fixed start. PROPOSED MAYBE (benefit) unproven — weight-based dosing has not been shown to achieve euthyroidism faster than fixed low-dose starting.

cards.headline: Chiardi 2025: across 11 studies (2,577 patients), only 33.9% were euthyroid at first follow-up after total thyroidectomy — weight-based dosing 29% vs fixed or algorithm-based 40%, not significant (the strategies made no difference)
cards.summary: Chiardi 2025: across 11 studies (2,577 patients), only 33.9% were euthyroid at first follow-up after total thyroidectomy — weight-based dosing 29% vs fixed or algorithm-based 40%, not significant (the strategies made no difference)
cards.people: 2,577 patients after total thyroidectomy in 11 studies (2000–2024) reporting the proportion achieving euthyroidism at first follow-up, covering fixed-dose, weight-based (dose/kg) and individualised algorithm-based levothyroxine starting strategies, for benign and malignant disease.
cards.result: The pooled euthyroidism rate at first follow-up was 33.9%, with high heterogeneity (I² = 82.68%). No dosing strategy consistently outperformed others: dose/kg methods achieved 29% euthyroidism, while fixed or algorithm-based approaches achieved 40%, without statistical significance. Meta-regression identified no significant predictor, and no significant differences emerged between benign and malignant disease or between retrospective and prospective designs. The authors conclude that only about one-third of patients achieve euthyroidism at first follow-up regardless of strategy, and that the guideline weight-based recommendation may not be adequate.
cards.watchOut: High heterogeneity (I² = 82.68%) and mixed benign/malignant populations mean the 29% vs 40% contrast is a subgroup description, not a randomised comparison; the robust finding is the low overall first-follow-up rate on every scheme.
cards.source: Chiardi I et al. Establishing the Adequate Levothyroxine Dose After Total Thyroidectomy: A Systematic Review With Meta-analysis. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2025. PMID: 40682434. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zaborek 2019: in 598 patients euthyroid after thyroidectomy for benign disease, standard weight-based dosing (1.6 µg/kg/day) predicted the right dose in only 51.3%
cards.summary: Zaborek 2019: in 598 patients euthyroid after thyroidectomy for benign disease, standard weight-based dosing (1.6 µg/kg/day) predicted the right dose in only 51.3%
cards.people: 598 patients who attained euthyroidism after total or completion thyroidectomy for benign disease, analysed retrospectively; seven published dosing schemes and thirteen machine-learning algorithms were compared by the proportion of predicted doses within 12.5 µg/day of the patient's eventual euthyroid dose.
cards.result: A novel Poisson regression model was most accurate, correctly predicting 64.8% of doses, significantly better than the best literature scheme (body-mass-index/weight-based, 60.9%; P = .031). Standard weight-based dosing (1.6 µg/kg/day) correctly predicted 51.3% of doses, and the least effective scheme (age/sex/weight-based) 27.4%. The authors conclude that a multivariable scheme outperforms weight-based dosing in estimating the euthyroid dose.
cards.watchOut: Prediction accuracy within 12.5 µg/day is a surrogate for speed: the study does not report time to euthyroidism or first-follow-up euthyroid rates by starting scheme, so it bounds how often weight-based dosing starts at the right dose rather than measuring faster achievement directly.
cards.source: Zaborek NA et al. The optimal dosing scheme for levothyroxine after thyroidectomy: A comprehensive comparison and evaluation. Surgery. 2019. PMID: 30413325. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Valenzuela 2021: in benign total thyroidectomy, weight-based dosing predicted the euthyroid dose with 53.8% accuracy and overdosed 32.1% of patients (over 25 µg too high)
cards.summary: Valenzuela 2021: in benign total thyroidectomy, weight-based dosing predicted the euthyroid dose with 53.8% accuracy and overdosed 32.1% of patients (over 25 µg too high)
cards.people: 406 patients undergoing total or completion thyroidectomy for benign disease at a single institution (2011–2019), of whom 184 had follow-up data confirming a euthyroid state (TSH 0.45–4.5 mIU/L) and formed the accuracy analysis; 85.9% women, 56.5% obese, median BMI 30.8 kg/m².
cards.result: The multivariable Poisson scheme's accuracy was 60.3% (n = 111) versus 53.8% (n = 99) for the weight-based standard — higher but not statistically significant (P = 0.21). Overdosing errors (over 25 µg) were more frequent with weight-based dosing: 32.1% vs 17.9% (P = 0.0025), and in obese patients 45.2% vs 19.2% (P = 0.0006). Predicted doses from the two schemes differed by an entire dose step on average (mean 16.0 µg) and disagreed in 76% of patients.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre and retrospective, with accuracy assessed only in the 184 patients documented euthyroid; the overdosing signal is concentrated in obesity, where actual-body-weight dosing predictably overshoots — a caution about weight-based dosing, not proof a fixed low dose is better overall.
cards.source: Valenzuela F et al. Comparison of Dosing Schemes for Thyroid Hormone Replacement Therapy After Thyroidectomy. The Journal of Surgical Research. 2021. PMID: 33845415. shelves.title: Ultrasound surveillance after benign thyroid cytology: it detects growth in 15.4% and cancer in 0.3% over 5 years, but no evidence shows it improves outcomes versus clinical follow-up alone (observational only)
shelves.question: In adults with a solitary thyroid nodule and benign cytology, does routine repeat ultrasound surveillance improve outcomes versus clinical follow-up alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Disease Progression · Female · Humans · Incidence · Incidental Findings · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Risk Factors · Thyroid Neoplasms · Thyroid Nodule · Ultrasonography
shelves.balance: No trial has ever compared the two strategies, so improved outcomes from routine repeat ultrasound are unproven; the observational record shows what surveillance finds and what it misses. In a prospective multicentre cohort under yearly ultrasound surveillance (Durante 2015, PMID: 25734734; 992 patients with benign nodules), growth occurred in 15.4% over 5 years and thyroid cancer was diagnosed in 5 original nodules (0.3%), only 2 of which had grown. In a large biopsy cohort with median 13.9 years of follow-up (Ng 2021, PMID: 33371796; 2,207 patients), the false-negative rate for benign cytology was 3.2% (1.5% excluding papillary microcarcinomas), and no patient with a false-negative diagnosis died of thyroid cancer. A major review (Durante 2018, PMID: 29509871) frames most benign nodules as safely managed with a surveillance programme aimed at the small subgroup harbouring significant cancer (about 10% as printed in the record), with the initial risk estimate determining follow-up intensity. All evidence is observational, which caps the stamp. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) unproven — observational only: routine ultrasound surveillance detects the rare missed cancer, but no evidence shows it improves outcomes versus clinical follow-up alone.

cards.headline: Durante 2015: under yearly ultrasound surveillance, benign nodules grew in 15.4% of 992 patients over 5 years, and cancer was found in 0.3% of original nodules — only 2 of the 5 cancers had grown
cards.summary: Durante 2015: under yearly ultrasound surveillance, benign nodules grew in 15.4% of 992 patients over 5 years, and cancer was found in 0.3% of original nodules — only 2 of the 5 cancers had grown
cards.people: 992 consecutive patients with 1 to 4 asymptomatic, sonographically or cytologically benign thyroid nodules (1,567 nodules), recruited at 8 Italian thyroid referral centres (2006–2008) and followed prospectively with yearly thyroid ultrasound for 5 years.
cards.result: Nodule growth occurred in 153 patients (15.4%; 95% CI, 14.3% to 16.5%); 174 of 1,567 nodules (11.1%) increased in size, by a mean of 4.9 mm in largest diameter over 5 years. Nodules shrank spontaneously in 184 individuals (18.5%). Thyroid cancer was diagnosed in 5 original nodules (0.3%; 95% CI, 0.0% to 0.6%), of which only 2 had grown; new nodules developed in 93 patients (9.3%), with one cancer detected among them. Growth was associated with multiple nodules (OR up to 8.9 for 4 nodules), larger baseline volume (OR about 3.0) and male sex (OR 1.7), and was less likely at age 60 or older (OR 0.5). The authors conclude the majority of benign nodules show no significant size increase during 5 years of follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Everyone in this cohort received surveillance, so it measures the yield of surveillance, not its benefit over clinical follow-up; growth itself was a poor cancer signal (3 of 5 cancers had not grown), which cuts both ways in the surveillance argument.
cards.source: Durante C et al. The natural history of benign thyroid nodules. JAMA. 2015. PMID: 25734734. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ng 2021: over a median 13.9 years, benign-cytology false negatives were 3.2% (1.5% excluding microcarcinomas) among 2,207 biopsied patients, and no false-negative patient died of thyroid cancer
cards.summary: Ng 2021: over a median 13.9 years, benign-cytology false negatives were 3.2% (1.5% excluding microcarcinomas) among 2,207 biopsied patients, and no false-negative patient died of thyroid cancer
cards.people: 2,207 patients with initial thyroid fine-needle aspiration biopsies at a US academic centre (1997–2004), reclassified by the 2017 Bethesda System and matched to institutional and California cancer registries; median follow-up 13.9 years (range 10.5–18.4 years), with 279 confirmed thyroid malignancies during follow-up.
cards.result: Kaplan-Meier estimates showed the risk of malignancy was low for nondiagnostic and benign categories, intermediate for atypia/follicular lesion of undetermined significance and follicular neoplasm, and high for suspicious and malignant categories. A total of 52 of 1,575 false-negative cases (3.2%) were identified; excluding papillary microcarcinomas the false-negative rate was 1.5% (23 of 1,575). No patient with a false-negative diagnosis died of thyroid cancer during follow-up. The authors conclude asymptomatic patients with low-risk features and initially benign or unsatisfactory biopsy are unlikely to develop thyroid malignancy and highly unlikely to die of thyroid cancer.
cards.watchOut: This cohort includes all cytology categories and multinodular glands, not only solitary benign nodules, and follow-up intensity was clinical practice rather than a protocol; it bounds the danger of a benign result rather than testing a surveillance schedule.
cards.source: Ng DL et al. A Large Thyroid Fine Needle Aspiration Biopsy Cohort with Long-Term Population-Based Follow-Up. Thyroid. 2021. PMID: 33371796. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Durante 2018: most thyroid nodules are benign and safely managed with surveillance aimed at the small significant-cancer subgroup — with follow-up intensity set by the initial ultrasound and cytology risk estimate
cards.summary: Durante 2018: most thyroid nodules are benign and safely managed with surveillance aimed at the small significant-cancer subgroup — with follow-up intensity set by the initial ultrasound and cytology risk estimate
cards.people: Narrative review of the diagnosis and management of thyroid nodules for the general clinical readership, covering nodules detected in up to 65% of the general population; no new patient data are reported in the record.
cards.result: The record reports no comparative effect size for surveillance versus clinical follow-up. Its framing: most nodules are benign and clinically insignificant; the main goal of initial and long-term follow-up is identification of the small subgroup that harbour a clinically significant cancer (about 10% as printed in the record), cause compressive symptoms (about 5%), or progress to functional disease (about 5%). The initial risk estimate, derived from ultrasound and (if performed) cytology, should determine the need for treatment and the type, frequency and length of subsequent follow-up; management ranges from simple observation to local treatments and surgery.
cards.watchOut: A review card is context, not outcome evidence: it shows expert practice endorses risk-stratified surveillance, but endorsement is not a demonstration that routine repeat ultrasound improves outcomes over clinical follow-up.
cards.source: Durante C et al. The Diagnosis and Management of Thyroid Nodules: A Review. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 29509871. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: surveillance finds growth in about 1 in 6 patients and cancer in about 0.3% of benign nodules over 5 years, but no study compares surveillance with clinical follow-up alone — outcome benefit is unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: surveillance finds growth in about 1 in 6 patients and cancer in about 0.3% of benign nodules over 5 years, but no study compares surveillance with clinical follow-up alone — outcome benefit is unproven
cards.people: The carded evidence: one prospective surveillance cohort (992 patients, 1,567 nodules), one long-term biopsy cohort (2,207 patients, median 13.9 years), and one narrative review (no patient data). Total documented participants exceed 3,100, so no small-N stamp labelling applies. All evidence is observational.
cards.result: Growth 15.4% and cancer in 0.3% of nodules over 5 years under yearly ultrasound (Durante 2015); benign-cytology false-negative rate 3.2% (1.5% excluding microcarcinomas) with no thyroid-cancer deaths among false negatives over 13.9 years (Ng 2021); expert framing supports risk-stratified follow-up without a comparative outcome estimate (Durante 2018). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) unproven — observational only.
cards.watchOut: The honest gap is comparative: because missed cancers after benign cytology are rare (0.3–1.5% on these records) and indolent enough that none caused death in 13.9 years, a trial proving surveillance improves outcomes would need to be very large — which is why none exists and why the stamp stays at POSSIBLE unproven.
cards.source: Synthesis of Durante C et al. JAMA. 2015 (PMID: 25734734); Ng DL et al. Thyroid. 2021 (PMID: 33371796); Durante C et al. JAMA. 2018 (PMID: 29509871).

shelves.title: Stopping biotin before thyroid testing (small volunteer studies): biotin falsely moved TSH, free T4 and thyroglobulin on Roche/Beckman/Siemens platforms, and accuracy recovered 8 hours to 2 days after stopping — no study enrolled hypothyroid patients
shelves.question: In adults with hypothyroidism taking biotin supplements, does stopping biotin before testing improve accuracy of thyroid function tests versus continuing it?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Biotin · Chromatography, High Pressure Liquid · False Negative Reactions · Female · Humans · Male · Mass Spectrometry · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Thyroglobulin · Thyroid Function Tests · Thyroid Hormones · Thyrotropin
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — stopping biotin before testing removes a real, platform-dependent interference, but the direct washout evidence is two small volunteer studies (N = 13 and N = 10) in healthy adults, not a trial in people with hypothyroidism. Ylli 2021 (PMID: 34042535) gave 13 adults biotin 10 mg/day for 8 days and found significant changes in thyrotropin (TSH), free thyroxine and total triiodothyronine on the Roche Cobas 6000 platform and falsely lower thyroglobulin on Siemens IMMULITE 2000, with maximal interference 2 hours after ingestion; Zhang 2020 (PMID: 32118725) gave 10 healthy adults 5 and 10 mg/day for 7 days and found interference on Roche and Beckman platforms but none on Abbott, lasting 8 hours after 5 mg/day and 1 to 2 days after 10 mg/day — so accuracy returns once biotin is stopped, on a timescale of hours to about 2 days at supplement doses. The clinical stakes are documented in Favresse 2018 (PMID: 29982406): across more than 150 reported patients with thyroid immunoassay interferences of all types, at least 50% led to misdiagnosis and/or inappropriate management. No carded study enrolled hypothyroid patients specifically, so the levothyroxine-titration risk is inferred from the assay data and the review, and is printed as such. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): stop biotin before thyroid testing on susceptible platforms; how long ahead depends on dose and platform (hours after 5 mg/day, up to 2 days after 10 mg/day in the washout study).

cards.headline: Ylli 2021: biotin 10 mg/day for 8 days significantly distorted TSH, free T4 and total T3 on the Roche platform and falsely lowered thyroglobulin on Siemens — interference was maximal 2 hours after each dose (N = 13, printed on the face)
cards.summary: Ylli 2021: biotin 10 mg/day for 8 days significantly distorted TSH, free T4 and total T3 on the Roche platform and falsely lowered thyroglobulin on Siemens — interference was maximal 2 hours after each dose (N = 13, printed on the face)
cards.people: 13 adult subjects (mean age 45 ± 13 years) in a prospective study, administered biotin 10 mg/day for 8 days. Blood was collected at three time points on day 1 and day 8 (baseline, 2 and 5 hours after biotin ingestion) and assayed on four platforms: Abbott Architect, Roche Cobas 6000, Siemens IMMULITE 2000, and liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Study N = 13.
cards.result: Significant changes in TSH, free thyroxine (fT4) and total triiodothyronine (TT3) measurements were observed after biotin exposure when the Roche Cobas 6000 platform was used, and biotin intake resulted in a falsely lower thyroglobulin level on Siemens IMMULITE 2000. Maximal biotin interference was observed 2 hours after biotin exposure on both day 1 and day 8. The record reports significance and direction but no numeric effect sizes, so none are printed here. The authors warn that altered TSH and thyroglobulin results can be particularly problematic in patients requiring careful titration of levothyroxine therapy, such as those with thyroid cancer.
cards.watchOut: Healthy volunteers, not hypothyroid patients, and only 13 of them: the study proves the assay moves, at one dose (10 mg/day) and on specific platforms — it does not measure how often levothyroxine doses are actually changed wrongly in clinic.
cards.source: Ylli D et al. Biotin Interference in Assays for Thyroid Hormones, Thyrotropin and Thyroglobulin. Thyroid. 2021. PMID: 34042535. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zhang 2020: after stopping biotin, interference cleared within 8 hours of a 5 mg/day course and within 1 to 2 days of a 10 mg/day course on Roche and Beckman platforms — and never appeared on Abbott (N = 10, printed on the face)
cards.summary: Zhang 2020: after stopping biotin, interference cleared within 8 hours of a 5 mg/day course and within 1 to 2 days of a 10 mg/day course on Roche and Beckman platforms — and never appeared on Abbott (N = 10, printed on the face)
cards.people: 10 healthy adults recruited to take biotin 5 and 10 mg/day for 7 days. Thyroid function analytes were measured at baseline before biotin and from 2 hours to 2 days after withdrawal, on Roche cobas e602, Beckman UniCel DxI 800 and Abbott Architect 2000 platforms. Study N = 10.
cards.result: Ingesting 5 or 10 mg/day of biotin for 7 days produced positive or negative interference in thyroid function tests on the Roche cobas e602 and Beckman UniCel DxI 800 systems, but no interference on Abbott Architect 2000. Interference from 5 mg/day lasted 8 hours on the Roche and Beckman systems, while 10 mg/day interfered for 1 day or 2 days. The record reports durations and platform patterns but no numeric effect sizes, so none are printed here; the authors present the study as guidance on biotin washout periods at over-the-counter supplement doses.
cards.watchOut: Ten healthy volunteers and short courses: washout times at higher doses, in kidney impairment, or in people actually taking levothyroxine may differ, and the record gives durations per platform without separating every analyte.
cards.source: Zhang Y et al. Assessment of biotin interference in thyroid function tests. Medicine (Baltimore). 2020. PMID: 32118725. Registry ID: ChiCTR1800020472 (from the record). cards.headline: Favresse 2018: across more than 150 reported patients with thyroid immunoassay interferences, at least 50% led to misdiagnosis and/or inappropriate management — biotin is one of six interference types reviewed
cards.summary: Favresse 2018: across more than 150 reported patients with thyroid immunoassay interferences, at least 50% led to misdiagnosis and/or inappropriate management — biotin is one of six interference types reviewed
cards.people: A review of the six main types of interference affecting TSH, free T4 and free T3 measurement (macro-TSH, biotin, antistreptavidin antibodies, anti-ruthenium antibodies, thyroid hormone autoantibodies, and heterophilic antibodies), drawing on reported data from more than 150 patients with documented thyroid interferences of all types — not biotin cases alone.
cards.result: On review of the reported data, at least 50% of documented thyroid interferences led to misdiagnosis and/or inappropriate management, including prescription of an unnecessary treatment (with adverse effects in some situations), inappropriate suppression or modification of an ongoing treatment, or unnecessary complementary tests such as an I123 thyroid scan. The review proposes a detection algorithm based on the pattern of test alterations, using assay method comparison, dilution procedures, blocking reagent studies and polyethylene glycol precipitation. No biotin-specific harm rate is reported in the record, so none is printed here.
cards.watchOut: The 50% misdiagnosis figure covers all six interference types pooled from published cases — published cases over-represent dramatic errors, and the biotin-specific share cannot be separated from this record.
cards.source: Favresse J et al. Interferences With Thyroid Function Immunoassays: Clinical Implications and Detection Algorithm. Endocr Rev. 2018. PMID: 29982406. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: biotin at supplement doses falsely moves TSH, free T4, total T3 and thyroglobulin on susceptible platforms, and stopping it restores accuracy within hours to about 2 days — but the washout studies total 23 healthy volunteers, and none enrolled hypothyroid patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: biotin at supplement doses falsely moves TSH, free T4, total T3 and thyroglobulin on susceptible platforms, and stopping it restores accuracy within hours to about 2 days — but the washout studies total 23 healthy volunteers, and none enrolled hypothyroid patients
cards.people: The carded evidence: two prospective volunteer studies of biotin dosing and withdrawal (N = 13 at 10 mg/day; N = 10 at 5 and 10 mg/day) and one review of thyroid immunoassay interferences (more than 150 reported patients, all interference types). Counting the review's reported patients the total exceeds 30; the direct experimental washout evidence is 23 people, printed here and in the stamp.
cards.result: Interference is dose-, time- and platform-dependent: maximal 2 hours after a dose, present on Roche and Beckman platforms, absent on Abbott in the washout study, and clearing 8 hours after 5 mg/day and 1 to 2 days after 10 mg/day (Zhang 2020; Ylli 2021). The documented downstream harm of thyroid assay interference in general is misdiagnosis or inappropriate management in at least 50% of reported cases (Favresse 2018). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — stopping biotin before testing improves accuracy on susceptible platforms; the hypothyroid-patient application is an inference from volunteer assay data, not a patient trial.
cards.watchOut: The honest gap on this shelf is the population: the question asks about adults with hypothyroidism, and every carded experiment was done in healthy volunteers — what is proven is that the test goes wrong on biotin and recovers off it, not how much levothyroxine mismanagement that causes.

synthesis the carded evidence: two prospective volunteer studies of biotin dosing and withdrawal (n = 13 at 10 mg/day; n = 10 at 5 and 10 mg/day) and one review of thyroid immunoassay interferences (more than 150 reported patients, all interference types). counting the review's reported patients the total exceeds 30; the direct experimental washout evidence is 23 people, printed here and in the stamp. interference is dose-, time- and platform-dependent: maximal 2 hours after a dose, present on roche and beckman platforms, absent on abbott in the washout study, and clearing 8 hours after 5 mg/day and 1 to 2 days after 10 mg/day (zhang 2020; ylli 2021). the documented downstream harm of thyroid assay interference in general is misdiagnosis or inappropriate management in at least 50% of reported cases (favresse 2018). proposed possible (benefit) — stopping biotin before testing improves accuracy on susceptible platforms; the hypothyroid-patient application is an inference from volunteer assay data, not a patient trial. the honest gap on this shelf is the population: the question asks about adults with hypothyroidism, and every carded experiment was done in healthy volunteers — what is proven is that the test goes wrong on biotin and recovers off it, not how much levothyroxine mismanagement that causes. synthesis of ylli d et al. thyroid. 2021 (pmid: 34042535); zhang y et al. medicine (baltimore). 2020 (pmid: 32118725); favresse j et al. endocr rev. 2018 (pmid: 29982406).

shelves.title: Cholestyramine added to methimazole in Graves disease: hormone levels fell faster in all three small randomised trials (T4 −61% vs −43% at 4 weeks) — but symptom relief itself was never measured
shelves.question: In adults with Graves disease, does adding cholestyramine to methimazole speed symptom control versus methimazole alone?
shelves.mesh: Cholestyramine Resin · Drug Therapy, Combination · Humans · Hyperthyroidism · Methimazole · Propranolol · Thyroxine · Triiodothyronine
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three small short randomised trials agree that adding cholestyramine makes thyroid hormone levels fall faster, but none measured symptom control directly, so the shelf answers the hormone-speed question and labels the symptom inference. Mercado 1996 (PMID: 8784067, N = 30) found 4 weeks of cholestyramine with methimazole and propranolol lowered total T4 by 61% versus 43%, free T4 by 78% versus 65% and T3 by 68% versus 50% compared with methimazole and propranolol alone. Solomon 1993 (PMID: 8435884, N = 15, double-blind crossover) found a more rapid decline in all thyroid hormone levels during cholestyramine phases in the first weeks of treatment. Kaykhaei 2008 (PMID: 18946743, N = 45, double-blind placebo-controlled) found even 1–2 g twice daily sped the decline, with every patient on 2 g twice daily euthyroid at 4 weeks. Total carded N = 90, follow-up 2–4 weeks, endpoints biochemical throughout. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cholestyramine speeds biochemical control in the first month; whether patients feel better faster is untested in the carded trials.

cards.headline: Mercado 1996: with cholestyramine added for 4 weeks, total T4 fell 61% versus 43%, free T4 78% versus 65% and T3 68% versus 50% versus methimazole alone (N = 30)
cards.summary: Mercado 1996: with cholestyramine added for 4 weeks, total T4 fell 61% versus 43%, free T4 78% versus 65% and T3 68% versus 50% versus methimazole alone (N = 30)
cards.people: 30 patients with newly diagnosed hyperthyroid Graves disease, randomly assigned to methimazole, propranolol and cholestyramine for 4 weeks (group I); methimazole and propranolol for 4 weeks (group II); or methimazole, propranolol and cholestyramine for 2 weeks followed by 2 weeks without cholestyramine (group III).
cards.result: At the end of the study, total and free T4 and T3 had decreased more in group I than group II: 61%, 78% and 68% in group I compared with 43%, 65% and 50% in group II (P = 0.037 for T4, P = 0.038 for free T4, P = 0.012 for T3) — these are percentage falls in hormone levels, printed as the record gives them. Group III behaved like group I while receiving cholestyramine, but once it was discontinued the rate of decline slowed. The authors conclude cholestyramine is an effective, well-tolerated adjunct producing a more rapid and complete decline in thyroid hormone levels. No symptom scores are reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: Thirty patients, 4 weeks, hormone endpoints only: faster hormone decline is a plausible route to faster symptom relief, but this trial did not measure symptoms, heart rate control or time to feeling well.
cards.source: Mercado M et al. Treatment of hyperthyroidism with a combination of methimazole and cholestyramine. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 1996. PMID: 8784067. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Solomon 1993: in a double-blind crossover, cholestyramine phases produced a more rapid decline in all thyroid hormone levels than placebo phases, with the greatest effect in the first weeks (N = 15, printed on the face)
cards.summary: Solomon 1993: in a double-blind crossover, cholestyramine phases produced a more rapid decline in all thyroid hormone levels than placebo phases, with the greatest effect in the first weeks (N = 15, printed on the face)
cards.people: 15 patients with thyrotoxicosis (14 Graves disease, 1 toxic adenoma) in a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover: standard therapy (atenolol 50 mg daily and individualised methimazole) plus cholestyramine 4 g or placebo powder four times daily for 2 weeks (Phase 1), a 1-week washout, then the opposite treatment for 2 weeks (Phase 2). Study N = 15.
cards.result: Seven patients received cholestyramine and eight placebo in Phase 1; a more rapid decline in all thyroid hormone levels was seen in the cholestyramine group (F = 4–7, P < 0.01) than the placebo group (F = 2–3.1, P = 0.05). In Phase 2, the eight patients crossing to cholestyramine showed an additional decline in free thyroxine from weeks one to two, but the overall rate of decline was not different between groups. Immunoglobulin levels were unaffected. The record reports test statistics rather than percentage falls for this trial, so none are printed here. The authors conclude the greatest efficacy may be during the first few weeks of treatment.
cards.watchOut: The smallest carded trial (N = 15, including one toxic adenoma rather than Graves disease), with a crossover design in a condition whose hormone levels fall over time anyway — period effects can flatter the second phase.
cards.source: Solomon BL et al. Adjunctive cholestyramine therapy for thyrotoxicosis. Clin Endocrinol (Oxf). 1993. PMID: 8435884. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kaykhaei 2008: even low-dose cholestyramine (1–2 g twice daily) sped the hormone decline, and every patient on 2 g twice daily was euthyroid at 4 weeks (N = 45)
cards.summary: Kaykhaei 2008: even low-dose cholestyramine (1–2 g twice daily) sped the hormone decline, and every patient on 2 g twice daily was euthyroid at 4 weeks (N = 45)
cards.people: 45 patients with newly diagnosed hyperthyroid Graves disease in a prospective, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial: group I cholestyramine 2 g twice daily, group II cholestyramine 1 g twice daily, group III placebo powder — all with fixed-dose methimazole 30 mg/day and propranolol 40 mg/day for 4 weeks.
cards.result: Serum total triiodothyronine and free thyroxine decreased more rapidly and to a greater extent in the cholestyramine-treated groups, and all patients in group I had achieved a euthyroid state by the end of the study. The record reports direction and the euthyroid count but no comparative percentages or hormone values, so none are printed here. The authors conclude low-dose cholestyramine is an effective and well-tolerated adjunctive agent in hyperthyroid Graves disease.
cards.watchOut: Fixed methimazole dosing and 4-week follow-up: the trial shows speed of biochemical response at low cholestyramine doses, not durability, relapse, or any patient-reported outcome.
cards.source: Kaykhaei MA et al. Low doses of cholestyramine in the treatment of hyperthyroidism. Endocrine. 2008. PMID: 18946743. Registry ID: NCT00677469 (from the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: three small randomised trials (total N = 90) consistently show cholestyramine makes thyroid hormones fall faster in the first 2–4 weeks of methimazole treatment — symptom speed was never the measured endpoint
cards.summary: Synthesis: three small randomised trials (total N = 90) consistently show cholestyramine makes thyroid hormones fall faster in the first 2–4 weeks of methimazole treatment — symptom speed was never the measured endpoint
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised trials in newly diagnosed Graves disease / thyrotoxicosis (N = 30, 15 and 45; total 90), all adding cholestyramine (1 g twice daily to 4 g four times daily) to a thionamide plus a beta-blocker for 2–4 weeks. No small-N stamp labelling applies at a total of 90, but each trial is small and short, which is printed here.
cards.result: The clearest numbers are Mercado 1996: falls of 61% versus 43% (total T4), 78% versus 65% (free T4) and 68% versus 50% (T3) at 4 weeks. Solomon 1993 and Kaykhaei 2008 confirm the direction with different designs and doses, including complete euthyroidism at 4 weeks in the 2 g twice-daily group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): faster biochemical control is consistently shown; faster symptom control is the reasonable but unmeasured inference.
cards.watchOut: Every carded trial is from the hormone-endpoint era and none exceeds 45 patients or 4 weeks: there is no carded evidence on symptoms, quality of life, time off work, or what happens after the first month.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mercado M et al. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 1996 (PMID: 8784067); Solomon BL et al. Clin Endocrinol (Oxf). 1993 (PMID: 8435884); Kaykhaei MA et al. Endocrine. 2008 (PMID: 18946743).

shelves.title: Radioiodine vs surgery in toxic multinodular goiter (indirect evidence only): radioiodine preserves long-term euthyroidism in roughly 27–59% depending on dose — no head-to-head trial exists
shelves.question: In adults with toxic multinodular goiter, is radioactive iodine better than surgery for long-term hypothyroidism-free survival?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Goiter, Nodular · Humans · Iodine Radioisotopes · Male · Methimazole · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — indirect evidence only, printed on the face: no head-to-head trial of radioiodine versus surgery for this outcome was found in the records fetched this session, so the comparison is assembled from each treatment's own literature. After radioiodine, a substantial minority stay off thyroid hormone long term: in the Azizi 2019 randomised trial's radioiodine arm, 37% were euthyroid and 41% hypothyroid at 60–100 months; with a calculated-dose regimen, Kahraman 2012 found hypothyroidism in 73% by the end of up to 8 years of follow-up, so the radioiodine figure depends heavily on dose strategy. Total thyroidectomy, the definitive surgical option, removes the whole gland — the surgical meta-analysis carded (Bharath 2023) compares total with less-than-total thyroidectomy on recurrence and complications and reports no hypothyroidism rates, printed plainly on its card; a total thyroidectomy leaves no thyroid tissue to sustain hormone-free survival, while less-than-total surgery trades a chance of remaining euthyroid against recurrence and re-operation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — indirect evidence only: radioiodine preserves a real chance of long-term hypothyroidism-free survival (roughly 27–59% across the carded series) that total thyroidectomy does not, but no direct comparison exists.

cards.headline: Azizi 2019: after radioiodine for toxic multinodular goiter, 37% were euthyroid and 41% hypothyroid at 60–100 months (randomised trial, radioiodine arm n = 54 completers)
cards.summary: Azizi 2019: after radioiodine for toxic multinodular goiter, 37% were euthyroid and 41% hypothyroid at 60–100 months (randomised trial, radioiodine arm n = 54 completers)
cards.people: 130 consecutive untreated patients with toxic multinodular goiter, aged under 60, randomised to long-term methimazole or radioiodine; 53 methimazole and 54 radioiodine patients completed 60–100 months of follow-up (median 72 and 84 months respectively). The comparator in this trial is a drug, not surgery — carded here as the radioiodine-arm evidence.
cards.result: In the radioiodine group, 22 of 54 (41%) became hypothyroid, 12 (22%) had persistence or recurrence of hyperthyroidism, and 20 (37%) became euthyroid after 16.7 ± 2.7 mCi of iodine-131. In the methimazole group, 51 of 53 (96.2%) remained euthyroid and 2 (3.8%) had subclinical hypothyroidism. No surgical arm exists in this record.
cards.watchOut: Patients were under 60 and the radioiodine dose was modest; older patients and ablative dosing push hypothyroidism rates up, as the next card shows.
cards.source: Azizi F et al. Treatment of Toxic Multinodular Goiter: Comparison of Radioiodine and Long-Term Methimazole Treatment. Thyroid. 2019. PMID: 30803411. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Female · Goiter, Nodular · Humans · Iodine Radioisotopes · Male · Methimazole · Middle Aged

cards.headline: Kahraman 2012: with a calculated 150 Gy radioiodine dose, hypothyroidism reached 73% by the end of follow-up (265 patients, up to 8 years) despite a 98% cure rate
cards.summary: Kahraman 2012: with a calculated 150 Gy radioiodine dose, hypothyroidism reached 73% by the end of follow-up (265 patients, up to 8 years) despite a 98% cure rate
cards.people: 265 consecutive patients with toxic nodular goitre treated with radioiodine using a calculated dose regimen (intended thyroid dose 150 Gy, with individual uptake, half-life and ultrasound volume measurements) between 2003 and 2004, followed for up to 8 years.
cards.result: Cure rates were 85% at 3 months, 98% at 1 year and 98% at the end of follow-up. Hypothyroidism incidence was 32% at 3 months, 55% at 1 year and 73% at the end of follow-up. Above an achieved thyroid dose of 120 Gy there was no significant association between dose and cure rate. The authors suggest intended doses could be lowered in future calculated regimens.
cards.watchOut: A high intended dose (150 Gy) chosen for cure: its 73% hypothyroidism figure is a property of that regimen, not of radioiodine as such — the two radioiodine cards bracket the dose-dependence rather than contradict each other.
cards.source: Kahraman D et al. Development of hypothyroidism during long-term follow-up of patients with toxic nodular goitre after radioiodine therapy. Clinical Endocrinology. 2012. PMID: 21854403. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bharath 2023: the surgical comparison on record is total vs less-than-total thyroidectomy (5 RCTs) — recurrence lower with total thyroidectomy; the record reports no hypothyroidism rates
cards.summary: Bharath 2023: the surgical comparison on record is total vs less-than-total thyroidectomy (5 RCTs) — recurrence lower with total thyroidectomy; the record reports no hypothyroidism rates
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Bharath 2023)
cards.people: Updated systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 randomised controlled trials comparing total thyroidectomy with less-than-total thyroidectomy for benign multinodular non-toxic goiter. Population is non-toxic goiter, not toxic multinodular goiter — printed plainly here; no radioiodine arm exists in this record.
cards.result: Recurrence was lower after total thyroidectomy. Temporary or permanent recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy and permanent hypoparathyroidism were similar between groups; temporary hypoparathyroidism was lower with less-than-total thyroidectomy, and re-operation for recurrence was significantly higher after less-than-total surgery in a single trial. The authors found no clear overall benefit or harm of either extent of surgery for recurrence and re-operation, and rate the evidence low to moderate quality. The record reports no postoperative hypothyroidism or levothyroxine-use rates — that absence is printed here rather than filled in.
cards.watchOut: This card cannot supply the surgery-side hypothyroidism number: it is carded to show what the surgical literature does and does not measure, and the shelf's comparison rests on radioiodine series plus the structural fact that total thyroidectomy removes the whole gland.
cards.source: Bharath S et al. Total vs less than total thyroidectomy for benign multinodular non-toxic goiter: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis. Langenbeck's Archives of Surgery. 2023. cards.headline: Synthesis: radioiodine leaves 27–59% of patients hormone-free long term depending on dose regimen; no head-to-head trial against surgery exists, and total thyroidectomy offers no hormone-free survival by construction
cards.summary: Synthesis: radioiodine leaves 27–59% of patients hormone-free long term depending on dose regimen; no head-to-head trial against surgery exists, and total thyroidectomy offers no hormone-free survival by construction
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial's radioiodine arm (54 completers, 60–100 months), one radioiodine cohort (265 patients, up to 8 years), and one surgical meta-analysis (5 RCTs, non-toxic goiter, no hypothyroidism reporting). No carded study compares radioiodine with surgery directly.
cards.result: Radioiodine: 37% euthyroid at 60–100 months with 41% hypothyroid (Azizi 2019); 73% hypothyroid by end of follow-up with a 150 Gy calculated regimen (Kahraman 2012) — i.e., hypothyroidism-free survival after radioiodine ranges from about 27% to about 59% across the carded regimens. Surgery: total versus less-than-total thyroidectomy differs on recurrence, not on any hypothyroidism outcome the record reports (Bharath 2023). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — indirect evidence only.
cards.watchOut: The honest gap: 'better than surgery' is inferred, never tested — a patient choosing between radioiodine and subtotal surgery for hormone-free survival has no direct evidence on either side.
cards.source: Synthesis of Azizi F et al. Thyroid. 2019 (PMID: 30803411); Kahraman D et al. Clinical Endocrinology. 2012 (PMID: 21854403); Bharath S et al. Langenbeck's Archives of Surgery. 2023 (PMID: 37204607).

shelves.title: Surgery vs radioiodine for compressive goiter symptoms — MAYBE (weak evidence): both relieve symptoms in separate uncontrolled series; never compared head-to-head
shelves.question: In adults with multinodular goiter and compressive symptoms, is surgery better than radioactive iodine for symptom relief?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Dose-Response Relationship, Radiation · Female · Goiter · Humans · Iodine Radioisotopes · Male · Middle Aged · Radiopharmaceuticals · Thyroid Function Tests · Thyrotropin · Time Factors
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no head-to-head comparison exists in the records fetched this session; each treatment's symptom relief is documented only in its own series, printed as such. Radioiodine: in Duick 2004, all 30 patients with symptomatic toxic or nontoxic multinodular goiter experienced symptomatic relief by 1–2 months after rhTSH-aided radioiodine; the Cochrane review of rhTSH-aided radioiodine (6 RCTs, 321 participants) found greater thyroid volume reduction than radioiodine alone (mean difference 11.9%) at the cost of more hypothyroidism (relative risk 2.53). Surgery: in Shires 2021, 60 patients undergoing thyroidectomy for benign goiter improved significantly on breathlessness, dysphagia and all 11 ThyPRO quality-of-life domains after surgery — the improvement concentrated in obese patients, who started worst. Neither literature measures the other treatment, and compressive-symptom patients are exactly those often steered to surgery, so the series are not comparable. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): both surgery and radioiodine relieve compressive symptoms in their own series; whether surgery is better is untested head-to-head.

cards.headline: Duick 2004: all 30 patients with symptomatic multinodular goiter reported symptomatic relief 1–2 months after rhTSH-aided radioiodine — a single-arm series, no surgical comparator
cards.summary: Duick 2004: all 30 patients with symptomatic multinodular goiter reported symptomatic relief 1–2 months after rhTSH-aided radioiodine — a single-arm series, no surgical comparator
cards.people: 30 patients with symptomatic nontoxic or toxic multinodular goiter given a single injection of recombinant human thyrotropin (0.1 mg in 21 patients, 0.3 mg in 9) followed by 30 mCi of iodine-131. Single-arm treatment series.
cards.result: All study patients experienced symptomatic relief by 1 to 2 months. Radioiodine uptake quadrupled by 72 hours after rhTSH (24-hour uptake from 22% to 43% with 0.1 mg, P < 0.001; from 16% to 37% with 0.3 mg, P = 0.002), with no significant difference between doses. The authors conclude radioiodine therapy after rhTSH alleviated compressive and thyrotoxic symptoms in all 30 treated patients; no effect size beyond the all-patient relief statement is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: Thirty selected patients, no control group and a symptom outcome reported as an all-or-none statement: regression to the mean and selection (patients chosen for radioiodine may have milder compression) are unmeasured.
cards.source: Duick DS et al. Significance of radioiodine uptake at 72 hours versus 24 hours after pretreatment with recombinant human thyrotropin for enhancement of radioiodine therapy in patients with symptomatic nontoxic or toxic multinodular goiter. Endocrine Practice. 2004. PMID: 15310544. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane 2021 (Huo): rhTSH-aided radioiodine shrank goiters more than radioiodine alone (volume mean difference 11.9%) but more than doubled hypothyroidism (relative risk 2.53) — 6 RCTs, 321 participants
cards.summary: Cochrane 2021 (Huo): rhTSH-aided radioiodine shrank goiters more than radioiodine alone (volume mean difference 11.9%) but more than doubled hypothyroidism (relative risk 2.53) — 6 RCTs, 321 participants
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of 6 randomised trials in non-toxic multinodular goitre: 197 participants allocated to rhTSH-aided radioiodine and 124 to radioiodine alone, follow-up 12–36 months. The comparator is radioiodine alone, not surgery — printed plainly here.
cards.result: RhTSH-aided radioiodine increased hypothyroidism versus radioiodine alone (32.5% vs 12.1%; relative risk 2.53, 95% CI 1.52 to 4.20; moderate-certainty evidence) and reduced thyroid volume more (mean difference 11.9%, 95% CI 4.4 to 19.4; moderate-certainty evidence). Adverse events were 59.9% versus 48.4% (random-effects relative risk 1.24, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.63; low-certainty evidence). Low-certainty evidence from one 85-participant study left quality-of-life effects uncertain for either intervention.
cards.watchOut: Volume reduction is a surrogate for symptom relief, and the population is non-toxic goiter: this card quantifies what radioiodine can do to gland size, not how it compares with an operation for a breathless patient.
cards.source: Huo Y et al. Recombinant human thyrotropin (rhTSH)-aided radioiodine treatment for non-toxic multinodular goitre. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2021. PMID: 34961921. Registry ID: NCT00275171, NCT00454220 (registry IDs listed in the record for included trials). cards.headline: Shires 2021: after thyroidectomy for benign goiter, obese patients (n = 37 of 60) improved significantly on breathlessness, dysphagia and all 11 quality-of-life domains — no radioiodine comparator
cards.summary: Shires 2021: after thyroidectomy for benign goiter, obese patients (n = 37 of 60) improved significantly on breathlessness, dysphagia and all 11 quality-of-life domains — no radioiodine comparator
cards.people: Prospective pre/post analysis of 60 patients undergoing thyroidectomy for benign goiter (single or multinodular): 37 obese, 13 overweight, 10 normal weight. Outcomes: MRC breathlessness scale, MD Anderson Dysphagia Inventory, and ThyPRO quality-of-life questionnaire, before and after surgery. Single-arm surgical series. The record carries no MeSH terms, so the source line prints the standard fallback.
cards.result: Obese patients scored significantly worse pre-operatively on all three surveys. After surgery, the obese group — but not the other groups — improved significantly on breathlessness and dysphagia scores (P < 0.0001) and on all 11 ThyPRO domains (P < 0.0001); the degree of improvement correlated with body mass index across all subjects (r = 0.60, P = 0.0005). The authors conclude obesity is a critical factor in the alleviation of compressive symptoms after thyroidectomy for goiter.
cards.watchOut: No control group and improvement confined to the subgroup that started worst: some of the gain is expected from regression to the mean, and nothing here measures radioiodine in comparable patients.
cards.source: Shires CB et al. Quality of life in obese patients after thyroidectomy for goiter. Gland Surgery. 2021. PMID: 33968685. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: surgery and radioiodine each relieve compressive symptoms in their own uncontrolled series — the 'which is better' question has never been randomised
cards.summary: Synthesis: surgery and radioiodine each relieve compressive symptoms in their own uncontrolled series — the 'which is better' question has never been randomised
cards.people: The carded evidence: one single-arm radioiodine series (30 patients), one Cochrane review of radioiodine versus radioiodine-plus-rhTSH (321 participants), and one single-arm surgical series (60 patients). No carded study enrols both treatments.
cards.result: Radioiodine: symptomatic relief in all 30 treated patients by 1–2 months (Duick 2004); volume reduction 11.9% greater with rhTSH aid, hypothyroidism relative risk 2.53 (Huo 2021). Surgery: significant post-thyroidectomy improvement in breathlessness, dysphagia and quality of life, concentrated in obese patients (Shires 2021). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Patients with severe compression are preferentially sent to surgery in practice, so even a future registry comparison will fight confounding by indication; only a trial in patients eligible for both could answer this question cleanly.

shelves.title: Denosumab versus zoledronic acid in hypercalcemia of malignancy (observational only for treatment): similar calcium lowering in the direct treatment cohort and better prevention in randomised trials — superiority for controlling established calcium is unproven — a partial completion of shelf #2904
shelves.question: In adults with hypercalcemia of malignancy, is denosumab more effective than zoledronic acid for controlling calcium?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Male · Retrospective Studies · Hypocalcemia · Hypercalcemia · Denosumab · Aged · Middle Aged · Bone Density Conservation Agents · Diphosphonates · Neoplasms · Calcitonin · Calcium · Prognosis · Follow-Up Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2904, which covers denosumab in bisphosphonate-refractory hypercalcemia of malignancy (HCM); this shelf homes the head-to-head comparison against zoledronic acid, and #2904's single-arm refractory-disease trial is cross-pointed, not re-carded. No randomised trial has compared the two drugs as treatment for established HCM in the records fetched. The direct treatment evidence is one retrospective cohort of 317 patients with established HCM (Kong 2025), in which denosumab lowered calcium by 2.0 mg/dL and intravenous bisphosphonate by 1.8 mg/dL — similar effectiveness — while bisphosphonate plus calcitonin lowered it most (2.7 mg/dL), and hypocalcemia was significantly less frequent with denosumab; that study's comparator was intravenous bisphosphonates as a class, not zoledronic acid alone, and that limit is printed on its card. The randomised head-to-head evidence is about prevention, not treatment: pooled phase III data (Diel 2015) showed denosumab delayed first on-study HCM versus zoledronic acid (1.7% vs. 2.7% of patients; hazard ratio 0.63, a 37% relative reduction in hazard). A bone-metastases dosing cohort (Nasser 2019) cuts the other way on calcium control, with more hypercalcemia episodes recorded on denosumab than zoledronic acid (8.5% vs. 3.1% of encounters). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for treatment of established hypercalcemia: denosumab looks at least as effective as bisphosphonate treatment and better at preventing HCM than zoledronic acid, but superiority for controlling established calcium is unproven by any randomised head-to-head trial.

cards.headline: Kong 2025: in 317 patients treated for established hypercalcemia of malignancy, denosumab lowered calcium by 2.0 mg/dL and intravenous bisphosphonate by 1.8 mg/dL — similarly effective — while bisphosphonate plus calcitonin lowered it most, by 2.7 mg/dL; hypocalcemia was significantly less frequent with denosumab
cards.summary: Kong 2025: in 317 patients treated for established hypercalcemia of malignancy, denosumab lowered calcium by 2.0 mg/dL and intravenous bisphosphonate by 1.8 mg/dL — similarly effective — while bisphosphonate plus calcitonin lowered it most, by 2.7 mg/dL; hypocalcemia was significantly less frequent with denosumab
cards.people: 317 patients treated for hypercalcemia of malignancy at a tertiary hospital, 2017–2022, in a retrospective cohort study; mean age 65 years, 37.5% female. Three treatment groups: denosumab, intravenous bisphosphonate only, and intravenous bisphosphonate combined with calcitonin. The record does not break the bisphosphonate group down by drug, so this card compares denosumab with intravenous bisphosphonates as a class, not zoledronic acid alone.
cards.result: After adjustment for age, sex, body mass index, creatinine, malignancy type and furosemide/steroid use, denosumab decreased calcium by 2.0 mg/dL (−15.9%) and intravenous bisphosphonate alone by 1.8 mg/dL (−13.9%); the largest reduction, 2.7 mg/dL (−20.9%), was with bisphosphonate plus calcitonin. Denosumab and bisphosphonate-plus-calcitonin reached their lowest calcium within 48 hours, versus 72 hours for bisphosphonate alone. Hypocalcemia occurred significantly less frequently in the denosumab group than in the other groups; the record gives no hypocalcemia rates. The authors conclude denosumab and intravenous bisphosphonate were similarly effective, with the calcitonin combination faster and larger.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and single-centre: sicker or bisphosphonate-refractory patients are preferentially given denosumab in practice, which biases the comparison against denosumab — and the comparator is bisphosphonates as a class, so this card cannot by itself answer the zoledronic-acid-specific question.
cards.source: Kong SH et al. Comparison of the Effectiveness and Hypocalcemia Risk of Antiresorptive Agents in Patients with Hypercalcemia of Malignancy. Endocrinology and Metabolism (Seoul). 2025. PMID: 39901808. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Diel 2015: in pooled randomised phase III data, denosumab delayed or prevented hypercalcemia of malignancy better than zoledronic acid — first HCM in 1.7% vs. 2.7% of patients, hazard ratio 0.63 (a 37% relative reduction in hazard) — but this is prevention in bone-metastases patients, not treatment of established hypercalcemia
cards.summary: Diel 2015: in pooled randomised phase III data, denosumab delayed or prevented hypercalcemia of malignancy better than zoledronic acid — first HCM in 1.7% vs. 2.7% of patients, hazard ratio 0.63 (a 37% relative reduction in hazard) — but this is prevention in bone-metastases patients, not treatment of established hypercalcemia
cards.type: Pooled analysis of two randomised phase III trials (Diel 2015)
cards.people: Patient-level data combined from two identically designed randomised, double-blind, active-controlled phase III trials in patients with advanced cancer and bone metastases (breast cancer and other solid tumours) or multiple myeloma, comparing denosumab with zoledronic acid; median time on study 12.9 months. The pooled total N is not documented in the record.
cards.result: Denosumab significantly delayed time to first on-study HCM versus zoledronic acid (hazard ratio 0.63; 95% confidence interval: 0.41–0.98; P = 0.042 — a 37% relative reduction in hazard) and reduced the risk of recurrent HCM (time to first and subsequent HCM rate ratio 0.48; 95% confidence interval: 0.29–0.81; P = 0.006 — a 52% relative reduction). Fewer patients on denosumab experienced an HCM event (1.7% versus 2.7%; P = 0.028). Of the 84 patients who had an HCM event, 40% of those on zoledronic acid had more than one event, versus 31% on denosumab.
cards.watchOut: These patients were receiving bone-metastases dosing to prevent skeletal events, and HCM was an on-study event outcome — preventing a first calcium rise in that setting is not the same question as treating a patient who presents with established hypercalcemia, and the absolute difference was 1.0 percentage point (1.7% vs. 2.7%).
cards.source: Diel IJ et al. The role of denosumab in the prevention of hypercalcaemia of malignancy in cancer patients with metastatic bone disease. European Journal of Cancer. 2015. PMID: 25976743. Registry ID: NCT00321464 and NCT00330759. cards.headline: Nasser 2019: in a bone-metastases dosing cohort, hypercalcemia was recorded more often on denosumab than zoledronic acid (8.5% vs. 3.1% of encounters, odds ratio 2.9 relative) — and hypocalcemia was also more frequent on denosumab (5.5% vs. 3.1%)
cards.summary: Nasser 2019: in a bone-metastases dosing cohort, hypercalcemia was recorded more often on denosumab than zoledronic acid (8.5% vs. 3.1% of encounters, odds ratio 2.9 relative) — and hypocalcemia was also more frequent on denosumab (5.5% vs. 3.1%)
cards.people: 271 adult cancer patients with bone metastasis from a solid tumour or multiple myeloma who received zoledronic acid or denosumab, contributing 1,141 administration encounters, in a retrospective cohort study of records from August 2015 to July 2016; other indications for bone-targeting agents were excluded. This is skeletal-event-prevention dosing, not HCM treatment dosing.
cards.result: The incidence of hypocalcemia was higher with denosumab than zoledronic acid (5.5% vs. 3.1%, odds ratio = 0.55 as printed in the record, 95% confidence interval [0.3–1.0]; P = 0.05). Hypercalcemia incidence was also higher in the denosumab group (8.5% vs. 3.1%, odds ratio = 2.9, 95% confidence interval [1.68–5.03]; P < 0.0001). Calcium supplementation was associated with a 16% relative reduction in hypocalcemia risk that was not significant (relative risk = 0.84, 95% confidence interval [0.55–1.20]; P = 0.39). The authors emphasise monitoring and supplementation on either drug.
cards.watchOut: Encounter-level calcium abnormalities during prevention dosing reflect underlying disease, renal function, supplementation and why each drug was chosen — not the drugs' power to correct established hypercalcemia; this card is carded as a caution against reading the prevention data as proof of treatment superiority, not as a treatment trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: denosumab prevents hypercalcemia of malignancy better than zoledronic acid in randomised data, and matches bisphosphonates in the one direct treatment cohort — but no randomised trial has tested it head-to-head for controlling established hypercalcemia
cards.summary: Synthesis: denosumab prevents hypercalcemia of malignancy better than zoledronic acid in randomised data, and matches bisphosphonates in the one direct treatment cohort — but no randomised trial has tested it head-to-head for controlling established hypercalcemia
cards.people: The carded evidence: one retrospective treatment cohort in established HCM (317 patients), one pooled analysis of two randomised phase III prevention trials (pooled N not documented in the record; 84 patients had an HCM event), and one retrospective bone-metastases dosing cohort (271 patients, 1,141 encounters). The bisphosphonate-refractory single-arm evidence is homed on live shelf #2904 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.result: For treatment of established HCM, denosumab lowered calcium by 2.0 mg/dL versus 1.8 mg/dL for intravenous bisphosphonate, with less hypocalcemia on denosumab (Kong 2025, observational). For prevention, denosumab beat zoledronic acid randomised head-to-head: first HCM 1.7% vs. 2.7%, hazard ratio 0.63 (Diel 2015). In prevention-dosing practice data, calcium excursions in both directions were recorded more often on denosumab (Nasser 2019). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for the treatment question.
cards.watchOut: The honest gap on this shelf is design, not direction: the randomised comparison answers a prevention question and the treatment comparison is retrospective, so 'more effective for controlling calcium' remains unproven in the strict head-to-head treatment sense the question asks.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kong SH et al. Endocrinology and Metabolism (Seoul). 2025 (PMID: 39901808); Diel IJ et al. European Journal of Cancer. 2015 (PMID: 25976743); Nasser SM et al. Journal of Oncology Pharmacy Practice. 2019 (PMID: 31694497).

shelves.title: Cinacalcet and bone in non-surgical primary hyperparathyroidism (PARTIAL): calcium normalises, bone does not — density unchanged against placebo and over 5.5 years, and no fracture data
shelves.question: In adults with primary hyperparathyroidism who do not meet surgical criteria, does cinacalcet improve bone outcomes versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bone Density · Calcium/blood · Cinacalcet · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hyperparathyroidism/blood · Hyperparathyroidism/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Naphthalenes/therapeutic use · Parathyroid Hormone/blood
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference to bone density) — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1753. That shelf covers cinacalcet for calcium and PTH normalisation and cards the pooled Peacock 2011 analysis, which mentions bone density only in passing (no significant change except a total-femur decrease at 1 year); its record is NOT re-carded here. This shelf covers the uncovered slice: bone outcomes, in the population that does not go to surgery. Against placebo in the 1-year randomised trial (n = 78), cinacalcet normalised calcium in 73% vs 5% but bone mineral density was unchanged, while bone resorption and formation markers increased (Peacock 2005). In the open-label extension, density z-scores at spine, hip and wrist did not change over up to 5.5 years (Peacock 2009). A randomised-trial meta-analysis in exactly this population — asymptomatic patients or those who decline surgery — found bone-density increases with alendronate, denosumab, vitamin D and estrogen, and reports no density increase for cinacalcet (Ye 2022); a medical-management review states bisphosphonates improved density while cinacalcet had no effect (Leere 2017). No carded record reports a fracture outcome for cinacalcet. Note the DENOCINA trial, which also reports bone outcomes with cinacalcet, is already carded elsewhere in the library and was therefore not carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference to bone density): cinacalcet is a calcium-and-PTH drug; on the carded evidence it does not improve bone outcomes.

cards.headline: Peacock 2005: in the 1-year placebo-controlled trial (n = 78), cinacalcet normalised calcium in 73% vs 5% — but bone mineral density was unchanged by cinacalcet, while bone resorption and formation markers increased
cards.summary: Peacock 2005: in the 1-year placebo-controlled trial (n = 78), cinacalcet normalised calcium in 73% vs 5% — but bone mineral density was unchanged by cinacalcet, while bone resorption and formation markers increased
cards.people: 78 patients with primary hyperparathyroidism randomised to cinacalcet (titrated from 30–50 mg twice daily during a 12-week dose-titration phase) or placebo, with efficacy assessed during 12-week maintenance and 28-week follow-up phases; plasma PTH, biochemistry, biochemical measures of bone turnover, bone mineral density and safety were assessed.
cards.result: 73% of cinacalcet-treated patients vs only 5% of placebo-treated patients achieved the primary endpoint of normocalcemia (serum calcium ≤10.3 mg/dL (2.57 mmol/L) with at least a 0.5 mg/dL (0.12 mmol/L) reduction from baseline; P < 0.001). Fasting predose plasma PTH decreased 7.6% on cinacalcet but increased 7.7% on placebo (P < 0.01). Bone mineral density was unchanged by cinacalcet (the treatment made no difference to bone density), but bone resorption and formation markers increased (P < 0.05). Adverse events were mild and similar between groups. The record prints no bone-density percentages or fracture outcomes.
cards.watchOut: This trial's population was primary hyperparathyroidism generally — the record does not restrict it to patients who did not meet surgical criteria — and bone density was a secondary measure over about a year; no fracture outcome was reported, so the bone question is answered for density only.
cards.source: Peacock M et al. Cinacalcet hydrochloride maintains long-term normocalcemia in patients with primary hyperparathyroidism. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2005. PMID: 15522938. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Peacock 2009: over up to 5.5 years of cinacalcet, calcium stayed normal and PTH fell — with no changes in bone mineral density z-scores at spine, hip or wrist
cards.summary: Peacock 2009: over up to 5.5 years of cinacalcet, calcium stayed normal and PTH fell — with no changes in bone mineral density z-scores at spine, hip or wrist
cards.type: Open-label extension study of a randomised trial (Peacock 2009)
cards.people: 45 subjects with primary hyperparathyroidism from a double-blind, placebo-controlled 1-year trial continued into a 4.5-year open-label extension at 14 US centres; after the parent study all subjects were treated with cinacalcet 30 mg twice daily, increasing to 50 mg twice daily if serum calcium was 10.3 mg/dL or higher, for up to 4.5 years. Assessments included serum calcium, PTH, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and areal bone mineral density.
cards.result: Compared with baseline, cinacalcet treatment reduced serum calcium and PTH and increased serum phosphate, with slight increases in alkaline phosphatase. No changes in z-scores of areal bone mineral density at spine, hip or wrist were seen in annual percent changes, consistent with reports for untreated postmenopausal women or primary hyperparathyroidism patients (the treatment made no difference to bone density over 5.5 years). Adverse events (most commonly arthralgia, myalgia, diarrhoea, respiratory infection and nausea) were mild to moderate. The record prints no fracture outcomes.
cards.watchOut: An open-label extension without a placebo group: 'no change' in density is reassuring against loss but cannot show benefit, and the 45 continuers are the survivors of the parent trial's 78 patients.
cards.source: Peacock M et al. Cinacalcet treatment of primary hyperparathyroidism: biochemical and bone densitometric outcomes in a five-year study. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2009. PMID: 19837909. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ye 2022: in patients not candidates for parathyroid surgery, cinacalcet probably reduced calcium and PTH — while the bone-density gains in the review belonged to anti-resorptive drugs, not cinacalcet
cards.summary: Ye 2022: in patients not candidates for parathyroid surgery, cinacalcet probably reduced calcium and PTH — while the bone-density gains in the review belonged to anti-resorptive drugs, not cinacalcet
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Ye 2022)
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials in primary hyperparathyroidism: for medical therapy, 11 trials reported in 12 publications including 438 patients proved eligible (three addressed alendronate, one denosumab, three cinacalcet, two vitamin D and two estrogen therapy), in asymptomatic patients or symptomatic patients who decline surgery; six surgery trials including 441 patients were also reviewed.
cards.result: Alendronate, denosumab, vitamin D and estrogen therapy all increased bone density. Cinacalcet probably reduced serum calcium and parathyroid hormone levels; the review does not report a bone-density increase for cinacalcet. Cinacalcet and vitamin D may have a small or no increase in overall adverse events. For surgery, biochemical cure was achieved in 96.1% (high quality), with no convincing evidence of an impact on fracture, quality of life, kidney stones or renal function, and surgery was associated with an increase in bone mineral density. The record prints no pooled bone-density effect size for cinacalcet.
cards.watchOut: This is the carded report whose population matches this shelf's question (patients not candidates for, or declining, surgery) — and even here the bone-density benefit is attributed to other drug classes; the absence of a cinacalcet density estimate is printed plainly rather than filled in.
cards.source: Ye Z et al. The Efficacy and Safety of Medical and Surgical Therapy in Patients With Primary Hyperparathyroidism: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Journal of bone and mineral research : the official journal of the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research. 2022. PMID: 36053960. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Leere 2017: across the medical-management literature, bisphosphonates improved bone mineral density while cinacalcet had no effect on it — cinacalcet's effect was on calcium (mean fall 0.37 mmol/L (about 1.5 mg/dL))
cards.summary: Leere 2017: across the medical-management literature, bisphosphonates improved bone mineral density while cinacalcet had no effect on it — cinacalcet's effect was on calcium (mean fall 0.37 mmol/L (about 1.5 mg/dL))
cards.people: Systematic review of contemporary pharmaceutical options for medical management of primary hyperparathyroidism: 1,999 articles screened and 54 included, with data extracted on serum calcium, serum PTH, bone turnover markers, bone mineral density and hard endpoints for each drug, including cinacalcet and the bisphosphonates.
cards.result: Weighted mean changes in serum total calcium were 0.37 ± 0.013 mmol/L (about 1.5 mg/dL) for cinacalcet, 0.31 ± 0.034 mmol/L for pamidronate, 0.20 ± 0.040 mmol/L for clodronate and 0.07 ± 0.05 mmol/L for alendronate, as printed (falls from baseline). A meta-analysis showed a significant decrease of effect on serum calcium with time for the bisphosphonates, while cinacalcet maintained its calcium effect over time. Bisphosphonates improved bone mineral density while cinacalcet had no effect. The review prints no fracture outcomes for cinacalcet.
cards.watchOut: A narrative systematic review without pooled bone-density effect sizes for cinacalcet: its value here is the direct class contrast — the drugs that improved density in this literature were the bisphosphonates, not the calcimimetic.
cards.source: Leere JS et al. Contemporary Medical Management of Primary Hyperparathyroidism: A Systematic Review. Frontiers in endocrinology. 2017. PMID: 28473803. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: cinacalcet controls calcium and PTH in primary hyperparathyroidism but does not improve bone outcomes — density was unchanged against placebo at 1 year and unchanged over 5.5 years, and no carded record reports a fracture benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: cinacalcet controls calcium and PTH in primary hyperparathyroidism but does not improve bone outcomes — density was unchanged against placebo at 1 year and unchanged over 5.5 years, and no carded record reports a fracture benefit
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised placebo-controlled trial (n = 78) and its open-label extension (45 continuers, up to 5.5 years), one systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials in patients not candidates for surgery (11 medical-therapy trials, 438 patients), and one systematic review of medical management (54 included studies). Unique randomised participants in the cinacalcet programme total 78, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Against placebo, cinacalcet normalised calcium (73% vs 5%) but bone mineral density was unchanged, while bone turnover markers rose (Peacock 2005). Over up to 5.5 years of treatment, density z-scores at spine, hip and wrist did not change (Peacock 2009). In the population this shelf asks about — patients not candidates for or declining surgery — a randomised-trial meta-analysis attributes bone-density increases to alendronate, denosumab, vitamin D and estrogen, not to cinacalcet (Ye 2022), and a medical-management review states plainly that bisphosphonates improved density while cinacalcet had no effect (Leere 2017). No carded record reports fractures on cinacalcet. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference to bone density) — a calcium drug, not a bone drug, on the carded evidence.
cards.watchOut: Absence of a density effect is not proof of absence of any bone effect — density was a secondary outcome, follow-up in the controlled trial was about a year, and fractures were never reported; but after 5.5 years and two reviews, a clinically useful bone benefit should have shown itself if it were large.
