shelves.title: Thyroid-hormone kinetics: most T3 is made outside the thyroid — conversion of T4 supplies ~22 µg/day by the classic tracer count and ~80% of production by compartmental analysis
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are thyroid-hormone kinetics — daily thyroxine production rate, the fraction of T4 converted peripherally to T3 versus reverse T3, and T3 production from conversion versus direct secretion — measured by radiolabelled-hormone tracer studies?
shelves.mesh: Thyroxine · Triiodothyronine · Triiodothyronine, Reverse · Kinetics · Thyroid Gland
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the architecture of thyroid-hormone production, framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong: the thyroid secretes mainly thyroxine (T4), and most of the active hormone T3 is generated in peripheral tissues by monodeiodination, with inner-ring deiodination yielding inactive reverse T3 (rT3) instead. The carded tracer record: conversion exists and is obligatory — athyreotic patients maintained on T4 alone have circulating T3 far above what contamination of the dose explains (Braverman 1970, N = 13). The classic quantification in 8 normal subjects put extrathyroidal conversion at 4% of the T4 pool per day — 33% of total T4 production — generating 22 µg of T3 daily, counted as 41% of daily T3 production (Pittman 1971). The later multicompartmental analysis, which added the plasma appearance curve of labelled T3 generated from T4, revised the partition: of total T3 production of 16.0 µg/day/m², the thyroid contributed 3.3 and the periphery 12.7 µg/day/m² — roughly 80% from conversion (Pilo 1990, 14 studies in normal subjects). The two figures are both on the face: the discrepancy is methodological (disappearance-only analysis misassigns conversion to slowly exchanging pools), and the shelf presents the modern compartmental partition as the better measurement while keeping the classic number visible. For rT3, the double-tracer study bounded production at 1.12–2.15 µg/h, with 65–90% degraded in rapidly exchanging peripheral tissues and all degradation yielding iodide (Pilo 1993). The daily T4 production rate itself (~80–100 µg/day in the textbooks' account) is presented as the textbook's account: the fetched records quantify conversion as fractions of T4 production rather than printing a single verified production figure, and the shelf says so rather than dressing the textbook number as measured fact.

cards.headline: Braverman 1970: athyreotic patients on T4 alone have real circulating T3 (243–680 ng/100 mL against a normal range of 170–270) — proof that T4 is converted to T3 outside the thyroid (N = 13)
cards.summary: Braverman 1970: athyreotic patients on T4 alone have real circulating T3 (243–680 ng/100 mL against a normal range of 170–270) — proof that T4 is converted to T3 outside the thyroid (N = 13)
cards.type: Human tracer study (labelled T4 conversion in athyreotic subjects), J Clin Invest 1970
cards.people: Thirteen patients, all but two athyreotic or hypothyroid, maintained on at least physiological replacement doses of synthetic sodium-L-thyroxine; in the tracer limb the oral dose was enriched with [125I]T4 for 8 or more days, and two further patients received daily intravenous labelled T4 for 7 days.
cards.result: Serum T3 was found in every patient at 243–680 ng/100 mL (normal range 170–270 ng/100 mL) — far above what T3 contamination of the administered T4 (<0.1% in the purified lot) could explain. Labelled T3 (and tetraiodothyroacetic acid) appeared in serum at ~2–5% of total radioactivity after labelled T4, by both oral and intravenous routes, with binding patterns confirming identity. The authors' conclusion, verbatim in substance: conclusive evidence of extrathyroidal conversion of T4 to T3 in man — raising the question of how much of T4's metabolic effect is mediated through peripherally generated T3.
cards.watchOut: Patients on replacement, not healthy volunteers — carded as the existence proof for conversion; the quantitative partitions rest on the Pittman and Pilo cards. ng/100 mL is ng/dL.
cards.source: Braverman LE, Ingbar SH, Sterling K. Conversion of thyroxine (T4) to triiodothyronine (T3) in athyreotic human subjects. The Journal of clinical investigation. 1970. PMID: 4986007. cards.headline: Pittman 1971: the classic count in 8 normal subjects — conversion runs at 4% of the T4 pool daily (33% of T4 production) and generates 22 µg of T3 a day, 41% of daily T3 production
cards.summary: Pittman 1971: the classic count in 8 normal subjects — conversion runs at 4% of the T4 pool daily (33% of T4 production) and generates 22 µg of T3 a day, 41% of daily T3 production
cards.type: Human radiotracer kinetic study (T4-to-T3 conversion in normal man), J Clin Invest 1971
cards.people: Eight normal subjects given tracer [14C]thyroxine by multiple injections, with serial blood sampling and chromatographic isolation of thyroxine, triiodothyronine and tetraiodothyroacetic acid fractions; complete paired T4/T3 kinetic studies in four of the subjects. Small classic study — N = 8 printed on the face.
cards.result: Only 1–2% of serum 14C radioactivity appeared in the T3 fraction (2–4% in the tetraiodothyroacetic acid fraction), yet the kinetic calculation gives a large flux: the average daily extrathyroidal conversion of T4 to T3 was 4% of the extrathyroidal thyroxine pool, i.e. 33% of total thyroxine production. The T3 so generated, 22 µg/day, contributed 31% of the extrathyroidal T3 pool and 41% of daily T3 production — making conversion, already in 1971, 'a major source of triiodothyronine production'.
cards.watchOut: N = 8, printed on the face. The 41% figure is the disappearance-curve era's partition; the Pilo card shows why the compartmental re-analysis assigns a larger share to conversion — both numbers stay on the face.
cards.source: Pittman CS, Chambers JB Jr, Read VH. The extrathyroidal conversion rate of thyroxine to triiodothyronine in normal man. The Journal of clinical investigation. 1971. PMID: 5578229. cards.headline: Pilo 1990: compartmental analysis of 14 studies in normal subjects — T3 production is 3.3 µg/day/m² from the thyroid and 12.7 µg/day/m² from peripheral conversion (~80%)
cards.summary: Pilo 1990: compartmental analysis of 14 studies in normal subjects — T3 production is 3.3 µg/day/m² from the thyroid and 12.7 µg/day/m² from peripheral conversion (~80%)
cards.type: Human tracer compartmental analysis (T3 production partition), Am J Physiol 1990
cards.people: Fourteen studies in normal subjects, analysed with a composite six-pool model of T4 and T3 kinetics that adds the plasma appearance curve of labelled T3 generated in vivo from precursor T4 to the two hormones' disappearance curves.
cards.result: Total T3 production partitioned as 3.3 µg/day/m² thyroidal secretion against 12.7 µg/day/m² peripheral production — about four-fifths from conversion. Conversion occurred mainly in rapidly exchanging peripheral tissues (10.7 µg/day/m²), with only 2.0 µg/day/m² in slowly exchanging tissues. The methodological lesson is printed in the record: analysing disappearance curves alone misassigns 10.9 µg/day/m² of conversion to the slow pools — which is why the classic-era partition (Pittman card) came out lower. The appearance curve is what makes the partition measurable.
cards.watchOut: Model-based partition: the numbers are only as good as the six-pool model's assumptions, which the record states. Values are per m² body surface area, as published.
cards.source: Pilo A, Iervasi G, Vitek F, Ferdeghini M, et al.. Thyroidal and peripheral production of 3,5,3'-triiodothyronine in humans by multicompartmental analysis. The American journal of physiology. 1990. PMID: 2333963. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pilo 1993: reverse T3 disposal by double tracer — production bounded at 1.12–2.15 µg/h, 65–90% degraded in rapidly exchanging tissues, and every degradative pathway yields iodide
cards.summary: Pilo 1993: reverse T3 disposal by double tracer — production bounded at 1.12–2.15 µg/h, 65–90% degraded in rapidly exchanging tissues, and every degradative pathway yields iodide
cards.type: Human double-tracer kinetic study (reverse T3 disposal), Am J Physiol 1993
cards.people: A group of normal subjects (number not documented in the record's abstract — printed as such) studied by simultaneous injection of [125I]rT3 and 131I, following three plasma curves — labelled rT3 disappearance, 131I disappearance, and 125I appearance from rT3 degradation — analysed with a six-compartment model.
cards.result: The double-tracer design uniquely determines fractional disposal and exchange rates where the disappearance curve alone leaves them unacceptably wide. Two physiological findings: all degradative pathways of rT3 generate iodide (the labelled dose was completely recovered as 125I in plasma), and most rT3 (65–90%) is degraded in peripheral tissues rapidly exchanging with plasma. Production rate and body mass could still only be bounded — 1.12–2.15 µg/h and 2.88–8.24 µg respectively — narrower than the disappearance-only bounds (1.12–5.07 µg/h; 2.88–23.7 µg) but bounds, not point values, and presented as such.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record, printed on the face. The production figure is a bounded range conditional on the tracer tracing all peripherally produced rT3 — the record's own caveat.
cards.source: Pilo A, Iervasi G, Vitek F, Turchi S, et al.. Disposal and distribution of rT3 in humans: a new double-tracer kinetic study. The American journal of physiology. 1993. PMID: 8447391. cards.headline: Synthesis: the thyroid is mainly a T4 gland — peripheral conversion supplies most T3 (~80% by compartmental analysis; 41% by the classic count), and the T4-to-rT3 limb runs at roughly 27–52 µg/day
cards.summary: Synthesis: the thyroid is mainly a T4 gland — peripheral conversion supplies most T3 (~80% by compartmental analysis; 41% by the classic count), and the T4-to-rT3 limb runs at roughly 27–52 µg/day
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human tracer studies above (Braverman 1970; Pittman 1971; Pilo 1990; Pilo 1993), framed by the Guyton & Hall / Ganong account of thyroid-hormone metabolism as textbook framing, not as an evidence card.
cards.result: Existence first: people with no thyroid at all, given only T4, circulate T3 made from that T4 — conversion is not a hypothesis. Quantity second, with the method-dependence kept visible: the 1971 disappearance-curve calculation assigned 41% of daily T3 production (22 µg/day) to conversion, while the 1990 compartmental analysis with T3 appearance data assigns ~80% (12.7 of 16.0 µg/day/m², against 3.3 secreted directly). The modern figure is the better measurement for the reason the record itself gives — disappearance-only analysis misplaces conversion into slow pools. The inactive limb: rT3 production bounded at 1.12–2.15 µg/h (≈27–52 µg/day by simple multiplication), disposed of in fast-exchange tissues with complete recovery as iodide. The daily T4 production rate is carried as the textbook's account (Guyton & Hall / Ganong, on the order of 80–100 µg/day) because the fetched records express conversion as fractions of production rather than verifying one production figure — labelled as textbook framing wherever it appears on this shelf. Radioisotope-era Ns are small and printed on every card.
cards.watchOut: Fractions of T3 production from conversion differ by method (41% vs ~80%) — quoting either without its method misstates the record. No animal deiodination data are carded.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 4986007, 5578229, 2333963, 8447391), with textbook framing as cited. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Orbital radiotherapy in Graves' orbitopathy: SPLIT — one sham-controlled trial positive on motility only (60% vs 31%), the other negative on all outcomes; equal to prednisone, better tolerated
shelves.question: In adults with active Graves' orbitopathy (thyroid eye disease), does orbital (retrobulbar) radiotherapy, compared with sham irradiation or oral prednisone, improve eye outcomes (motility, diplopia, soft-tissue signs)?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Body Weight · Double-Blind Method · Eye Diseases · Female · Graves Disease · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prednisone
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the sham-controlled trials disagreed with each other, and that disagreement is the balance. Mourits (2000) found radiotherapy successful in 18 of 30 (60%) versus 9 of 29 (31%) on sham (relative risk 1.9; absolute difference 29 percentage points), driven by diplopia/motility only, with no effect on proptosis or eyelid swelling. Gorman (42 patients, internally controlled) found no clinically or statistically significant difference on any main outcome at 6 months. Against oral prednisone, radiotherapy was equally successful (13 of 28 versus 14 of 28; Prummel 1993) and better tolerated. Harms lead the other side: retinopathy risk, especially with diabetes, and a theoretical secondary-malignancy risk. The trial base is old (1993–2001) and small.

cards.headline: RCT of prednisone versus radiotherapy (Prummel 1993): successful outcome in 14 of 28 prednisone patients and 13 of 28 irradiated patients with moderately severe Graves' ophthalmopathy — equally effective, radiotherapy better tolerated
cards.summary: RCT of prednisone versus radiotherapy (Prummel 1993): successful outcome in 14 of 28 prednisone patients and 13 of 28 irradiated patients with moderately severe Graves' ophthalmopathy — equally effective, radiotherapy better tolerated
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial, oral prednisone + sham irradiation vs retrobulbar radiotherapy (20 Gy) + placebo capsules
cards.people: 56 patients with moderately severe Graves' ophthalmopathy randomised double-blind: 28 to a 3-month course of oral prednisone plus sham irradiation, and 28 to retrobulbar irradiation (20 Gy) plus placebo capsules; outcome was assessed 24 weeks after starting treatment by change in the highest NOSPECS class.
cards.result: A successful outcome was observed in 14 prednisone-treated and 13 irradiated patients. Responders in both groups improved in total and subjective eye scores and eye-muscle volume; the response was due largely to soft-tissue involvement and eye-muscle motility. In radiotherapy responders, mean elevation rose from 18.5 degrees (95% CI 14.8 to 22.2) at baseline to 21.8 degrees (18.6 to 25.0) at week 24 (P=0.003), but did not change in prednisone responders. Side effects were more frequent and severe during prednisone than during radiotherapy, and the authors judged radiotherapy the treatment of first choice on tolerability.
cards.watchOut: An active-comparator trial with no untreated/sham-only arm: 'equally effective' cannot distinguish both treatments working from the disease's natural course improving both groups — that is what the sham-controlled trials (next cards) were for, and they disagreed with each other.
cards.source: Prummel MF et al. Randomized double-blind trial of prednisone versus radiotherapy in Graves' ophthalmopathy. Lancet (London, England). 1993. PMID: 8105213. cards.headline: Sham-controlled RCT (Mourits 2000): radiotherapy was successful in 18 of 30 (60%) versus 9 of 29 (31%) on sham irradiation at 24 weeks (relative risk 1.9) — driven by diplopia/motility, not proptosis or eyelid swelling
cards.summary: Sham-controlled RCT (Mourits 2000): radiotherapy was successful in 18 of 30 (60%) versus 9 of 29 (31%) on sham irradiation at 24 weeks (relative risk 1.9) — driven by diplopia/motility, not proptosis or eyelid swelling
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-(sham-irradiation-)controlled trial, orbital radiotherapy 20 Gy vs sham
cards.people: 60 patients with moderately severe Graves' orbitopathy randomised double-blind: 30 to radiotherapy (20 Gy in ten fractions) and 30 to sham irradiation (ten fractions of 0 Gy); outcomes at 24 weeks included qualitative major/minor criteria and quantitative measures (eyelid aperture, proptosis, eye movements, subjective eye score, clinical activity score).
cards.result: Qualitative treatment success at week 24 was 18 of 30 (60%) irradiated versus 9 of 29 (31%) sham-irradiated patients (relative risk 1.9, 95% CI 1.0 to 3.6; P=0.04) — an absolute difference of 29 percentage points. The difference was caused by improvements in diplopia grade, not by reduction of proptosis or eyelid swelling; quantitatively, elevation improved significantly with radiotherapy and all other variables were unchanged. The field of binocular single vision enlarged in 11 of 17 irradiated versus 2 of 15 sham patients, yet only 25% of irradiated patients were spared additional strabismus surgery. The authors concluded radiotherapy should be used only to treat motility impairment.
cards.watchOut: A positive result on a composite qualitative outcome driven by one component (diplopia/motility): proptosis and soft-tissue signs did not improve, and three-quarters of irradiated patients still needed strabismus surgery. The other sham-controlled trial (next card) found no benefit at all — that disagreement is this shelf's balance.
cards.source: Mourits MP et al. Radiotherapy for Graves' orbitopathy: randomised placebo-controlled study. Lancet (London, England). 2000. PMID: 10801172. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sham-controlled RCT (Gorman 2001 trial, carded from its Ophthalmology 2020 Seminal Article record, PMID 32200817): no clinically or statistically significant difference between the irradiated and sham-treated orbit in any main outcome at 6 months in 42 patients
cards.summary: Sham-controlled RCT (Gorman 2001 trial, carded from its Ophthalmology 2020 Seminal Article record, PMID 32200817): no clinically or statistically significant difference between the irradiated and sham-treated orbit in any main outcome at 6 months in 42 patients
cards.type: Prospective randomised double-blind placebo-(sham-)controlled internally-controlled trial (one orbit irradiated, the other sham; crossover at 6 months) — the Gorman trial, carded from the Ophthalmology 2020 record (PMID 32200817)
cards.people: 42 of 53 consecutive eligible patients enrolled (ethnically diverse men and women over 30, moderate symptomatic Graves' ophthalmopathy, mean clinical activity score 6.2; no optic neuropathy, diabetes, recent steroid treatment, previous decompression or muscle surgery). One randomly selected orbit received 20 Gy external beam therapy and the other sham therapy; at 6 months the therapies were reversed, with measurements every 3 months for 1 year (extraocular muscle and fat volume, proptosis, range of motion, diplopia fields, lid fissure width).
cards.result: No clinically or statistically significant difference between the treated and untreated orbit was observed in any main outcome measure at 6 months. At 12 months, muscle volume and proptosis improved slightly more in the orbit treated first; the authors concluded they were unable to demonstrate any beneficial therapeutic effect in this group — representative of those for whom radiotherapy is frequently recommended — and that the slight 12-month improvement in both orbits may reflect natural remission or radiotherapy and is of marginal clinical significance.
cards.watchOut: Bibliographic confirmation, as the commissioning row directed: the record fetched from PubMed this session for PMID 32200817 is Gorman CA et al., Ophthalmology 2020, titled as in the source line — the journal's Seminal Article record of the Gorman et al. trial — and it is that record which is carded here. The internally-controlled (orbit-versus-orbit) design is elegant but small (42 patients), and patients with diabetes were excluded, so it cannot inform the retinopathy-risk question in diabetes.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the two sham-controlled trials disagreed — Mourits found a motility/diplopia benefit, Gorman found no benefit on any main outcome — and the prednisone comparison showed equal success rates with better tolerability for radiotherapy
cards.summary: Synthesis: the two sham-controlled trials disagreed — Mourits found a motility/diplopia benefit, Gorman found no benefit on any main outcome — and the prednisone comparison showed equal success rates with better tolerability for radiotherapy
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The randomised base is three old trials (1993–2001). Against an active comparator, radiotherapy matched oral prednisone (successful outcome 13 of 28 versus 14 of 28) with fewer and less severe side effects (Prummel). Against sham irradiation the trials split: Mourits found success in 60% versus 31% (relative risk 1.9, absolute difference 29 percentage points), driven by diplopia/motility with no effect on proptosis or eyelid swelling; Gorman (internally controlled, 42 patients) found no difference on any main outcome at 6 months. That disagreement — not a pooled gloss — is the honest balance. On harms, radiotherapy carries a retinopathy risk (especially with diabetes, a group Gorman excluded) and a theoretical secondary-malignancy risk, which lead the harm side alongside prednisone's well-known systemic effects in the comparator trial. No card on this shelf uses the retracted mycophenolate record (PMID 27484048), which belongs to a different question and is fenced library-wide.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Normal thyroid volume by ultrasound: German equations give upper limits of 38.7 mL (men) and 28.6 mL (women) vs conventional 25 / 18 mL — Spanish median 7.31 mL, Cuban mean 6.6 mL
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what is the normal thyroid volume on ultrasound — median, mean and upper reference limits by sex — how much do age, body size (weight, height, body surface area) and population iodine status move it, and how far do individualised reference equations move the enlargement threshold away from the conventional fixed limits (25 mL in men, 18 mL in women)?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Male · Reference Values · Cross-Sectional Studies · Thyroid Gland/pathology,diagnostic imaging,anatomy & histology · Middle Aged · Adult · Germany/epidemiology · Aged · Organ Size · Young Adult · Body Weight · Body Height · Goiter/epidemiology,diagnosis · Adolescent · Aged, 80 and over · Health Surveys · Cohort Studies · Age Factors · Iodine/urine · Sex Factors · Spain · Thyroid Gland/diagnostic imaging · Ultrasonography · Asian People · Esophagus/anatomy & histology,diagnostic imaging · Functional Laterality/physiology · Thyroid Gland/anatomy & histology,diagnostic imaging · Thyroid Nodule/diagnostic imaging,pathology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, on three independent population datasets (plus one supporting lobe-asymmetry report, not counted). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, thyroid sections — brief framing only; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. The German SHIP/KORA equations (8,606 thyroid-healthy reference individuals) put the individualised upper limit at 38.7 mL (men) and 28.6 mL (women) — the conventional fixed limits (25 / 18 mL) would label 34% of that population enlarged, vs 7% by the equations, and both sets of limits print on the face. Central values in non-iodine-deficient populations are far lower (Spanish median 7.31 mL; Cuban mean 6.6 mL), men exceed women in every dataset, and body size (weight, height, body surface area) moves volume in every dataset that tested it. Iodine status is a population property, not a caveat: the German limits come from a previously iodine-deficient region and are never presented as universal, and datasets are carded per population, never merged.

cards.headline: German population equations (Ittermann 2025): individualised 95th-percentile thyroid-volume limits are 38.7 mL (men) and 28.6 mL (women) — far above the conventional 25 / 18 mL cut-offs, which would label 34% enlarged vs 7% by the equations
cards.summary: German population equations (Ittermann 2025): individualised 95th-percentile thyroid-volume limits are 38.7 mL (men) and 28.6 mL (women) — far above the conventional 25 / 18 mL cut-offs, which would label 34% enlarged vs 7% by the equations
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population reference equations, three German cohorts pooled in one report — counted as one dataset)
cards.people: 11,549 individuals (51% women) from three independent German population cohorts — SHIP-START, SHIP-TREND (northern Germany) and KORA-F4 (southern Germany); 8,606 individuals (45% women) formed the thyroid-healthy reference population for the equations. Germany is a previously iodine-deficient region.
cards.result: Sex-stratified quantile-regression equations for the 95th percentile of thyroid volume used age, body weight and height. The overall reference value was 38.7 mL for men and 28.6 mL for women. By the established fixed cut-offs (25 mL men, 18 mL women), 34% of the overall population would have had goitre, compared with 7% when the individualised equations were used. The authors conclude the fixed upper limits are too low for an adult, previously iodine-deficient population and do not consider age, body weight or height.
cards.watchOut: Population-bound by construction: these are limits for a previously iodine-deficient German population, derived from three cohorts pooled in a single paper (counted as one dataset, its composition stated) — never print 38.7 / 28.6 mL as universal limits.
cards.source: Ittermann T et al. Thyroid volume-new reference values for defining thyroid enlargement. European journal of endocrinology. 2025. PMID: 40424555. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Non-iodine-deficient Spanish population (Maravall 2004): median thyroid volume 7.31 mL overall — 9.19 mL in men vs 6.19 mL in women
cards.summary: Non-iodine-deficient Spanish population (Maravall 2004): median thyroid volume 7.31 mL overall — 9.19 mL in men vs 6.19 mL in women
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population reference values, ultrasound)
cards.people: 268 representative healthy adults (after exclusions from 880 randomly selected residents of L'Hospitalet de Llobregat, Spain, a non-iodine-deficient population; mean urinary iodine excretion 154.23 µg/L); thyroid volume by ultrasonography, with age-decade tables by sex published.
cards.result: Reference thyroid volume was median 7.31 mL, mean 8.22 mL (95% CI 7.75 to 8.69). In men: median 9.19 mL, mean 9.87 mL; in women: median 6.19 mL, mean 6.57 mL (P < 0.0001 for the sex difference). Thyroid volume differed across age decades in men (younger men had lower volumes, P = 0.0034) but not in women. These central values sit far below the German upper reference limits — a population and iodine-status difference, not a contradiction to be averaged away.
cards.watchOut: A second report from this same 268-subject L'Hospitalet cohort exists (PMID 11106925) and is counted as the SAME dataset, not a fourth population. Spanish central values and German upper limits answer different questions in different populations and are never merged.
cards.source: Maravall FJ et al. Reference values of thyroid volume in a healthy, non-iodine-deficient Spanish population. Hormone and metabolic research = Hormon- und Stoffwechselforschung = Hormones et metabolisme. 2004. PMID: 15486817. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Healthy Cuban adults (Turcios 2015): mean thyroid volume 6.6 mL (men 7.3 vs women 6.4 mL), with body surface area the only significant anthropometric determinant on multivariate analysis
cards.summary: Healthy Cuban adults (Turcios 2015): mean thyroid volume 6.6 mL (men 7.3 vs women 6.4 mL), with body surface area the only significant anthropometric determinant on multivariate analysis
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population reference values, ultrasound)
cards.people: 100 healthy adults (21 men, 79 women) aged 18–50 years living in a non-iodine-deficient area of Havana, Cuba; thyroid volume by ultrasound, correlated with anthropometric measures.
cards.result: Average thyroid volume was 6.6 ± 0.26 mL; it was higher in men (7.3 mL) than in women (6.4 mL; P = 0.15). In univariate analysis volume correlated with all anthropometric measures, but in multivariate analysis body surface area was the only significant anthropometric parameter. Volume was also higher in current or former smokers and in persons with blood group AB or B. The authors propose reference values as a function of body surface area.
cards.watchOut: The smallest of the three datasets (N = 100, only 21 men) and restricted to ages 18–50: its sex difference did not reach significance, and its values describe a non-iodine-deficient Caribbean population — carded per population, never pooled with the European datasets.
cards.source: Turcios S et al. Thyroid volume and its relation to anthropometric measures in a healthy cuban population. European thyroid journal. 2015. PMID: 25960963. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Supporting report — lobe asymmetry only (Ying 2009): in 62 healthy Chinese adults with normal glands, the right thyroid lobe (6.8 mL) was significantly larger than the left (5.66 mL) on three-dimensional ultrasound
cards.summary: Supporting report — lobe asymmetry only (Ying 2009): in 62 healthy Chinese adults with normal glands, the right thyroid lobe (6.8 mL) was significantly larger than the left (5.66 mL) on three-dimensional ultrasound
cards.type: Supporting primary human physiology study (lobe asymmetry, three-dimensional ultrasound) — not counted in the three datasets
cards.people: 105 healthy Chinese subjects were scanned; 43 with thyroid nodules were excluded, leaving 62 subjects with normal thyroid glands assessed by three-dimensional ultrasound after exclusion of nodules. This report is NOT counted among the three population datasets.
cards.result: For normal thyroids, the right lobe (6.8 mL) was significantly larger than the left lobe (5.66 mL) (P < 0.05). Right-handed subjects had a significantly larger right lobe (mean 7.11 mL) than left-handed subjects (mean 5.82 mL), and subjects with an oesophagus deviated to the left had a larger right lobe (mean 7.15 mL) than those with a centrally located oesophagus (mean 5.7 mL); left-lobe volume did not differ by handedness or oesophageal position.
cards.watchOut: A lobe-asymmetry card only: total gland volume norms come from the three population datasets above, and a single-lobe measurement should never be doubled and read as total volume without this asymmetry in mind.
cards.source: Ying M et al. Asymmetry of thyroid lobe volume in normal Chinese subjects: association with handedness and position of esophagus. Anatomical record (Hoboken, N.J. : 2007). 2009. PMID: 19051270. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: normal thyroid volume is sex- and body-size-dependent and population-bound — German equation limits 38.7 / 28.6 mL vs Spanish median 7.31 mL and Cuban mean 6.6 mL central values; the conventional fixed 25 / 18 mL limits mislabel a third of the German population as enlarged
cards.summary: Synthesis: normal thyroid volume is sex- and body-size-dependent and population-bound — German equation limits 38.7 / 28.6 mL vs Spanish median 7.31 mL and Cuban mean 6.6 mL central values; the conventional fixed 25 / 18 mL limits mislabel a third of the German population as enlarged
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, thyroid sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. Three independent populations are carded: the German cohorts (11,549 individuals; 8,606 thyroid-healthy; 95th-percentile equations on age, weight and height giving overall limits of 38.7 mL in men and 28.6 mL in women, with 34% labelled enlarged by the conventional cut-offs vs 7% by the equations), the Spanish population (268 adults; median 7.31 mL, men 9.19 vs women 6.19 mL) and the Cuban population (100 adults; mean 6.6 mL, body surface area the sole multivariate determinant). A supporting Chinese report (62 normal glands) adds lobe asymmetry only (right 6.8 vs left 5.66 mL) and is not counted as a dataset. Iodine status is a population property: the German limits come from a previously iodine-deficient region and must never be printed as universal, and no card merges populations or methods eras. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: the direction of the physiology (larger in men, rising with body size) is consistent across all three populations, while every numeric limit stays population-specific, as printed on each card.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards: each limit carries its population, iodine context and method with it; an unbanded universal 'normal thyroid volume' is exactly the error these datasets document.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
